name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippians will soon be able to participate in a school-choice tax credit program. Here’s what to know
description: Proponents of school choice policies say a new federal tax credit program is a win for the state. Opponents say it undermines Mississippi voters' rejection of school choice.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Starting next year, Mississippi families can get a break on their taxes for donating to scholarships that will largely benefit private schools, experts say. 
The federal program, created by President Donald Trump’s 2025 “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” will give people a break on their taxes for contributing to scholarships that can pay for education expenses at private schools, charter schools or public schools. Experts expect most of the money will flow toward private schools and families who could already afford, or were on the cusp of being able to afford, a private school education. 
Proponents of school-choice policies — which are aimed at giving families more educational options, often funding those choices with public money — say it’s a win for the state. 
But school-choice opponents argue the policies siphon money away from the public education system, which must serve every child, and force Mississippi into a program its residents have already said they don’t want. 
Republican state lawmakers, led by House Speaker Jason White, made a full-court push to expand school-choice policies in Mississippi earlier this year. However, House Bill 2, his lengthy school-choice bill, passed by a thin margin in the House and was killed by the Senate. 
Before that, in January, Gov. Tate Reeves announced that Mississippi would be participating in the federal tax credit scholarship program starting in 2027. States must opt in to that program. 
House Speaker Jason White, R-West, addresses state representatives as the House prepares to debate House Bill 2 on Thursday, Jan. 15, 2026, at the Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Douglas Carswell described it as an “awesome” program that allows the state to correct the Senate’s failure to expand school-choice options. He heads up the Mississippi Center for Public Policy, a conservative think tank that backs the expansion of school-choice policies.
Nancy Loome, a public school advocate and founder of The Parents’ Campaign, disagrees with Reeves’ decision. 
“Voters made it clear when House Bill 2 was debated in the 2026 legislative session that they don’t want this,” she said.
How does the federal tax credit program work?
The federal program allows taxpayers to contribute up to $1,700 each, or $3,400 for a married couple filing jointly, to an organization that awards school scholarships.
The governor designates scholarship-granting organizations, or SGOs, to award money to a school to cover costs of a child’s education. Taxpayers can’t direct their money to a particular student or school, but SGOs can focus on a particular group of students, like students who attend religious private schools. 
Reeves has not yet finalized his list of SGOs for Mississippi, according to the Mississippi Center for Public Policy, which is tracking and publishing the state’s eligible SGOs. The governor’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment. 
Donors will get a dollar-for-dollar tax credit, a break on their taxes equal to the amount they contribute, which is about three times as much as people receive from donating to a children’s hospital or other causes. 
Families who earn up to 300% of the area’s median income qualify to participate in the scholarship program. That’s six figures in Mississippi, or about $150,000. 
The House of Representatives debate House Bill 2 on Thursday, Jan. 15, 2026, at the State Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Paige Shoemaker DeMio, a senior policy analyst at Center for American Progress, a progressive policy and research institute, said the people who will benefit those most from the tax credit program are wealthy and owe $1,700 or more in taxes. Research about existing state tax credit scholarship programs back that up. 
“Statistically, people who are higher income owe that much in taxes,” she said.
There’s no set amount for the scholarships. The scholarship-granting organization sets the amount. 
And across the country, school-choice scholarships and vouchers provide anywhere between $4,000 to $9,000. Nationally, private school tuition averages about $13,000. That means while federal scholarships may make it easier for families on the cusp of being able to afford private schools, that education still may be unaffordable to the neediest families.
Will federal tax credit scholarships help students from low-income families?
There’s no requirement to prioritize the scholarships for low-income students. A majority of private school vouchers across the country go to students who could already afford and were attending private schools, according to research.
Carswell recognized the reality that the scholarships may miss low-income students. 
“We need to ensure that we have SGOs that provide access to private education for low-income families, too,” he said. “That’s why we need a broad range of SGOs that offer smaller schools, and not just established ones, access to the new source of funding.”
However, the governor has little power to tailor the program to the state’s students, Shoemaker DeMio said.
The federal regulations require Reeves to approve any SGOs that meet the minimum requirements. He can’t impose additional reporting or standards.
The lack of transparency and reporting requirements is a “huge lost opportunity,” said Mike Petrilli of the Fordham Institute, a national conservative-leaning education policy think tank.
“It’s very much a light touch,” he said. “We may never know if this is making a difference for kids.”
How will tax credit scholarships for private schools affect public ones?
There’s been some movement nationally to use the program to divert money to public schools, including public charter schools, Shoemaker DeMio said, but it’s tricky to understand how that would play out. Public schools do not charge students to attend. 
And the federal guidance regulating that part of the program hasn’t been made public yet, she said. It’s also unclear how much it will cost states to administer the program, which could include monitoring fraud, reviewing audits and other duties. 
The U.S. Department of Treasury estimates the tax-credit scholarship program, which begins all over the country in 2027, will cost taxpayers $26 billion in its first three years. That would make it the federal government’s largest education expense — more than Title I, which ensures that economically disadvantaged children receive a high-quality education, and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, which guarantees children with disabilities receive an equitable education.
Members of the House of Representatives vote on House Bill 2, a school-choice proposal, on Thursday, Jan. 15, 2026, at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“We’d be spending as a country more on private schools than any other (public education) program,” Shoemaker DeMio said. That could mean spending less on public education in the future, which could be especially detrimental to a state like Mississippi that heavily relies on federal funding. 
But most concerning to DeMio is that Mississippi voters have already rejected school-choice programs through legislative action. 
“Any time school choice has been on a ballot, it has failed,” she said. “This is clearly not a popular program, but people have now found a way to get around the voters and ignore what Americans want. It’s incredibly frustrating.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: These purple WA districts are trending blue. What changed?
description: This is the story of how Democrats came to win over (most of) Washington’s suburbs. Over the past decade, Democrats have amassed power in Olympia through areas further and further from their urban bases.  These are places like east King County suburbs where Republican Dino Rossi’s tenure as a state senator nearly carried him to […]
text:
The Tacoma Narrows Bridge, as seen from the east side, leads into the 26th Legislative District, where Democrats have gained momentum in recent years. (Photo by Aspen Ford/Washington State Standard)This is the story of how Democrats came to win over (most of) Washington’s suburbs.
Over the past decade, Democrats have amassed power in Olympia through areas further and further from their urban bases. 
These are places like east King County suburbs where Republican Dino Rossi’s tenure as a state senator nearly carried him to the governor’s office; northern Whatcom County, not long ago a redder shade of purple; part of the Kitsap Peninsula that has been a rare split district but may soon be represented by three Democrats; and Island County, where Democrats are gaining strength.
The shifts allow Democrats to continue expanding and strengthening a foundation for a supermajority in the Legislature, which could lead to transformational changes to state law. 
However, these new Democratic lawmakers also tend to be among the most moderate in their party, willing to buck the progressive wing of their caucuses on some of their biggest policy priorities, like this year’s income tax on high earners.
Two main factors have driven the trend. One is Donald Trump. As moderate Republicans and independent voters have soured on the president’s brash rhetoric, Democrats have provided refuge. Other Republican candidates have followed the president’s lead to some extent.
“The nonstop degrading of our neighbor, I think, is really irritating people,” said Ray Shjerven, chair of the 26th Legislative District Democrats. 
Alex Hays, a Republican campaign consultant, put it differently: “Democrats have convinced voters not to pay attention to their job performance and to instead focus on Donald Trump’s performance.”
The second reason is the suburban districts have been the recipients of new Democrat-leaning voters, driven further from urban cores by the high cost of living and the promise of hybrid or remote work. Think of Seattleites moving across the water to Port Orchard, or Tacoma residents going across the Narrows into more suburban communities for the 26th District. Urbanites have similarly been seeking refuge on Whidbey Island in the 10th District. Bellingham residents are heading north and east into the 42nd. 
“COVID really drove the crazies out of the city, and they’re bringing crazy with them where they go,”  said Tim Hazelo, a Republican candidate for state House in the 10th District.
This has helped Democrats overcome the fact that fewer voters than ever are persuadable amid intense polarization.
Republicans have also struggled to recruit strong candidates, sometimes turning to hopefuls who align more with the national party but may not be as electable in suburbia, according to Democrats and some Republicans.
“The type of person that Trump motivates to be more involved is also just not the person that is as close a fit to swing voters as a lot of people would like,” said Hays, the Republican consultant.
Dean Nielsen, a veteran Democratic consultant, said Trump “essentially traded the suburbs for a greater share of rural America.” The problem for Republicans is that rural Washington is a small piece of the state, and Latino voters are keeping some of those areas at least somewhat competitive, he added.
If Nielsen were a Republican strategist, he’d try to find business-oriented candidates who were vocally supportive of abortion and LGTBQ+ rights.
State Rep. Jim Walsh, who chairs the state Republican Party, disagrees with the premise that his allies are sputtering in these areas. He believes these are still swing districts, and politicos will be able to properly assess voting patterns in 2028. The Senate race in the 42nd and a House race in the 26th are the two most expensive campaigns for state Legislature this year.
“Trump Derangement Syndrome is intense but it has a short halflife,” Walsh wrote in a text message. “Normal people are tired of the lies and bad-faith rhetoric coming out of Olympia.”
Eastside swing
All of these examples were preceded by the 5th Legislative District in east King County. Fifteen years ago, Republicans ruled this combination of rural exurbs and affluent suburbs. Now, it’s not all that competitive as Democrats have swept all three seats, along with flipping the congressional seat that represents the area in 2018. 
Republican Dino Rossi served alongside two Republican state representatives, and even served in the Senate when Republicans had a majority. He helped write the state budget. Minority Republicans are now largely shut out of those negotiations. Rossi also came oh-so-close to the governor’s mansion.
But after rounds of redistricting, a presidential term and a half for Donald Trump and housing growth in these areas, the 5th is reliably blue. Democrats have been sailing to reelection. Rep. Zach Hall, who was appointed to the role, faces a strong challenger in longtime police leader Michelle Bennett, but she has little chance to beat him this year due to the district’s tilt.
The 5th might qualify as the first shoe to drop for Republican power in these areas, as Democratic reign has now spread far and wide.
Island breeze
The year 2022 portended a good future for Democrats in the 10th District. They’d already wrested one state House seat out of Republican hands four years earlier and took another in 2022. 
And they did so despite a damaged Democratic candidate. In the final days of the campaign, Clyde Shavers faced blockbuster allegations from his father that he’d inflated his military record. Shavers still won, unseating the Republican incumbent, but by only a couple hundred votes.
Winning in such headwinds indicated a turn toward Democrats in a district that covers Island County and parts of Skagit and Snohomish, local politicos say.  Republicans had held both House seats since the early 2000s.
Sen. Ron Muzzall, R-Oak Harbor, on the Senate floor on Wednesday, April 16, 2025. (Photo by Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero/Washington State Standard)
In two years, all eyes will be on the state Senate race, where Republican Sen. Ron Muzzall, faces a fight for another four-year term, if he runs again, given the Democratic momentum there. 
Muzzall’s 2024 run was the most expensive legislative race in the state that year, with over $1.5 million contributed to the campaigns and $2 million more spent on independent efforts to sway voters. Muzzall won by 2 percentage points, while his Democratic colleagues in the state House were reelected more comfortably. 
“We’ll do everything we can to make sure that we flip it,” said state Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad.
Northern expedition
To the north, Sharon Shewmake broke the ice, first by defeating a Republican incumbent to win a seat in the state House in 2018 and then four years later narrowly winning a race for state Senate after Doug Ericksen, the incumbent Republican, died. 
That solidified the Democrats’ flipping of all three legislative positions in the 42nd District, which covers the north side of Bellingham all the way to the Canadian border and the more rural east side of Whatcom County. The margins of victory for Democrats have only grown in recent years.
Republicans held the Senate seat in the 42nd for nearly 20 years before Shewmake’s victory in 2022.
The shift coincided with a buildout of housing on open land on the north side of Bellingham, said Jamie Douglass, chair of the district Democratic Party.

Shewmake isn’t running for reelection this year, but her chosen replacement, Michael Shepard, is poised to take her place after a strong primary for Democrats. Flipping the seat is among Republicans’ top priorities statewide.
The other side of the water
One year ago, 26th District Democratic state Sen. Deb Krishnadasan faced a tough race to retain her state Senate seat against longtime Republican state Rep. Michelle Valdez in an off-year election. 
Krishnadasan won by about 5 percentage points. This year, she won her primary over a lesser-known Republican by 12. 
Renee Hernandez Greenfield is now seeking to replace Valdez, who isn’t running for reelection, and deliver a Democratic triumvirate there, erasing one of the few remaining districts with split representation. Like the 42nd just a decade ago, all three seats in the 26th were held by Republicans.
State Sen. Deb Krishnadasan, D-Gig Harbor, outside the House chamber at the Washington state Capitol on Jan. 13, 2026, following Gov. Bob Ferguson’s State of the State address. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Standard)
Hernandez Greenfield faces Katy Cornell, a Republican pastor. Cornell may serve as a recent example of GOP troubles recruiting candidates. She recently found herself in hot water over resurfaced videos of sermons in which she equates abortion to murder and implies religions other than Christianity are akin to witchcraft.
The 26th covers parts of Kitsap and Pierce counties, including Port Orchard, Purdy, Gig Harbor and parts of Bremerton. Like the development in Whatcom County in recent years, the district has seen a big boost in housing since the newest Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in 2007. 
Looking forward
Despite their successes, Democrats in these areas aren’t getting too confident.
“When I moved here, they were all Republican,” said Douglass, chair of the 42nd Legislative District Democrats. “Now all three are Democrats, and I still think, though, that it takes an incredible amount of hard work and diligence for it to stay that way.”
Next week’s elections will indicate how far Democrats have come in these areas, and how close they’ll be to supermajority power in the Legislature. 
These same factors are at play in southwest Washington, where four Democratic challengers in the August primary led Republican state House incumbents handily in areas near Vancouver and Portland. A sweep for Democrats next week would leave just Sen. Paul Harris, of the 17th, as the lone Republican remaining across those two neighboring districts. Two years ago, the GOP held all six. 
In 2022, Harris won a state House reelection bid by nearly 10 percentage points. Two years later, when he ran for Senate, that was down to just over 2 percentage points.

This creep could continue to extend, with Democrats showing electoral strength in central Washington’s 12th District, which now crosses the Cascades into exurbs like North Bend and Monroe, and the 35th District in Mason County. Rising costs in Gig Harbor and Bremerton in the 26th could force people to move into the cheaper 35th.
But looking that far ahead is hard to predict in a world where Trump is no longer the Republican standard-bearer.
“Until Trump is retired, it is very difficult to model or describe or plan what the next steps for the Washington Republican Party is,” Hays said. “That’s like an event horizon.”

title: Commentary: Five questions about Missouri’s election. Some are easier to answer than others.
description:
A polling location in Jefferson City (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri voters keep rejecting some of the GOP’s biggest ideas. Then they keep electing Republicans to run the state.
Two years ago, voters protected abortion rights and approved paid sick leave. In August, they overwhelmingly rejected proposals to overhaul the tax system and make c[...]
text:
A polling location in Jefferson City (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri voters keep rejecting some of the GOP’s biggest ideas. Then they keep electing Republicans to run the state.
Two years ago, voters protected abortion rights and approved paid sick leave. In August, they overwhelmingly rejected proposals to overhaul the tax system and make constitutional amendments harder to pass.
Yet Republicans hold every statewide elected office, six of eight congressional seats and supermajorities in both legislative chambers.
On Tuesday, voters will revisit several of those disagreements. Here are five questions I’m watching.
 1. Didn’t we already settle the abortion question?

You’d think so.
In 2024, voters approved Amendment 3, enshrining abortion rights in the state constitution. Republican lawmakers responded by putting another amendment on the ballot.
So we’re doing this again?
Yes, but not quite the same way.
Amendment 3 would repeal those protections and restore a ban on most abortions, with limited exceptions. It would also constitutionally prohibit gender-affirming medical care for minors.
Wait, it’s also Amendment 3?
Yes. Missouri recycles amendment numbers. Political arguments, too.
This time around, a yes vote bans abortion and a no vote keeps it legal. 
What do the polls say?
An August SLU/YouGov poll found 43% in favor, 44% opposed and 13% undecided.
A small but vocal minority of anti-abortion activists oppose the amendment, arguing the proposed ban doesn’t go far enough. Meanwhile, Amendment 3’s supporters have mounted a more organized campaign than they did two years ago, particularly through churches working to mobilize voters.
The question is whether the coalition that protected abortion rights in 2024 will hold together in the face of that effort.
 2. Can Ann Wagner survive another Democratic wave?

Wagner has seen this movie before.
In 2018, Democrats gained dozens of U.S. House seats. Wagner survived, winning her suburban St. Louis district by about four points. She’s won every election since.
At some point, Democrats might wonder whether the district is actually competitive or just enjoys making them think it is.
So why is this year different?
An October Emerson College poll showed Democratic challenger Fred Wellman leading Wagner 51% to 46%. Other surveys have shown tighter margins.
Last week, Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved the district from leaning Republican to a toss-up. The result could offer a window into whether the suburban backlash against Republicans that defined 2018 is returning eight years later.
 3. Is Missouri’s redistricting fight finally over?

That depends on your definition of over.
After more than a year of Republican maneuvering and courtroom battles, the gerrymandered version of Missouri’s congressional map is finally on the ballot. The GOP-drawn map, designed to help Republicans win seven of eight U.S. House seats, won’t be used Tuesday.
But Proposition A will determine its fate in future elections.
Remind me how that works.
A yes vote approves the Republican-drawn map for future elections. A no vote rejects it.
So a no vote ends the whole thing?
Not necessarily.
Some Republicans have already floated trying again in 2027.
If voters reject Proposition A, another item on the ballot called Amendment 6 could — if it passes — make another gerrymander much, much harder. But more on that later.
 4. Will Democrats win control of the legislature?

No. No, they will not.
Democrats haven’t controlled either chamber of the Missouri legislature since 2002. And nobody is talking seriously about a Democratic takeover this year.
But they don’t need one to change how Jefferson City operates.
What does that mean?
A net gain of three House seats or two Senate seats would end the GOP’s two-thirds majority in the respective chamber.
That would mean Republicans could no longer override a governor’s veto or pass emergency clauses allowing new laws to take effect immediately without Democratic support.
And Republicans are taking the threat very seriously, spending heavily to defend districts that weren’t considered competitive just a few months ago.
Where should we look Tuesday?
The suburbs, obviously. But also rural Missouri.
Democrats haven’t won a predominantly rural House district since 2010. Whether they can expand beyond their traditional strongholds may tell us more about the party’s future than the final seat count alone.
 5. Will Missouri voters keep rejecting Republican priorities while electing Republicans?

Back where we started.
Missourians have voted for abortion rights, Medicaid expansion, a higher minimum wage and paid sick leave. Republican lawmakers have tried to reverse or limit nearly all of them.
Which brings us to Amendment 6?
Exactly.
Amendment 6 would require 80% support in both legislative chambers and another statewide vote to change laws or constitutional amendments approved by initiative, or enact laws similar to those rejected by referendum (see also: Proposition A).
But are Missouri voters turning against Republicans themselves?
Consider the auditor’s race, the only statewide office on the ballot.
Republican Scott Fitzpatrick won by nearly 22 points in 2022. He has substantially outraised Democratic challenger Quentin Wilson, and the contest has attracted relatively little attention.
Yet an August poll showed Fitzpatrick ahead by just two points, within the margin of error.
The result could be revealing even if Fitzpatrick wins. Does he approach his margin from four years ago, or is the race closer?
One result won’t establish a political realignment. But taken with the Wagner race, legislative contests and ballot measures, it could tell us whether rejecting Republican ideas is starting to translate into rejecting Republican candidates.
Or whether Missourians will keep saying no to Republican policies and yes to Republican politicians.

text:
The Fairview mansion, built around 1901 for William Jennings Bryan and his wife, Mary, is now up and off of its foundation and ready to be relocated Nov. 7, weather permitting. (Courtesy of Bryan Health)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s capital city is preparing for an unprecedented spectacle Saturday. 
One of Lincoln’s two prestigious National Historic Landmarks — the 125-year-old Fairview mansion built for political heavyweight William Jennings Bryan and his wife, Mary — will be relocated to a different corner of the hospital campus that grew around it.
At an earlier time, the William Jennings Bryan home shown here illustrates how a modern hospital grew up around the mansion built around 1901. (Courtesy of Bryan Health)
That’s 2.3 million pounds of brick house, moving at one mile per hour atop 34 specialized remote-controlled dollies, each with eight semi-truck-size tires. Crews will be laying out a temporary path of gravel, rock and steel plates between the mansion’s current and future sites.
It’s expected to take about 10 hours for the home to travel about a third of a mile from the south side of Bryan East Campus to its northeast corner at 52nd and A streets.
Bryan Health officials are inviting the public to watch from 7:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. and participate in related “fun zone” activities including food and information booths. They’ve put safety and traffic measures in place and said ongoing construction should not disrupt voting Tuesday at a campus polling place. 
‘Landlocked’ medical campus
For a few days at the start of this week, roughly 500 tons of rock is to be hauled daily into a lot on the medical center campus lot, with a truck arriving every 15 or so minutes. The material is to be used to create the makeshift road. 
Moving the Fairview risked its historic designation, but Bob Ravenscroft, Bryan Health’s vice president and chief development officer, said hospital leadership saw it as the best option to satisfy community health needs and growth demands of a “landlocked” medical campus.
Fairview mansion was lifted off the ground in recent days using a unified hydraulic jacking system to prepare for relocation across Bryan East Campus Nov. 7. (Courtesy of Bryan Health)
Another alternative was demolition, an option Ravenscroft said neither the hospital nor community members wanted. He said expanding or relocating hospital components elsewhere on campus was cost-prohibitive.
It was important, he said, to preserve the storied structure — which over the decades has served also as student dorms, daycare, a museum — and put it back into use. 
The move will enable expansion of Bryan East’s emergency department — which is adjacent to the mansion — and the neonatal intensive care unit. Emergency patients more than doubled in the last decade, Ravenscroft said. And, he said, the NICU is “routinely full, dang near overflowing.”
“We have over 50 counties in the state that no longer have obstetric services,” Ravenscroft said. “It’s compromising  prenatal care. … We need to expand the capacity to treat these tiniest babies.”
‘Parade of political personalities’
Ravenscroft lauded the “tremendous donation” from William and Mary Baird Bryan a century ago that started the hospital.
William Jennings Bryan is shown here in the basement of the Fairview. (Courtesy of R.B. Hindmarsh via Bryan Health)
The story goes back to 1901, when, according to an account in the Nebraska State Historical Society archives, the Bryans broke ground on their Lincoln home that would be known as Fairview. Proceeds from the internationally known lawyer and U.S. congressman’s publications helped build the mansion Bryan envisioned as a new Monticello. He accepted the 1908 presidential nomination on its front steps.
“Woodrow Wilson visited here during the 1912 campaign and a steady parade of political personalities came to consult with ‘The Great Commoner,’” the Explore Nebraska History team wrote in a passage about Fairview. Bryan, a three-time Democratic presidential nominee, served as secretary of state under President Wilson through 1915. 
His wife’s health led the family to move in 1921 from Nebraska to Florida, and the following year they deeded Fairview and a portion of surrounding land to the local Methodist Conference for construction of a hospital. Four years later, Bryan Memorial Hospital opened its doors, named in Bryan’s honor after his death in 1925.
In 1926, the Bryan Memorial Hospital dedication at the home built for William Jennings Bryan and his wife, Mary. (Courtesy of Bryan Health)
Bryan is one of 28 members of the Nebraska Hall of Fame.
The mansion became a student dormitory for the Bryan School of Nursing and for four decades was home to hundreds of future medical professionals, a hospital statement said. 
In 1963, the National Park Service named Fairview a National Historic Landmark for its exceptional significance in American history and culture. Nebraska has 23 such designations; the only other Lincoln one is the State Capitol.
While a recognition of notoriety, the federal landmark designation doesn’t automatically offer protection from demolition or relocation.
“Being reverent of the original gift remains important to us,” said Ravenscroft. 
Confident of designation
He said Bryan officials have consulted and worked with the city of Lincoln and the city’s Historic Preservation Commission on the relocation project, and are confident the federal designation will be retained. The Lincoln Lancaster Planning Commission voted in April to support the mansion move.
Shown here is where the Fairview mansion is to settle. (Courtesy of Bryan Health)
Guidance from experts, including a preservation architectural firm, led to “meticulous” removal, digital cataloging and storage of basement woodwork and other materials, he said. The plan is to rebuild the mansion basement at the new site. That area reportedly served as a family living area and also was where Bryan wrote his speeches, books and newspaper editorials for “The Commoner.” 
“We feel really really really good about this (effort to retain the federal designation) because of the due diligence we’ve done and the feedback,” Ravenscroft said, though he added that a reevaluation process is required after the home is relocated and put back into use.
The relocated structure will not be occupied for a few years, Ravenscroft said. 
It is to be the centerpiece of an expanded Bryan College of Health Sciences and used for administrative offices, a welcome center and student services. Fundraising is ongoing for that initiative, he said.
Yellow line shows route the Fairview mansion will take from the south side of Bryan East Campus to the northeast corner. (Courtesy of Bryan Health)
Several days ago, in preparation for the Nov. 7 move, the Fairview was lifted off the ground using a unified hydraulic jacking system. Steel beams were inserted through foundation openings to form a supportive framework beneath the surface. The foundation then was filled with rock.
Some street closures, as early as Tuesday night, will be required to accommodate the move, said Jeff Bliemeister, Bryan director of safety and security. Volunteers will be on hand the day of the event to direct the public to the activity hub and to areas with “up-close views” of the mansion as it is relocated. 
Bliemeister and Ravenscroft offered an update of the project and road closures during a virtual news conference Friday.
A rendering depicts the future site of the William Jennings Bryan home, scheduled to be moved on Nov. 7. (Courtesy of Bryan Health)
An online auction is currently active — featuring furnishings from when the home was recreated in the 1990s, Ravenscroft said. About 300 objects are for sale, among them an R.J. Horner style buffet, a Victorian-style carved oak table and chairs, a vintage LaBarge Louis XVI style mirror, rugs and wall hangings.
The public will be able to view auction items in person the day of the move. Proceeds are to go toward refurbishing the mansion. 
Pet cemetery?
A popular conversation surrounding the project has centered on what will happen to a pet burial ground on the Fairview property, Ravenscroft said. He said a dog and a horse were buried on the premises.
A pet tombstone, at center, was still on the site this summer as construction was ongoing. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
“Here’s our pickle: The gravestones have not been in the same spot all of these years, so we’re as curious as anybody to see … what we’ll find.”
He said that since the remains are not human, there were no legal implications.
David Kracman of Lincoln is among those monitoring and questioning the fate of the mansion as well as the pet graves. He told Ravenscroft in an email that while he was saddened by the house relocation, he was sympathetic to growth and modernization needs of the hospital.
Kracman referenced a 1924 newspaper clip about a pair of dogs, Tiny and Major, that were considered members of the Bryan family and buried on the property. He suggested moving their remains and grave marker to the same spot relative to the house at the new location.
At an earlier time, the William Jennings Bryan statue shown with Fairview in the background. (Courtesy of Bryan Health)
“Given the importance of these two dogs to the Bryans, I think some extra effort is required to show proper respect to the family,” Kracman wrote. 
Ravenscroft said two pet tombstones have been moved to a safe location and that any excavation won’t occur until later construction phases. He said pet remains won’t be relocated and hospital officials will decide later what to do with the headstones.
The lifesize statue of Bryan that was on Fairview property has been removed and preserved. 
In the case of bad weather or unforeseen circumstances, hospital officials said the relocation of the mansion will push back a week. Work will continue in the days after the move to position Fairview into its new spot with a new view.
“Fingers are crossed for good weather,”Ravenscroft said. “It’s kind of a once-in-a-lifetime thing that impacts the community’s ability to access emergency care.”





 

Fairview mansion built for William Jennings Bryan around 1901 shown here in August. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)







 

One of the pet tombstones as shown on the Fairview property earlier this summer. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)







 

Fairview mansion built for William Jennings Bryan around 1901 shown here in August. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)







 

Fairview mansion show in the background shows its relative proximity to the emergency area that hospital officials say needs to be expanded. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner) 







 

Fairview mansion built for William Jennings Bryan around 1901 shown here in August. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)







 

The Fairview mansion, built around 1901 for William Jennings Bryan and his wife, Mary, is now up and off of its foundation and ready to be relocated Nov. 7, weather permitting. (Courtesy of Bryan Health)

title: Commentary: Ayoub: Sounds of silence return after costly campaigns
description:
(Getty Images)While broadcasters, social media and others who make money during political campaigns back their cash-filled trucks up to the bank, silence is returning. It’s a welcome sound. We may argue over results, laugh at new conspiracy theories and breathe sighs of relief or resignation, but the political advertising avalanche goes quiet this week. 
The[...]
text:
(Getty Images)While broadcasters, social media and others who make money during political campaigns back their cash-filled trucks up to the bank, silence is returning. It’s a welcome sound. We may argue over results, laugh at new conspiracy theories and breathe sighs of relief or resignation, but the political advertising avalanche goes quiet this week. 
The 2026 midterms were the most expensive ever. Nearly $12 billion alone was spent on political advertising. Television broadcasters will add over $4 billion to their coffers, about a sixth of local television’s aggregate revenue for the year. Nice work if you can get it. 
Throw in direct mail, arena rentals, transportation and sundry other costs and you have yourself historically high spending to win a seat in Congress or the corner office in a statehouse or the last say in how we run this railroad we call democracy. 
I suppose you get what you pay for, but if the fare we were served in Nebraska is any indication, good information was at a premium among the gazillions ponied up for politics this go-round.
To wit: I learned little new from political advertising about Nebraska’s candidates or the ballot referendums we are supposed to decide this election. Yes, there were a couple of clever turns, including one catchy tune, but in aggregate the ads were an incessant parade of the usual: name-calling, innuendo, guilt by association, oversimplification, bandwagoning, straw men, non sequiturs, false dilemmas and slippery slopes. They starred actual candidates, a few paid actors and some real, earnest Nebraskans looking right into the camera telling us how they were going to vote or yukking it up over some perceived duplicity.
We heard a lot about a little, too. For example, boys in girls locker rooms is now apparently a critical cog in the civic health of the state although no one really showed that was even a thing. Meanwhile, the cost of gas and groceries — a thing indeed — kept climbing.
To be fair, making a cogent argument in 30 seconds is not easy, even with AI and other wizardry now available to creators. The “issues” — fodder for debates, candidate forums and thoughtful interviews (hat tip to those who participated) — are rarely fleshed out in half a minute of air time. 
Nebraska candidates, even with holes in their arguments, were on relatively good behavior compared to some of their office-seeking cousins across the country. Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP candidate for governor in Ohio, ran an ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent, who said her daughter lied about her childhood and the sexual abuse she suffered as a preteen, rape charges that have been part of the official record for years. When he was rightly taken to the woodshed for a well-earned public whooping, JD Vance came to his defense, the vice president telling Republicans critical of the Ramaswamy ad to “stop whining.” Response to the veep’s backstopping was tepid at best, perhaps because too many remember that Vance also told us immigrants in Ohio were eating pets.
A Michigan Democratic candidate who happens to be Muslim is poised to win a Senate seat there. He has been met with a barrage of racist swill and accusations of terrorism from the president to the HHS secretary to Texas Sen. Ted Cruz. No telling what the allegations would have been if he were a Lutheran or a Catholic. Right?
Malice has always been a political campaign bottom-feeder, but its abject cruelty seems to have surfaced, giving many pause in wondering just what are the limits of political discourse? Are there limits? 
Coincidently, new research into empathy — a hen’s tooth in a political campaign — indicates the concept and the practice have fallen into disfavor among a significant portion of the population, including some who think it’s “dangerous.” The assertion is based on the belief that unbridled empathy leads us to make seriously bad moral decisions, that we will find ourselves empathizing with the wrong people for the wrong reasons. You can check out the research here. 
Where that leaves those of us who live in the friendly and dare-I-say empathetic confines of “Nebraska Nice” is an open question. Yes, we get after each other pretty good during an election season but then seem to forgive the diss, the disparagement, the disinformation and even the defamation a political campaign can engender. Or maybe not.
All of which makes one wonder why we do it in the first place? Especially since we have plenty of other things to talk about, discuss, question and, for those up for it, debate. I’m guessing we could probably do everything a lot cheaper too … you know … what with gas and groceries.

title: Democrats highlight healthcare affordability on campaign trail
description: Enrollment in Get Covered NJ, the state's health insurance marketplace, began Nov. 1. State officials say help and funding are available, but rates have risen and federal subsidies have been cut. (Photo courtesy of Elizabeth Public Schools)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?] As Democrats hoping to regain control [...]
text:
Enrollment in Get Covered NJ, the state's health insurance marketplace, began Nov. 1. State officials say help and funding are available, but rates have risen and federal subsidies have been cut. (Photo courtesy of Elizabeth Public Schools)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?] As Democrats hoping to regain control of Congress argue on the campaign trail that Republicans have let healthcare grow unaffordable, consumers seeking private insurance plans on New Jersey’s marketplace are finding rates have skyrocketed.
Enrollment in New Jersey’s health insurance marketplace began Sunday. The state Department of Banking and Insurance warned last month that the 2027 rates for plans sold through Get Covered NJ, the state’s marketplace, are set to increase nearly 20% on average over the current monthly cost, with policies sold through United Healthcare spiking nearly 36%.
Consumers can compare plan options in advance of purchasing them. People have until Jan. 31 to find a plan.
The rate hike comes after GOP leadership in Congress declined in 2025 to extend financial subsidies created under former President Joe Biden for the comprehensive commercial plans sold through the state and federal marketplaces created in the 2010 Affordable Care Act. President Donald Trump and the GOP objected to the cost of continuing this aid, estimated to total $335 billion over a decade.
Acting Department of Banking and Insurance Commissioner Susan Ochs called the funding changes “devastating,” and said New Jerseyans will lose nearly $500 million in tax credits as a result. That loss can already be seen in the lower enrollment numbers for 2026, she said, the first year-over-year decline in the program’s short history.
“The challenges are real, but so is our commitment to meeting them. Financial assistance is still available through Get Covered New Jersey, including our state subsidy and the remaining federal tax credits. Many consumers enrolling in coverage will still qualify for financial help, and we are working to ensure they have clear information, trusted assistance, and a path forward,” Ochs told the Senate health committee last week during a hearing about the impact of these federal changes.
The rising cost of healthcare coverage is driving up the number of people who are uninsured, studies show. More than 9% of New Jersey residents under age 65, when they can qualify for Medicare, now lack health insurance.
The lapsed subsidies have become a key talking point for Democrats on the campaign trail in advance of Election Day on Tuesday.
U.S. Sen. Cory Booker (D), who is seeking a third full term, raised the issue in a recent debate against Republican challenger Justin Murphy. Democrat Rebecca Bennett has made healthcare affordability a central theme in her push to unseat Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. in the highly competitive 7th District.
“He has voted to take healthcare away from tens of thousands of people in our district,” she said at a recent campaign event in Rahway.
Harrison Neely, a spokesperson for Kean, said it is Bennett who has reduced access to care as an executive with several health technology firms.
“She made hundreds of thousands in corporate healthcare while partnering with companies accused of putting profits over patients,” he said.
New Jersey funds subsidies for lower-income consumers on its marketplace, and aid is available for those who earn nearly $96,000 annually for an individual or close to $164,000 for a family of three. Those figures are equal to 600% of the federal poverty level.
With less federal assistance, the percentage of people paying just $10 a month for plans fell from 48% in 2025 to 11% this year, the department said. The average cost of a Get Covered plan without subsidies is now nearly $724 a month, Ochs said. Other federal changes set to take effect in January will limit subsidies for noncitizens.
“Rising premiums, reduced financial assistance, and shifting eligibility requirements are sowing confusion and forcing families to make difficult choices about their health care and their household budgets,” Ochs told lawmakers.
It’s a concern New Jerseyans know well. Three in four people here said they worried about affording healthcare in the future, according to a survey by Healthcare Value Hub in July, and nearly two-thirds said they had delayed or skipped care because of cost sometime in the past year.

The rate hikes approved in New Jersey outpace the 15% average increase nationwide, said Laura Waddell, the healthcare program director for advocacy group New Jersey Citizen Action, and come after double-digit rate hikes last year.
Waddell said the price hike is a “double whammy” after subsidies were slashed, which had put the cost of care within reach for millions nationwide.
Federal funding cuts to Medicaid are also expected to force as many as 330,000 New Jerseyans off of NJ Family Care and reduce funding for hospitals, doctors, public health programs, and more by up to $6 billion annually.

The Medicaid cuts have also been a target for Democrats this fall.
Zack Mullock, a Democrat seeking to unseat Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R) in South Jersey’s 2nd District, highlighted Van Drew’s vote to cut Medicaid funding in a Facebook ad that features video of the Republican disputing that claim. Van Drew has defended his vote, saying that people who are eligible will still have access to Medicaid coverage.
To ease Obamacare enrollment this year, the state provided $5 million to 33 organizations — healthcare clinics, disability advocates, faith and community groups, including New Jersey Citizen Action — so they can help people find the right plan, collect the documents they need, and navigate the sign-up. Assistance is available in 10 languages.
“We will continue doing everything we can to help eligible New Jerseyans understand their options, get assistance and most importantly, get the coverage and care they need,” Ochs said.
Enrollment in New Jersey’s marketplace nearly doubled after its first full year of state operation in 2021, from nearly 270,000 consumers that year to more than 513,000 in 2025, department data shows.
But that trend reversed this year, when about 509,000 had signed up for 2026 plans. By the end of June, enrollment dropped to 434,700.
Consumers have also shifted away from gold and silver-level plans, which have higher monthly payments but lower out-of-pocket costs. Interest in bronze plans, which have lower monthly rates but skimpier benefits, doubled between 2025 and 2026, data shows.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Commentary: The quiet rewrite of America’s signature preservation law could harm SC’s historic places
description:
An aerial photo of the Charleston peninsula, with White Point Garden and The Battery at the southern tip, looking up the Cooper River to the Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge. (Photo by Vanessa Kauffmann/Courtesy of Preservation Society of Charleston)Historic preservation is more than old mansions and dusty artifact displays.
It is a way of thinking about the places[...]
text:
An aerial photo of the Charleston peninsula, with White Point Garden and The Battery at the southern tip, looking up the Cooper River to the Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge. (Photo by Vanessa Kauffmann/Courtesy of Preservation Society of Charleston)Historic preservation is more than old mansions and dusty artifact displays.
It is a way of thinking about the places where we live and work every day. It is caring for community gathering places like post offices and churches. And it is seizing the opportunity we have to pass down pride for the places that define us as South Carolinians and Americans across generations.
At present, this reflection is more than an academic exercise.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, while well-meaning in name, contains the most significant change to federal preservation law in 60 years. The law has been introduced in the U.S. Senate and is slated for a vote soon after the midterm elections.
In 1966, Congress declared preservation a national policy.
The National Historic Preservation Act was devised in an age when downtowns were carelessly being severed by interstates.
Hulking modern towers suddenly appeared next to stately courthouses. Grand buildings were erased to make way for more efficient alternatives like which have not stood the test of time. Think: New York’s Penn Station.
Federal preservation law rests on a basic idea: Those who know their communities best have the right to be heard on how to reduce harm to historic sites as projects are planned.
The 1966 law is a case study for how principles of federalism are modeled in legislation.
When American history is on the line, hearing from the boots on the ground matter. The law also enshrines rights for tribes and indigenous communities to speak up for the protection of ancestral sites on federal lands.
The check in the preservation act to prevent federal overreach, known as Section 106, is now under attack. The required consultation process uniquely embraces in-person dialogue over written reports. Those with localized knowledge have a platform to share information with federal officials early in project planning when federal funds or permits are required.
This conversation reduces harm, helps avoid surprises, and generates buy-in to make projects more successful.
This consultation is now on the chopping block.
For the last several months, the threat was a proposed regulatory overhaul. But when broad opposition emerged, including nearly 1,000 community groups that joined the 106Strong Coalition, the sweeping overhaul was quietly stuffed into a permitting reform bill.
But to characterize the change as reform is misleading. It is hollowing out of accountability for federal action with profound potential consequences for our history.
Under the bill, local consultation all but goes away unless the federal agency elects to a dialogue on its initiative.
The substitute is a report — a new paperwork requirement for federal officials that simply outlines expected harms. Ultimately, the project could move forward for any plausible reason the agency decides.
The change would clear the way for some of the most contentious recent projects around the nation’s capital. But the impacts would be both far-reaching and close to home.
South Carolinians don’t have to go far to find Section 106 success stories: A scaled-back federal courthouse in downtown Charleston, a Confederate stockade in Florence where American prisoners are buried, and the discovery of a Revolutionary battlefield in Chester County all relied on local knowledge informing federal permitting agencies.
Here in the Lowcountry, citizen input from the Preservation Society of Charleston, in consultation with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, has been critical to develop a sensitive plan for a storm surge barrier called the Battery Extension project.
Working with the Corps and the city of Charleston, Section 106 amplifies local voices to make sure this major resilience project is more than a rudimentary concrete wall.
The proposed solution will be a multifunction amenity, integrating seamlessly with history and protecting Charleston’s architectural legacy — a key economic driver for the state.
The new law would clear the way for much less sensitive development by rewriting what harm to a historic place entails. Under the proposed process, the visual, atmospheric and auditory effects of a large industrial site would be irrelevant.
In other words, the hands of the permitting agency would be tied regardless of project’s proximity to a significant historic place.
Across the country, Section 106 has proved time and again that direct engagement produces win-win solutions.
Let’s defend this dialogue and ensure that the places that bind community life can survive short-term pressures to cut corners and hide behind another report.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska candidates, ballot measures exceed $63M in fundraising before Nov. 3 election
description: The 2026 Nebraska candidates running for: governor and lieutenant governor (first row); attorney general, secretary of state, state treasurer, auditor of public accounts and Public Service Commission (second row); Legislature (rows three through six, arranged by legislative district); and State Board of Education and University of Nebraska Board of Regents ([...]
text:
The 2026 Nebraska candidates running for: governor and lieutenant governor (first row); attorney general, secretary of state, state treasurer, auditor of public accounts and Public Service Commission (second row); Legislature (rows three through six, arranged by legislative district); and State Board of Education and University of Nebraska Board of Regents (bottom row, from left, arranged by district). (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — As Nebraskans head to the polls Tuesday, they will vote in some of the most expensive races in state history — and in a year when candidates and statewide ballot measure campaigns have already raised more than $63 million.
Campaign finance data available as of Sunday afternoon indicates general election candidates across 43 state-level offices, from the governor to two statewide education boards, had raised $36.5 million. Of the total, 75% is from Nebraska, and 11% is from Washington, D.C. Money has come in from all states but Alaska, Delaware and New Hampshire.
Meanwhile, four groups for or against three statewide ballot measures have raised nearly $26.9 million — 21.3% is in-state while 38.6% is from New York and 36.5% is from Massachusetts. The out-of-state lean is primarily because outside gambling groups are the sole donors to the campaign to legalize and regulate online sports betting (Initiative Measures 440 and 441).
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and the tools you need to cast your vote in Nebraska’s Nov. 3 general election.]
In addition to campaign-specific spending, political action committees have spent $3.68 million to support or oppose the same state-level candidates or issues. This total doesn’t include administrative spending or funds already reported on candidate-disclosed donation reports.
‘Unfortunate reality’
The race for Legislative District 4 in west Omaha has so far exceeded $1.2 million in direct spending. Lawmakers are paid just $12,000 each year, 100 times less than the campaign spending total.
An additional $323,000 in outside PAC money has been spent to support or oppose incumbent state Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn and challenger Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek of Omaha.
“It’s the unfortunate reality that we live with right now,” said von Gillern, who is facing a tough reelection. His fate could have a cascading effect on legislative leadership positions next year as multiple senators have asked him to consider the open speakership.
State Sen. Brad von Gillern and Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek are facing off again for to represent west-central Douglas County’s Legislative District 4. They are pictured in Omaha in early October 2026. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Von Gillern, a Republican, is in a rematch with Maxwell-Ostdiek, a registered nonpartisan. She came ahead of von Gillern in the spring primary by about the same margin that von Gillern won by four years ago. 
The incumbent said candidates largely have two missions aided by campaign finance: Tell people about yourself and ensure voters understand your opponent.
“The hope is, obviously, that that inspires someone to ask good questions and consider the facts,” von Gillern said. “The challenge is that so often the advertising is misrepresentation or is 1% of the truth and is incredibly misleading.”
Maxwell-Ostdiek said it was “wild” to see this much money being spent on an officially nonpartisan race. She was outspent in 2022 and has been outspent so far this year.
“It is meant to be representation where you’re really learning and visiting and talking with your neighbors, and this outside money is just, it’s very, it’s surprising,” said Maxwell-Ostdiek.
She added: “These amounts of money, I think, are a reflection of concern about performance, and so I’m trying to keep my eye on what’s important, which is talking to voters every day and listening and trying to get my message out. That’s my focus.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen and former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont are the 2026 Republican and Democratic candidates for Nebraska governor. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In Nebraska, party affiliation for candidates for the Legislature, State Board of Education and University of Nebraska Board of Regents does not appear on the ballot. However, nearly all candidates in those races are registered with a party or endorsed by Republicans or Democrats.
Of the seven nonpartisans in those races, all but two are endorsed by the Nebraska Democratic Party. The exceptions are Dan Winter of Bradshaw, who is running for Legislative District 24, and Shaylee Scranton of Thedford, who is running for Legislative District 42.
Top donors in Nebraska 2026 elections
Democratic and Democratic-endorsed nonpartisans have largely benefited from a network of centralized groups this cycle. Former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, who is challenging Republican Gov. Jim Pillen’s reelection, is also among the benefactors.
The top Democratic donors this year, so far, are:

Democracy Nebraska, a Lincoln-based PAC, donated $1.39 million across 17 state-level candidates (14 Democrats and three nonpartisans, including $351,000 to Walz).
Dianne Lozier, co-founder of the Lozier Foundation in Omaha, donated $1.38 million across 15 state-level candidates (15 Democrats and four nonpartisans, including $1 million to Walz).
NU Regent Barbara Weitz, co-founder of the Weitz Family Foundation in Omaha, donated $1.26 million across nine state-level candidates (six Democrats and three nonpartisans, including $750,000 to Walz).
Way Back PAC, based out of Wyoming, donated $653,000 to 11 state-level candidates (nine Democrats and two nonpartisans, including $498,000 to Walz).

On the right, the largest donors are Guy Ellsworth of Pierce ($465,000 to Pillen alone), Shawn Peed of Lincoln ($400,000 to five candidates) and Tom Peed of Lincoln ($326,000 to four candidates). The Peeds each gave Pillen $300,000.
The 2026 candidates for Legislative District 18, from left: Jess Goldoni of Omaha and Taylor Royal of Bennington. State Sen. Christy Armendariz of Omaha declined to seek reelection. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Union Pacific Railroad Co. has given $426,500 to 13 Republicans, including $375,000 to Pillen. UP has also given $2,000 to Democratic state Sen. John Fredrickson.
Pillen has received $2 million from the Republican Governors Association, too, so far the single-largest contributor to a candidate this year. Walz has received $507,500 from the Democratic Governors Association. She’s also been boosted by the Government that Works PAC in Washington, D.C., with $800,000.
Another major donation: $400,000 from the Republican Attorneys General Association and the RAGA Action Fund to Attorney General Mike Hilgers. He faces Democrat Jocelyn Brasher this fall. Brasher’s top two donors are Weitz ($314,600) and Democracy Nebraska ($125,400).
Candidates receiving nonitemized contributions from individuals totaling less than $250.01 account for $1.27 million across 51 candidates on the general election ballot.
Outside PAC spending
When including indirect PAC spending, another legislative race, Legislative District 18, also in Douglas County, has exceeded $1.1 million between Jess Goldoni and Taylor Royal. They are seeking to succeed state Sen. Christy Armendariz of Omaha, who decided not to run again. 
Outside spending accounts for $562,600 in LD 18, about 48% for or against Goldoni compared to 44% for or against Royal (an additional 8% came in the primary when a second Republican was in the race). However, more PAC money has supported Goldoni (53% of her total) than opposed her. More PAC money has opposed Royal (76% of his total) than supported.
Bill Bowes of La Vista and SuAnn Witt of Papillion are the 2026 candidates for Legislative District 14 in Sarpy County. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Legislative District 14, between Bill Bowes of La Vista and SuAnn Witt of Papillion ($991,214.35), to succeed Speaker John Arch of La Vista, is also less than $10,000 away from $1 million in spending. The race has, in total, seen nearly $400,000 in outside PAC spending, mostly negative (45% for or against Bowes, 34% for or against Witt and 22% for or against a second Republican who did not advance from the primary, similar to LD 18).
Of the LD 14 PAC spending, nearly $140,000 has been against Bowes, and nearly $123,000 has been spent to oppose Witt.
The five most active Nebraska PACs this year in total spending: Nebraska United ($1.57 million spent), Preserve the Good Life ($1.13 million), Nebraskans for a Stronger Future group ($988,000, We Are Nebraska ($667,000) and the Nebraska Conservative Leadership Fund ($600,000). 
The 2026 candidates for Legislative District 36, from left: State Sen. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue and Darin Tompkins of Papillion. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Nebraska United, We Are Nebraska and the Conservative Leadership Fund have supported Republicans and opposed Democrats or Democratic-supported nonpartisans. Preserve the Good Life and the Nebraskans for a Stronger Future Group have done the opposite.
Other expensive legislative races
The other most expensive legislative races this year, based on available records:

Legislative District 36, between incumbent state Sen. Rick Holdcroft of Bellevue and Darin Tompkins of Papillion ($826,237.59).
Legislative District 10, between Cindy Johnson of Omaha and Rebecca Rens of Bennington ($763,617.34), to succeed state Sen. Wendy DeBoer of Omaha.
Legislative District 12, between incumbent state Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston and Christy Knorr of Omaha ($725,442.22).
Legislative District 2, between Dean Helmick of Plattsmouth and Caitlin Knutson of Lincoln ($614,801.45), to succeed state Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood.
Legislative District 20, between incumbent state Sen. John Fredrickson and Chris Anderson, both of Omaha ($559,198.19).
Legislative District 26, between incumbent state Sen. George Dungan and Tobias Howard, both of Lincoln ($305,019.75).

Fredrickson and Dungan are looking to avoid close elections as they had in 2022 when they first won. Fredrickson was outspent in 2022 and won by 82 votes. Fredrickson and Dungan are Democrats. This time around, they’ve heavily outspent their Republican opponents.
The 2026 candidates for Legislative District 20, from left: State Sen. John Fredrickson and Chris Anderson, both of Omaha. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Fredrickson and Anderson have spent $440,000 between them, and Fredrickson accounts for 88% of that. Of an additional $114,000 in indirect PAC spending, $31,000 has supported Fredrickson. About $43,000 has supported Anderson, with almost $40,000 more in opposition.
For Dungan, he is the only candidate in the race with a financial disclosure committee (a legal requirement after directly raising or spending $5,000). About $40,000 has been spent indirectly to support either Dungan (just shy of $7,000) or Howard (almost $33,000).
Two other rural races to watch: Legislative District 32, between Mark Schoenrock of Diller and Shay Smith of Crete, and Legislative District 30, between Janet Bock of Beatrice and Cally Ideus of Filley. LD 32 is represented by state Sen. Tom Brandt of Plymouth, while state Sen. Myron Dorn of Adams represents LD 30. Brandt and Dorn are term-limited.
Schoenrock and Ideus are Republicans, while Smith is a registered nonpartisan. Bock is a Democrat. Smith has outspent Schoenrock by nearly $100,000, and in outside spending, the Nebraska Conservative Leadership Fund has spent $7,675 in support of Schoenrock.
Importance of canvassing
Despite the money, von Gillern, Maxwell-Ostdiek and dozens of other candidates say they continue to meet voters where they’re at, primarily door to door or at listening sessions.
The 2026 candidates for Legislative District 12, state Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston and Christy Knorr of Omaha, in the district on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Von Gillern described canvassing as “by far the most impactful thing that we do.” He described going to 108 doors in one night, and maybe 35 homeowners answered. Of those, he said he had decent conversations with 25 and is convinced he won at least 15-20 votes that night.
“Yes, it’s old-fashioned. Yes, it’s not a lot of fun, particularly on a 100-degree day, or when it’s raining, or I don’t know, three weeks it could be snowing,” von Gillern said in early October. “It’s not the most fun, but interacting with people and meeting folks, and some of the conversations are so incredibly rewarding and uplifting.”
Maxwell-Ostdiek agreed. In early October, she said candidates are asking voters to give their trust, which must be earned. She said her focus is also on good ideas, no matter the source.
“I think that going around and talking to people in person is part of how we’re going to build community again and try to bring people together because more people actually have in common many of the same issues and the same concerns and priorities than they don’t,” Maxwell-Ostdiek said.
Candidates and ballot measures unite
Two regents and one legislative candidate did spend millions supporting an anti-abortion measure in 2024, and one legislative candidate spent more than $1 million for an abortion-choice measure. 
The 2026 candidates for Legislative District 2, from left: Dean Helmick of Plattsmouth and Caitlin Knutson of Lincoln. State Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood is term-limited. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Candidates can buy cheaper ads in competitive ad markets than ballot question committees. The Legislature voted against ending the strategy this spring.
This year, candidates for and against Initiative Measures 440 and 441, to legalize and regulate online sports wagering, have purchased ads to spread the word about the proposals. The supporting group is Tax Relief Nebraska. The main opposing group is Save Nebraska Sports.
Tax Relief Nebraska is already the most expensive petition campaign, even outside of intermingling with candidates. The campaign had raised nearly $22.5 million through Oct. 29.
The group is the main reason for the out-of-state lean in ballot measure finance, due to funding from Boston’s DK Crown Holdings (the parent company of DraftKings) and New York’s FanDuel Inc. Each gave $10.4 million to Tax Relief Nebraska.
On Oct. 27, Tax Relief Nebraska gave $750,000 to legislative candidate Tim Anderson of Sutton. New ads are running under Anderson’s name in support of online sports wagering.
The 2026 candidates for Legislative District 38, from left: Tim Sutton of Sutton and Janell Anderson Ehrke of Orleans. State Sen. Dave Murman of Glenvil is term-limited. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Anderson is running for Legislative District 38 in central Nebraska to succeed term-limited state Sen. Dave Murman of Glenvil. Anderson faces Janell Anderson Ehrke of Orleans. She, like Murman and Anderson, is a Republican. Anderson and Anderson Ehrke both said they are in favor of letting voters decide whether to legalize online sports betting.
State Treasurer Joey Spellerberg of Fremont has received nearly $1 million from Common Sense Nebraska, which is the same group that helped funnel money to candidates for the anti-abortion constitutional amendment in 2024. Spellerberg is part of Save Nebraska Sports.
Because of Anderson’s connection to Tax Relief Nebraska, Spellerberg, State Auditor Mike Foley and U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts have withdrawn their endorsement of Anderson.
This appears to be the first year where legislative and regents candidates will exceed $1 million in funds raised or spent for their races, excluding any intermingling with ballot measures. Unlike the Legislature, regents have no salary.
Breaking through the noise
Other races likely to make history this year are two NU Board of Regents races, one an open seat for the first time in 18 years in Lincoln (NU Regents District 1) and the other a special election for a four-year term in Omaha (NU Regents District 4). 
Brent Comstock and Dr. Jeremy Hosein, both of Lincoln, are facing off for an open seat on the NU Board of Regents. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In the Lincoln race, candidates Brent Comstock and Jeremy Hosein have already raised more than $950,000 and spent more than $670,000. And in Omaha, candidates Susanne Shore and Justin Solomon have raised more than $555,000 and spent more than $529,000. 
The previous regents’ record was nearly $779,000 raised and more than $772,000 spent in 2008, also for NU Regents 1.
The third and final regents race this year is for NU Regents District 2, between Jill Wolfe of Elkhorn and Elizabeth Butler of Papillion. Wolfe has given her campaign $190,000, and she’s taken out nearly $30,000 in loans. Her next largest donation is from U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts ($15,000). Butler’s top donors are Lozier ($30,000) and Weitz ($26,742). Wolfe and Butler have together raised $380,000.
Susanne Shore and Justin Solomon, both of Omaha, are facing off in a special election for an open seat on the NU Board of Regents. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Comstock said NU is critical for the state, with a $6 billion annual economic impact. He said voters want a “good, solid person in this seat,” which is open for the first time in 18 years after NU Regent Tim Clare, who ran in 2008, decided not to run again. 
Regents often serve multiple six-year terms, Comstock noted, and they have no term limits.
“Like every other campaign for office, things are getting more expensive, but when you think about the importance of the university to our state, I think that it’s a good example of why it is costing so much,” Comstock said.
Hosein and Comstock encouraged voters to do their own research and look at candidates’ ideas, supporters and how candidates have conducted themselves before voting.
“I’m an open book because we deserve better leaders with honesty, character and competency,” Hosein said in a statement.
Said Comstock: “The university is too important for people to skip out on filling in this oval.”
Voting ends at 8 p.m. Central time Tuesday. Early voting is underway.

text:
Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak invited Daron Wyatt, a reserve deputy for his office and the Republican candidate for Albany County sheriff, to a Laramie meeting featuring FBI Director Kash Patel. Albany County Sheriff Aaron Appelhans, Wyatt’s Democratic opponent, called the candidate’s presence “a little out of place.” 
The FBI organized the Wednesday meeting at the University of Wyoming’s War Memorial Stadium, billing it as a capabilities briefing in the morning and a “special fireside chat” in the afternoon with Patel, FBI Denver Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski, U.S. Attorney for Wyoming Darin Smith and Wyoming’s U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman, according to the meeting invitation. The fireside chat was “an opportunity for open dialogue on priorities, challenges, and future collaboration,” the invitation states. 
It’s unclear what brought Patel to the meeting, or why it was held in Laramie. An FBI spokesperson didn’t respond to WyoFile’s specific inquiries, instead referring to statements posted on X by Patel and FBI Denver. Roundtable discussions like the one held Wednesday aren’t unusual at national conferences, but this one was “fairly unique” because of the location, Appelhans said. 
Patel’s presence in Wyoming follows a U.S. Department of Justice and FBI initiative called Operation Steadfast Promise, which aimed to address violent crime specifically in tribal communities across the country. As part of the national campaign, which occurred from April through September, the FBI assigned an additional 15 agents to Lander.
While the FBI initially extended meeting invitations in early October only to the first and second in command of each Wyoming law enforcement agency, the agency later opened the invitation to all Wyoming law enforcement personnel, according to emails shared by Appelhans. The gathering was closed to the general public — an FBI agent turned away a photographer for the Branding Iron, which first reported on the event, when he entered the stadium’s public lobby. 
Wyatt, a cop who retired from full-time policing in California over six years ago, attended the meeting in his capacity as a reserve deputy for the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office. Kozak said in a call to WyoFile that he brought Wyatt on as a reserve deputy about six months ago. “He’s been volunteering in the jail, working in the pods just to learn our procedures here,” Kozak said. 
Wyatt isn’t paid in his role as a reserve deputy, according to the sheriff. 
Kozak, who donated $75 to Wyatt’s candidate committee, invited the candidate to the FBI meeting for the capabilities briefing. “He invited me so that I could hear the briefing, so that in the event that I am elected, I would have the information,” Wyatt said in a call to WyoFile. “I don’t know when they will come and do another briefing like that.” 
Wyatt said he had also hoped to network at the event “so that if something ever happens, there’s already a face to the name and a name with a telephone number.”
Appelhans, the Albany County sheriff since 2020, said in a call to WyoFile that he felt Wyatt’s attendance was “a little out of place” and noted that, according to his observation, no other reserve deputies from other agencies attended the event, which primarily hosted “higher-level law enforcement administrators and executives.” 
The Albany County sheriff pointed to Wyatt’s post to his campaign Facebook page thanking Kozak for inviting him to the event. “I think that kind of speaks for itself,” Appelhans said. When asked to clarify what he meant, the sheriff said it highlights an agency outside of Albany County “trying to kind of put their 2 cents in and dip their fingers in some of the local politics that we have here in Albany County.” 
In addition to thanking Kozak for the invite, the post includes a number of hashtags related to the election and photos of Wyatt with Kozak and Patel.
The race between Appelhans and Wyatt has been heated, with each throwing barbs primarily over jail deaths and use of force. The election is Tuesday.
