title: Race contrasts two approaches for the low-visibility state treasurer’s office
description: From left, Republican John Leiber and Democrat Yee Leng Xiong are running for state treasurer in Tuesday's election. Leiber is the incumbent. (Leiber, campaign photo; Xiong, Marathon County Board photo)The 2026 race for Wisconsin state treasurer is a contest between two visions for the office — a Republican incumbent who has centered his case on doing the jo[...]
text:
From left, Republican John Leiber and Democrat Yee Leng Xiong are running for state treasurer in Tuesday's election. Leiber is the incumbent. (Leiber, campaign photo; Xiong, Marathon County Board photo)The 2026 race for Wisconsin state treasurer is a contest between two visions for the office — a Republican incumbent who has centered his case on doing the job without “growing government,” and a Democratic challenger who believes the position could take a higher profile.
The campaign website for Republican incumbent John Leiber, who is seeking reelection, says that in his first term he “hasn’t added programs or built a bigger office,” but instead stuck to the list of duties assigned to the state treasurer.
Democratic challenger Yee Leng Xiong is a Marathon County Board member and treasurer of the DC Everest School Board in Weston, Wisconsin, southeast of Wausau. His campaign website says he intends to “act as an independent watchdog for Wisconsin taxpayers” advocating “transparent management and investment of public funds.”
The state treasurer’s office is among those identified in the Wisconsin Constitution. “The office was first imagined by the state’s founders as a check on the government’s financial decisions and a steward of its public lands,” the treasurer’s office website states.  
Over the years lawmakers have transferred or eliminated many of its duties, including cash and debt management, the state’s 529 education savings plan and the state local government investment pool. 
In 2018, however, Wisconsin voters rejected an amendment that would have eliminated the elected office from the constitution.
After that vote, Sarah Godlewski, who had led the campaign against the amendment, ran for state treasurer in 2018 and won, stating the agency should be a fiscal watchdog. In office, Godlewski took on public-facing roles, including working with county treasurers and promoting retirement security programs.
Godlewski didn’t seek a second term, instead joining three other Democrats seeking the party nomination to run for U.S. Senate in 2022. In early 2023 Gov. Tony Evers appointed her as Wisconsin Secretary of State when the incumbent, Doug La Follette, resigned shortly after taking office for his 12th consecutive term. Godlewski is now the Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor. 
The state treasurer’s remaining official duties include signing state checks (technically done by machine) and serving with the secretary of state and the attorney general on the state Board of Commissioners of Public Lands.
The board manages 75,000 acres of former federal land now held in trust for Wisconsin schools and also manages four trust funds. The largest, the Common School Fund, makes annual donations to school library systems. Over the last four years the Common School Fund has grown to about $1.6 billion, and the annual payments to libraries from the fund have grown each year, reaching $73.5 million in 2025-26.
Republican John Leiber
When John Leiber ran in 2022 against a Democrat who campaigned on continuing Godlewski’s approach, Leiber emphasized instead focusing on the job of treasurer as it was outlined in the state constitution and statutes. Other than Sen. Ron Johnson, Leiber was the only Republican that year to win a statewide office in Wisconsin.
Leiber has been a state legislative aide and has worked in the state Department of Revenue in the tax division. On the job since 2023, he has emphasized maintaining a lean office and focusing on his role on the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands. 
“This is the only dedicated funding for school libraries statewide and my top priority is to ensure the fund continues to thrive in the future,” Leiber said when he announced his reelection campaign a year ago.
Leiber’s campaign website states that in office, he “has not built a bureaucracy or invented new programs. He has administered the constitutional duties of the office, advocated for fiscal restraint with the Legislature, and focused on the assets he is charged to oversee.”
Democrat Yee Leng Xiong
Yee Leng Xiong has built a resume that includes election to multiple levels of state government as well as experience in running a nonprofit and membership on a state financial literacy council appointed by Gov. Tony Evers.
Xiong is a Wausau native whose parents were Hmong refugees from Southeast Asia. If elected he would be the first Hmong official elected to a Wisconsin statewide office.
Xiong says he can act as an independent watchdog over state finances.
“As Treasurer, you don’t answer to the Governor or the Legislature — you answer directly to the people,” Xiong said in January when he announced his candidacy. “I’m running to be an independent voice for taxpayers and to make sure Wisconsin’s money is managed responsibly, transparently, and in the public interest.”
On his campaign website, Xiong says that he has “experience managing budgets at every level of government” and is committed to “transparency and accountability.”
He also says he can bring his school board experience to bear in the decisions by the public lands board because he “understands firsthand how trust fund decisions impact local schools and students.”

title: Collins, Jackson make their closing appeals in Maine’s pivotal US Senate race
description: Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins speaks to reporters outside the Winthrop Police Department on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)The communications equipment for Winthrop’s emergency dispatch network had been failing almost daily, leaving the roughly 18,000 people across Kennebec County who rely on it with unreliable service. So, the [...]
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins speaks to reporters outside the Winthrop Police Department on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)The communications equipment for Winthrop’s emergency dispatch network had been failing almost daily, leaving the roughly 18,000 people across Kennebec County who rely on it with unreliable service. So, the town manager reached out to U.S. Sen. Susan Collins. 
Collins, from the helm of the Senate Appropriations Committee, walked them through the process to secure federal earmarks, getting them a little more than $1.1 million earlier this year to purchase new equipment, including a tower that will more than double the range of wireless emergency communications. 
“It’s not a want. It’s a need,” Paul Ferland, police chief of both Monmouth and Winthrop, said after giving Collins a tour of the department on Thursday. “And for this community to take it upon themselves monetarily, it was just not feasible to get it done any time in the future.” 
This is one of several local stops Collins has made in her final days on the campaign trail before the Nov. 3 election, when she hopes to secure a sixth term. Meanwhile, her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, has spent his last days hosting public forums, events with high-profile national figures and press conferences highlighting Collins’ ties to President Donald Trump.  
Democrats view Collins’ seat as a key pickup opportunity in their efforts to gain more control in the U.S. Senate, and they’re hoping time has run out on the senior senator’s staying power given the Trump administration’s increasing unpopularity. 
“There are folks in the United States Congress, in the House and the Senate, that will not stand up to this president, regardless of what he decides to do,” U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona said while stumping for Jackson in Brunswick on Wednesday. “It’s not right.”
Coupled by a late burst of ads, the last leg of the most expensive race in state history has underscored the two opposing approaches each candidates’ campaigns have centered on. 
“That’s what it boils down to,” Collins said in Winthrop. “I’ve been able to bring $1.5 billion dollars to Maine to support projects just like this one. That’s a pretty powerful argument.” 
After the event with Kelly in Brunswick, Jackson said, “People that think that Senator Collins has been doing all this, bringing in all this money, I mean, look, it’s a pittance compared to what we’re losing.” He posed the following question to voters: “Do you think the government’s working for you?” 
U.S. Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona, left, campaigns for Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson, right, at Flight Deck Brewing in Brunswick on Oct. 28, 2026. (By Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
Final appeals
Vietnam veteran Bill Jefferson was drafted into a war he opposed. Now, the Buxton resident harbors similar resentment about the United States’ war with Iran. That’s part of why he supports Jackson, who has publicly opposed the conflict. 
During an event Jackson held with veterans at Flight Deck Brewing in Brunswick, Jefferson also said Jackson’s support of universal healthcare and eliminating U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement factor into his support. 
A lifelong Democrat, Jefferson previously worked as an immigration inspector on the Canadian border. He saw an ad for the job after 9/11 and thought he could do something positive, he said. He felt he did, but now he is reluctant to talk about his time in that role because he is appalled by how federal immigration enforcement is being run today, noting a lack of training and respect for human rights. 
“We all know right now that what’s happening in this country is completely wrong,” Jackson told the crowd of about 30 people. 
Speaking next to Kelly, who said he is considering running for president in 2028, Jackson said he wants to work with him to help “get our democracy back, get our government back, get things in place that actually helps everyday people instead of the billionaire class.”
Jackson has gotten boosts from several prominent Democrats, including Democratic U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, and Democratic U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts. Meanwhile, former U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia, a Democrat turned independent, has campaigned with Collins. Trump has not visited Maine, but Vice President JD Vance praised Collins during his trip in August. 
As he has throughout the campaign,  during a press conference with the Maine Democratic Party on Friday in Portland, Jackson focused on Collins’ record of siding with the president the vast majority of the time. He also repeated his criticism of Collins voting to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who had a hand in overturning Roe v. Wade, during a fireside chat in Kittery with Planned Parenthood Action Fund President and CEO Alexis McGill Johnson on Thursday. 
At the same time, Collins was touting her federal earmarks in Winthrop. She pushed back on a reporter’s question about voters who said they want her to do more to stand up to Trump, listing off instances where she has clawed back funding, like the Sea Grant, and the rural healthcare fund she got put into the president’s signature spending law, which won’t offset the larger healthcare cuts in the law.   
“What I find that people are more interested in is the question, ‘Who can do more for the people of Maine?’” Collins said. “I think when I frame the question that way, the choice becomes very obvious.”  
Collins went on to say that even if Democrats win back the U.S. Senate, and she wins re-election, she’ll still have power. She’d then be vice chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, as she was before her current role as chair. 
“Given the bad decisions that have been made in Augusta, given the fact that we’re a low-income state and that we’re also a heavily taxed state and the state with the oldest population by median age in the country, we need that help,” Collins said. “We desperately need the help.”
The senator continued to spotlight the help she’s been able to provide by way of federal earmarks in subsequent stops, which included what will soon be a new childcare building in Greenville and the ribbon cutting of a new public safety building in Milo.
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and staff in front of her campaign bus after visiting the Winthrop Police Department on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
Eleventh-hour ads
Halloween provided both candidates with opportunities to speak directly with voters. At Cross Point Church’s trunk-or-treat in Bangor, Collins displayed a trunk decorated in honor of America 250. Meanwhile, Jackson trick-or-treated with families in Portland, dressed up as a “cord of wood,” a reference to an ad Collins’ campaign aired last week that he and others have criticized as classist. 
It features retired broadcaster Bill Green, who was also in an earlier Collins ad. In the new ad, Green says, “we’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here. We’re sending someone to the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective.”
In response, Jackson told reporters in Brunswick on Wednesday, “Well, if taking away healthcare for people, getting us into foreign wars, and giving billionaires tax cuts are the tools, then yeah, no, I don’t have those tools.”
He added, “I’m a working class person, got into the Maine Legislature, ended up being the Senate president for six years. I know how to get shit done. She’s just scared that she’s going to lose.”
This comes after most of the negative advertising in Maine’s U.S. Senate race had come from outside groups. More than $260 million has been spent on ads, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact, surpassing the previous state record of $200 million spent in the 2020 race between Collins and Democrat Sara Gideon.

title: Lawsuit could save Medicaid for 140,000 in Ohio
description: Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, speaks at the Department of Health and Human Services in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)The American Medical Association says the Trump administration has unlawfully imposed a rule that could threaten health coverage for at least 140,000 Ohio Medicaid r[...]
text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, speaks at the Department of Health and Human Services in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)The American Medical Association says the Trump administration has unlawfully imposed a rule that could threaten health coverage for at least 140,000 Ohio Medicaid recipients. 
The AMA made that statement last week in a friend-of-the-court brief in support of a lawsuit in which Columbus is a plaintiff. It seeks to stop an element of planned Medicaid work requirements that the city said will burden taxpayers and city services.
The requirements are a part of President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, which was passed with only Republican support in summer 2025. 
The bill cut taxes on the richest 1% of Americans by $1 trillion over 10 years. It cut a similar amount from Medicaid and SNAP — healthcare and nutrition programs for the poor — over the same period. 
A major way the Trump bill seeks to make cuts to Medicaid is through work requirements that mostly go into effect on Jan. 1. Past experiments with work requirements failed to produce additional employment, and the Congressional Budget Office estimates that they will cause 7.5 million Americans to lose healthcare by 2034. An analysis by the Commonwealth Fund said cuts to Medicaid and SNAP will actually result in job losses by reducing states’ economic output.
Bad as those predictions are, Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Department of Health and Human Services took an unlawful step further, Columbus and a group of health advocates said in a Sept. 18 lawsuit. 
The Trump law was meant to exempt from the work requirement the “medically frail” who have coverage under Obamacare’s Medicaid expansion in states such as Ohio, said the suit, which was filed in U.S. District Court in Maryland.
But in its rules implementing the law, Health and Human Services requires such people to prove that their medical frailties make them unable to work, the suit said.
It defined “medically frail” as those who were “blind or disabled,” “with a substance use disorder,” “with a disabling mental disorder,” “with a physical, intellectual, or developmental disability that significantly impairs their ability to perform one or more activities of daily living,”; or those “with a serious or complex medical condition.”
The lawsuit said placing the burden on such recipients to prove their medical frailties make them unable to work will cause millions more to lose coverage than the Trump law contemplated.
“Independent experts project the statute, as enacted, would cause about 6.4 million people to lose coverage on an average annual basis between 2027 and 2034,” it said. “With the (rule’s) additional restrictions, those losses are estimated to increase to around 8.2 million people each year — a roughly 30 percent increase.”
Cleveland-based Center for Community Solutions in July said that 143,000 Ohioans who have coverage under Ohio’s Medicaid expansion are medically frail and another 172,000 would have to undergo additional evaluation before it can be determined whether they are or not. And it said many of the medically frail would have a tough time proving their frailties make them unable to work.
“The people most likely to qualify for medical frailty protections may also be individuals least able to navigate additional paperwork, documentation requests, and administrative reviews,” the Center for Community Solutions said in an appeal to loosen the requirements. “If the exemption process becomes too complex, coverage losses could occur even among individuals the exemption was intended to protect.”
The lawsuit said resulting coverage losses would fall on Columbus and the taxpayers who finance its medical and social infrastructure.
Among its services, the city operates a community health center that serves people regardless of ability to pay. 
“Columbus receives compensation when it provides these services to Medicaid beneficiaries, but it is not compensated when it provides these services to uninsured individuals,” it said. “The increase in the number of uninsured individuals resulting from the rule would lead to a greater burden on those city services and lower reimbursement, which, in turn, will impose additional costs on the city.”
The friend-of-the-court brief was filed Tuesday by the American Medical Association and eight other doctors’ groups, including ones representing oncologists, emergency doctors and obstetricians. It said the rule promulgated by Kennedy’s agency stands the intent of the Trump law on its head when it comes to the medically frail.
“The statutory language of (the Trump law) excludes medically frail individuals from Medicaid work requirements, including everyone with a serious or complex medical condition or substance use disorder,” it said. “But — contrary to the statute — (the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services) added the requirement that individuals prove their medical condition significantly impairs their ability to work. This additional requirement converts what Congress intended to be an exclusion based on one’s medical status into an exclusion based on the individual’s ability to work.” 
The rule also would add to the flood of paperwork which is already drowning practitioners, the AMA and other doctors’ groups said.
“At a time when excessive administrative tasks are a leading contributor to gaps in patient care and physician burnout, these additional responsibilities create new burdens for medically frail patients and the physicians who care for them,” it said.

title: Ohio Auditor of State candidates seek to enhance agency’s role in different ways
description:

text:
A voter fills out a ballot at the Portland Expo in Maine’s June 9, 2026, primary election. (Photo by Jim Neuger / Maine Morning Star)The race for Ohio’s auditor of state will come down to a small town mayor with years of experience working with the state office, or the current Ohio Secretary of State.
Democrat Annette Blackwell and Republican Frank LaRose are vying for the seat, as the current auditor, Keith Faber, runs to become the next state attorney general.
The auditor of state is the Ohio’s chief compliance officer, overseeing tax and spending audits for governmental agencies and offices, including the state, counties, cities, villages, and school districts.
The auditor also has a seat on the Ohio Redistricting Commission when the redrawing of state voting district maps for legislative and congressional seats is conducted. Current Auditor of State Keith Faber even stood as co-chair of the commission during the most recent redistricting effort.
In more recent news, the auditor’s office has had to deal with alleged cybercrimes, as the web server for the agency was “attacked by overseas cybercriminals and potentially foreign state actors,” according to a statement from Faber published on the auditor’s office website.
The website was shut down “out of an abundance of caution,” and web server and online accounts were taken offline while the office determines the level of the threat.
Faber’s statement went on to say they do not believe the attack was ransomware, and the data contained by the office had been backed up. The office said it does not have reason to believe financial information for government entities audited by the agency are at risk.
“Based on the nature of the files attacked, we have no evidence this cyberattack put the personal financial information of Ohioans at risk,” according to the statement.
The auditor’s office plays an important role in the day-to-day inner workings of the state, but it’s not one that Ohioans are generally familiar with. Because of that, candidates have spent time on the campaign trail not only helping voters get to know them, but the office itself.
  Annette Blackwell 
Democrat Annette Blackwell has more experience with the auditor’s office than the average Ohioan, because of her current position as mayor of Maple Heights. The city struggled under a fiscal emergency designation from the state auditor’s office, causing Blackwell to hit the ground running to undo the financial crisis she inherited when she was elected to the office.
Annette Blackwell.(Photo courtesy of the Blackwell campaign)
She and her team were able to get out from under the designation, eventually earning praise from the auditor’s office for their financial standing. But Blackwell said the process allowed her some perspective on what the state auditor could be doing to help communities who aren’t struggling with fraud or some other nefarious financial downfall, but rather the state of the economy, and lack of help from their state and federal counterparts.
“In our city, there was no fraud, waste, and abuse, but we lost significant revenue with reappraisal, with the middle class moving out … and skilled workforce (moving out), and then the companies that hired those skilled workers moving out,” Blackwell told the Capital Journal. “And then of course the local government fund being cut and never being totally restored, so our tax base was decimated.”
Talking to voters on the campaign trail included talking to school district representatives and township officials who are approaching fiscal concern, or have just climbed out from under it, she said.
“What I don’t hear is they felt supported (by the auditor’s office),” Blackwell said. “They felt audited, they didn’t feel audited and supported.”
As data centers become a larger and larger discussion, and mixed-use development becomes a competitive race across the country, Blackwell said financial modeling has to meet the challenge, so local governments can retain the companies, but also understand the impact of tax incentives that attract industries. While she campaigns, she is working on the Maple Heights budget as well, which involves looking at how tax abatements are impacting the bottom line for her city, and the forecast for the next five years with regular municipal costs still in need of funding, like police forces and fire engines.
“We have to negotiate in a way that keeps us whole,” she said. “We want to encourage investment and development, but not at the risk of having a fiscal crisis that leads us to some kind of designation from the auditor’s office.”
  Frank LaRose 
Secretary of State Frank LaRose’s campaign did not respond to multiple requests for an interview with the Capital Journal.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose. Official photo.
In campaign events and speeches, he has touted his experience as the chief elections officer for the state, and pledged transparency and accountability in the office of auditor.
He told attendees of an event with the Akron Press Club in May that trust “is at an all-time low in institutions of all kinds: the government, the churches, the press, businesses, civic organizations.” He said in some ways the lack of trust is “well-founded.”
LaRose said the leader of the auditor’s office should filter through the “chaotic information ecosystem” that exists in the state and nationally, and “make sure that taxpayers are empowered with accurate information about how their local, county, and state government entities are operating.”
On his campaign website, LaRose released an “accountability and affordability plan” as part of his bid to become the next auditor.
“Ohio families are facing rising property taxes, higher living costs, and government spending that keeps growing,” the 10-point plan states. “Taxpayers deserve more than another audit report gathering dust on a shelf.”
The plan includes “affordability audits” to “examine spending growth against inflation, population changes, and household costs,” along with identifying “unnecessary bureaucracy, excessive administrative expenses, and opportunities to lower costs in state agencies, school districts, and local governments.”
LaRose’s goals also include new dashboards for public spending, using artificial intelligence to “examine government transactions,” creating a program to encourage reports of public corruption called the “Ohio Taxpayer Fraud Bounty Program,” expanding the fraud investigation authority within the auditor’s office, and creating other programs aimed at efficiency, accountability, and investigation of “AI-enabled financial fraud.”
The general election in Ohio is Nov. 3, and early voting ends Nov. 1. Absentee ballots must be received by local boards of elections by Nov. 3. In-person voting on election day begins at 6:30 a.m. and ends at 7:30 p.m.

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye

• Measles in Ohio. The Columbus Dispatch reports, “Measles cases in Ohio nearly 600% higher in 2026 compared to 2025.”
Ohio is experiencing its third measles outbreak of 2026, with cases surging in Southern Ohio. Measles cases in Ohio and nationwide have reached a 35-year high, driven by declining vaccination rates. The vast majority of measles cases in Ohio are among individuals who have not been vaccinated.
• Fracking waste in Ohio drinking water. Rolling Stone reports, “Ohio Denies Evidence of Fracking Waste in Drinking Water. Its Own Records Show Otherwise.”
“In Ohio’s rural southeastern corner, Marietta College geology professor David Jeffrey was among the residents worried that industry activity in America’s booming natural gas region could be polluting their drinking water. That’s “the biggest fear,” he said at an August meeting with top Ohio officials.
When Jeffrey and residents from advocacy groups Buckeye Environmental Network and Washington County for Safe Drinking Water met with Ohio officials, those state officials repeatedly assured residents that despite the up to 1.4 billion gallons of oil and gas wastewater injected in underground wells in their county and across Ohio each year, the state was unaware of any resulting drinking water contamination there…
What officials did not tell the group that day is that five years earlier, the state did receive a call and, on Vendel’s orders, investigated a drinking water well for oil and gas wastewater contaminants in eastern Ohio, roughly 80 miles away from Washington County. Independent experts say the results are consistent with fracking wastewater contamination. Despite that and the water well’s location near two oil and gas wastewater injection wells, ODNR concluded fracking wastewater was not to blame, according to documents DeSmog and Rolling Stone obtained via public records request.
• Healthcare. NBC News reports, “Many with ACA coverage face a new crisis in 2027: Insurers fleeing the market.”
Many Americans are heading into ACA open enrollment with the likelihood of higher premiums and fewer insurance companies to choose from…
Insurers that offer ACA plans are proposing a premium increase of about 15%, on average, for 2027 — the second straight year of double-digit increases, according to an analysis from KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group, that looked at public filings from insurers across all 50 states and Washington, D.C.
At the same time, 11 insurers have announced plans to leave the ACA marketplaces in 2027 in at least some states where they currently offer coverage, according to KFF.
• Trump v. Veterans. NPR reports, “Trump’s VA killed a home loan program. Thousands of veterans are paying the price.”
Thousands of military veterans with VA-backed mortgages have been hit with higher interest rates and monthly payments since last year, when the Trump administration shut down a low-interest program designed to help them.
Among veterans who had their loans modified after a financial hardship, more than 15,000 saw their monthly payments increase by at least $150, according to an NPR investigation that obtained previously unreported data from the Department of Veterans Affairs.
• Retaliation. The Washington Post reports, “She spoke about her husband’s ICE custody death. Now she could face deportation.”
A Maryland woman who spoke publicly about her husband’s death in ICE custody has been placed in deportation proceedings, according to documents shared with The Washington Post.
Veronica Ramirez received media attention this month after her husband, Julian Curo Churata, died in an ICE detention center in Louisiana. Curo Churata, originally from Peru, had lived in the United States for more than a decade before he was detained by immigration officers in June. He died Sept. 29.

title: Democratic governors rally support for Sand in a final push before Election Day
description: Rob Sand speaks to supporters Nov. 1, 2026 at an event in Des Moines, urging them to make a final push in support of his candidacy for governor. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Rob Sand, Democratic candidate for Iowa governor, said Sunday night that whatever his supporters have going on over the next 48 hours leading up to Election Day, it’s “pro[...]
text:
Rob Sand speaks to supporters Nov. 1, 2026 at an event in Des Moines, urging them to make a final push in support of his candidacy for governor. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Rob Sand, Democratic candidate for Iowa governor, said Sunday night that whatever his supporters have going on over the next 48 hours leading up to Election Day, it’s “probably less important” than encouraging people to vote. 
Sand spoke with supporters at an event in Des Moines alongside Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and former Iowa governor and former U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Tom Vilsack on the same day President Donald Trump stopped in Dubuque to support Sand’s opponent, Zach Lahn, and other Republicans on Tuesday’s ticket. 
While encouraging attendees to get out the vote ahead of the election, Sand said they could tell undecided voters that with him in Iowa’s Capitol, it would “force” policymakers to work together by returning the state to a divided government instead of single-party control.
 “We’re on the cusp of returning Iowa to a balanced government, where everything that happens has to be a bill that has bipartisan support,” Sand, the current state auditor, said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sand and Lahn are competing in an open race as Gov. Kim Reynolds is not running for reelection. If Sand wins, he would be the first Democrat in the seat since 2011. He argued a Democratic governor would balance what will likely remain a Republican majority in the state Legislature. 
Sand pointed to Iowa’s history as a state that for many years elected U.S. senators from both parties, that created an independent redistricting commission and initiated a merit-based judicial nomination system.
Former Iowa Gov. Tom Vilsack speaks Nov. 1, 2026 at an event in Des Moines in support of Rob Sand and Democrats on Iowans’ ballots. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“People on the other side right now, they want you to think that we have been a state that’s been about right versus left – no, we have been a state about right versus wrong,” Sand said. “We have been a state about people working together, regardless of partisanship, who recognize that the real divide is not between neighbors who vote differently, but between regular Iowans and the people who have the responsibility to be representing all of us.” 
Beshear, who chairs the Democratic Governors Association and has campaigned in support of Sand in the past, said he and Sand understand that people “aren’t as partisan as the national media wants to tell us they are.” 
He said voters aren’t thinking about elections every day —  they’re thinking about problems related to the roads they drive on, the schools they take their children to or whether or not they feel safe.
“What Rob gets, is when we move the needle on those things, we don’t move a state to the right or the left, we just move it forward,” Beshear said. “We lift everyone up. We leave no one out, and we move the needle in ways that improve Iowa, Kentucky, and the United States of America.” 
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear speaks in support of Rob Sand Nov. 1, 2026 at an event in Des Moines. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Beshear is not the only Democratic governor who has flown in to support Sand. Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly stopped in Iowa in support of Sand’s campaign, and Beshear said the Democratic Governors Association has “been all in” and invested more than $10 million to “get Rob Sand elected.”
Beshear has been governor of Kentucky since 2019, winning reelection in 2023. He was rumored to have been a potential vice president candidate when Kamala Harris ran for president in 2024 and has generated speculation about a 2028 presidential run. 
At the Sunday night event, Beshear asked voters if they were ready to win the U.S. Senate, the U.S. House and the governor’s race. 
“And after we do all that, in 2028 are you ready for a Democratic president?” Beshear shouted above the cheers in the room.
On the eastern side of the state Sunday evening, President Donald Trump supported Iowa’s Republican candidates, including Lahn, during his second visit to the state in as many weeks. 
Iowa has a number of races that election forecasters and some polls indicate could flip congressional majorities in favor of Democrats. The Cook Political Report has listed the race between Sand and Lahn as “lean Democrat.” 
At the event in Dubuque, Trump said Lahn was Iowa’s “only choice” for governor. 
“On election night, Iowa is going to prove that America does not belong to those who hate it,” Trump said before inviting Lahn and U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson on stage. “America belongs to those who love it.”
Before rallying with Sand, Beshear was in Council Bluffs Sunday to support Josh Turek, the Democratic candidate running against Hinson for U.S. Senate. 
Sarah Trone Garriott joined Rob Sand and other Democrats at an event Nov. 1, 2026 in Des Moines. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Iowa Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, who is running against incumbent U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn to represent Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, also rallied with Sand, Beshear and Vilsack on Sunday night. 
Trone Garriott said her goal is to be someone who is “showing up” for Iowans. 
“We need a new governor,” Trone Garriott said. “And we also need to make sure that there is a Legislature that is not going to get in the way of our new governor’s efforts to make life better for our neighbors. And we’ve got to send some people to Washington who are going to be showing up for the people of this state.” 
Vilsack said he was “grateful” and “proud” of the Democrats across the ballot, but that he was “most grateful” for Sand and his work to present a “blueprint for a different politics.” 
The Democrat and former governor said Sand’s campaign has shown that it’s “not the party label at the end of the day, it’s the character of the candidate.” 
“It’s the vision of the candidate that matters, and that leadership involves understanding that when you are the governor of this great state, you are not the governor of a specific party or a specific part of the state, you are governor of all of the state.” 
Encouraging attendees in the final push for the vote, Sand said that democracy is “not a spectator sport.” 
“I don’t know what’s on your to-do list for tomorrow or the day after that … It’s probably less important than winning a new direction for Iowa for literally decades to come,” Sand said.

title: UConn’s big problem (and it’s not Matt Ritter)
description:

text:
Last week the University of Connecticut’s board revealed that it voted not to continue President Radenka Maric’s term as president and to offer an interim presidency to House Speaker Matt Ritter.  
UConn is a great university and no matter whom it chooses as its next president, it will continue to be for some time.  Students will continue to have transformative educational experiences, and athletic teams will continue to win championships.  Under the leadership of President Maric, the university has thrived in most current metrics that matter.  Except for one – the university rankings, particularly in U.S. News and World Report.

Thomas Katsouleas

Rankings are flawed in many ways, but they are nevertheless important.  They affect in the long term the quality of faculty and students and leadership that a university can attract.  USNWR is particularly significant because the largest factor in that ranking is peer rating by other university presidents.  That is, by the people who know most about what is going on in higher education.  
Universities move up or down in perceived and actual quality on seven- to ten-year time scales.  UConn has had five presidents over the past seven years.  That instability has not gone unnoticed by our peers, donors and others.  Over that same period, UConn’s ranking has fallen from the low 20’s to the low 30’s among public institutions.   Long the highest ranked public university in New England, UConn no longer is.  That distinction goes to UMass Amherst by a significant margin now.  At some point, the Board of Trustees, who have made those choices has to take responsibility for their long-term outcomes.  There are many paths forward for UConn but none of them will succeed without significant upgrades to its board and practices.
To reverse the downward trend will require visionary and stable leadership and a board that guides and supports its president in the high-level decisions that affect UConn’s long-term future.  This will not happen without major reforms to the UConn board and the way that it operates.
Improve its training
While UConn’s Board members are well-meaning and talented in their respective fields, they lack training in what it takes to be a successful university board.  
There are time-tested best practices that other boards have learned through formal training by consultants such as the Association of Governing Boards of Universities and Colleges.  
This shortcoming of the UConn board has been noted by UConn’s outside accreditors among others.  However, the UConn board has yet to accept any recommendation to receive training or outside assessment.  Whether the current board continues or not, the governor should insist on this best practice.

Give strategic plans time 
The board needs to give time for whomever it chooses to finish their strategic plans.
Rarely if ever do boards have the expertise to know what it takes to move a great university forward and upward in the competitive landscape of higher education.  They must instead choose a proven leader who does and then give them the room to make it happen.  
Without this longer-term approach, UConn will continue to lose ground as other universities carry out their plans.

Allow shared governance 
A flagship public university is a large and complex ecosystem.  To move it significantly forward requires the collective wisdom and support of many constituencies to align around shared goals.  
To that end, the best universities have a long tradition of shared governance between their boards, administrators and faculty with additional vital input from students, parents, staff, donors and other stakeholders.  
The UConn board’s latest move to offer the presidency to Speaker Ritter by fiat without a public search is a dangerous abandonment of that principle.  Although this has been framed as an interim appointment, I don’t think that anyone believes that the Speaker of the House would resign his post to take a temporary role somewhere.  
It is unlikely for any university to choose the best leader for its future nor for that leader to succeed without the broad input of the university community.

Revisit the Ritter decision 
I hope that the Board of Trustees or the governor will revisit the decision not to allow President Maric to carry out her strategic plans.  The Board’s inability to stick with and support its own choices is doing unquestionable harm to the university and its students.  
If UConn changes leaders again now, yet another promising strategic plan will be left unfulfilled, nascent research initiatives will be left without their most vocal champion and a talented faculty and staff will be left bewildered if not justifiably angered.
If there becomes a need for an interim leader, they should be truly interim to allow for an open and consultative presidential search process.  I also urge the Governor and whatever board he decides to appoint to make the reforms above to bring it in line with best practices. Only in that way will UConn be able to regain its upward arc.
Thomas Katsouleas is a Professor of Electrical Engineering and Physics and served as the President of the University of Connecticut from August 1, 2019, through June 30, 2021.

text:
Every year, Americans throw away more than 100 million gallons of paint. 
Read that number again and let it sit for a moment. One hundred million gallons. That is enough to fill roughly 150 Olympic swimming pools. And none of it simply disappears.
Instead, it gets poured down drains, tossed into trash cans, and dumped at the curb. From there, it steadily seeps into the soil and, ultimately, into the groundwater that families drink. Research has shown that a single gallon of paint can contaminate up to 250,000 gallons of water. Frankly, we are poisoning our own wells one brushstroke at a time, and most of us never give it a second thought.
I have spent the past 16 years proving there is a better way. In 2010, I founded Global Paint for Charity with a deliberately simple idea. Rescue the paint America throws away, and put it to work where it is needed most. Since then, we have recovered more than 5 million gallons of surplus paint. We have delivered it across 44 countries and underserved communities here at home. And along the way, we have improved more than 15 million lives.
Those numbers, however, only tell half the story. The other half is quieter and, honestly, more moving. Over the years, more than 625,000 volunteer hours have powered this work. Roughly 70 percent of the paint we recover goes to high-need regions around the world, while the remaining 30 percent stays here, donated free to domestic nonprofits, veterans, and families rebuilding their neighborhoods.
Time and again, I have watched what happens when that paint arrives. Take a broken-down classroom in a poor village, for example. The walls go from gray to bright almost overnight. Gradually, the girls studying inside start earning better grades. They show up to school more often. More of them graduate. Meanwhile, their teachers, the same ones who had nearly given up, suddenly feel proud to teach again. Remarkably, a single gallon of paint sets all of this in motion at once. It protects the earth, creates good-paying jobs, saves lives, helps other charities stretch further, and keeps small businesses alive.
On October 1, Connecticut gave this idea the force of law. The state became the first in America to expand its paint stewardship program to aerosol paints, the pressurized spray cans piling up in garages and basements everywhere (Connecticut General Assembly, 2026). Under the new law, every producer selling paint in Connecticut must join the stewardship program and pay its fair share. If a company refuses to participate, its products cannot be sold in the state. It is, quite simply, producer responsibility with teeth.
This matters enormously, and for good reason. Paint is one of the largest hazardous waste streams coming out of American homes. About 10 percent of the roughly 2 billion gallons sold each year goes unused, and latex paint alone makes up nearly 40 percent of hazardous household waste. For years, the handful of states with stewardship programs covered only architectural paint, the gallons in cans. Aerosols were left out, even though they are pressurized, chemical-filled, and nearly impossible to dispose of safely. Connecticut just closed that gap, and consequently it has set the national precedent.
And yet collecting paint is only half the battle. Here is the uncomfortable truth about most stewardship programs today. They are built to collect and recycle, which is genuinely important. But they stop there. They do not get the recovered paint into the hands of the communities that desperately need it. In other words, we have built a system that keeps paint out of landfills but leaves it sitting in warehouses, while millions of families who cannot afford a single gallon watch from the sidelines. The World Health Organization estimates that 80 percent of homes in underserved areas remain unpainted, and 170 million children have never seen a painted classroom. Clearly, collection without redistribution is an unfinished job.
That is precisely why I designed the Nevada Paint Recycling and Community Care Act, known as the NPRCCA. It is the policy proposal at the heart of my doctoral research at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and in my view it is the best option America has for leftover paint. The reason is straightforward. The NPRCCA does what existing programs do not. It combines collection, recycling, and redistribution into a single framework. 
The proposal calls for a one-time investment of 5 to 10 million dollars, while the status quo already burdens taxpayers with more than 10 million dollars every single year in hazardous waste costs. To put it bluntly, cleaning up contaminated groundwater can cost between 1.7 and 5 million dollars for every 1,000 gallons of water, according to the EPA. Prevention is not merely kinder. It is dramatically cheaper. Recovered paint would flow directly to schools, affordable housing, veteran housing, and neighborhood projects, both statewide and around the world. In short, the act treats paint as what it truly is. Not trash, but a resource.
So here is my call, plain and simple. To state legislators: copy Connecticut, and then go one step further. Add redistribution the way the Nevada law does, so recovered paint reaches people instead of sitting in warehouses. To the paint industry: stewardship is not punishment. It is partnership, and frankly the companies that step up now will be the ones communities remember. To federal policymakers: the states are leading because Washington has not. A national framework would finish the job Connecticut started.
Sixteen years ago, I started with one idea: waste, turned into hope. On October 1, Connecticut turned that idea into law for every kind of paint. The NPRCCA shows how to carry it the rest of the way. The rest of America should follow.

Rony Delgarde is the founder and CEO of Global Paint for Charity and the author of How to PAINT Change.

text:
New Haven is a port town and, since its inception, has had a long and rich history of its citizens opening the doors of their private properties to travelers, explorers, and wanderers. Its doors have been faithfully open and welcoming to those who seek shelter — not just homeowners, but housing providers as well.
A famous housing provider was William Lanson, an African American engineer, builder, and leader in New Haven. He achieved projects too difficult for others, namely extending New Haven’s Long Wharf, the longest in the country at that time.
He owned multiple rental houses and accommodated temporary guests. Similarly to Airbnbs today, he provided accommodations to people who faced discrimination elsewhere, lacked the credentials to get leases, could not afford hotels, or needed accommodations that hotels could not provide.
But Lanson was accused of disorderly conduct, sexual impropriety, and other alleged offenses at his lodging properties. A New Haven police officer, hostile newspaper publishers, and segments of the city’s white political and business establishment turned against him.
The properties where Lanson provided housing were in the Wooster neighborhood. Over time, the area had become desirable real estate, and there was a pressing need for housing workers from the factories nearby.
New Haven turned against Lanson. The Columbian Register portrayed Lanson as leading an establishment associated with vice, mockingly characterizing his operation as an “African college” of criminality. Other New Haven publications also helped amplify opposition to Lanson.
He was subjected to repeated police surveillance, prosecution, arrests, and public hostility. Officer Jesse Knevals repeatedly investigated Lanson’s lodging properties, keeping them under surveillance for months. Historian Stacey Close reported in an April 2026 lecture that Knevals testified he had observed no improper conduct in houses owned by Lanson, despite the sustained investigations.
In the end, Lanson was ruined. He was jailed five times in six years on petty charges and spent 450 days in jail. He lost everything. In 1851, he died in the almshouse in his 70s.
Years later, in 2020, New Haven formally acknowledged its mistreatment of William Lanson. On September 26, Mayor Justin Elicker publicly apologized for the historical discrimination and false accusations against him, offered a posthumous pardon for falsely brought municipal charges, and declared September 26 William Lanson Day. A seven-foot bronze statue honoring him was unveiled in New Haven.
Now, fast-forward six years to 2026. During this same time of year, under Mayor Elicker’s watch, an ordinance was proposed to restrict the ability of housing providers to offer short-term rentals. Ordinance OR-2026-0039 was formally submitted on October 5. On October 23 the Board of Alders Legislation Committee advanced the measure to the full board for a vote in November. 
Particularly poignant is that one of the alders that presented the ordinance is Mandy Martinelli, representing the very same Wooster neighborhood where Lanson provided lodging so many years ago.
The persecution Lanson endured must not be diminished. His story should make us examine how readily a city can portray housing providers and their guests as threats while overlooking the people they serve.
The city cannot undo what happened to Lanson. But an apology should be more than a ceremony and a statue. It should change how we examine accusations, whose voices we listen to, and whether we recognize the community value of opening doors to people who have few other options.
What would the mayor who apologized to William Lanson say to a housing provider offering similar accommodations today? Would that provider be honored for opening doors, or be told to close them?
In the spirit of Halloween, will the ghosts of New Haven’s past remind us to examine the decisions we make today? Honoring our history should mean carrying its lessons forward, including fairness toward those who open their doors to others.
If passed, this will negatively affect thousands of people – immigrants, displaced persons, and patients annually — individuals who can only be helped by the service the city is trying to ban.
Local businesses stand to lose millions in annual income. Thousands of workers that support local businesses will also suffer. That figure does not capture the full network of people supported by short-term rentals, including maintenance workers, cleaners, greeters, local soap makers, artists, and other small producers and service providers.
Contact your alder and urge opposition to ordinance OR-2026-0039 as written. Ask for an approach that addresses problem properties while allowing responsible local housing providers to continue serving our community.
Naomi Freeman lives in New Haven.

title: President Donald Trump doubles down on bid to lift Roger Marshall’s campaign with Kansas rally

text:
President Donald Trump speaks at a Nov. 1, 2026, rally in Salina, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)SALINA — President Donald Trump slotted Kansas into his final midterm campaign stop Sunday to make one more swing at salvaging the reelection campaign of U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall.
Trump brought Air Force One to the tarmac in Salina, a community of 46,000 people known for hosting the world’s largest frozen pizza plant, as a follow-up to his MAGA celebration in October at Park City. The president’s road show reboot in Kansas was designed to reinforce his support for Marshall, a Republican displaying unblemished loyalty to Trump. The senator’s reelection campaign also received in-person boosts from Vice President JD Vance, who also came to Kansas twice, and a roster of Trump administration officials dispatched to the heartland.
“Just two days from now, the people of Kansas are going to reelect Roger Marshall to the United States Senate,” Trump said. “I had to come here to make sure that Roger got it. One of the most respected people in Washington. I didn’t want to take a chance.”
The president said he managed 30 rallies in 32 days, and decided to wrap up his national tour in central Kansas.
“I’ve done it for one simple reason. To stop America-hating communists and jihadists from taking over the United States government,” he said. “The Democratic Party is dominated by the most extreme and dangerous radicals in American history. They’re openly promising to abolish your borders and let millions and millions of Third World migrants ransack, rape and plunder your communities.”

“They want to steal your wealth and give it to fraudsters,” he added. “They want to raise your taxes by trillions and trillions of dollars. They want to defund your police, abolish oil and gas. Wipe out your savings. Bankrupt your families. Take away your guns.”
Trump called off a Saturday rally in Salina after expressing confidence in Marshall’s reelection prospects, but decided to set up Sunday’s outdoor gathering after polling indicated Democrat Adam Hamilton held an advantage over Marshall.
Kansas voters have declined to elect a Democrat to the U.S. Senate for nearly a century. Marshall’s struggle might be puzzling to those aware of the overwhelming support Kansa voters have given to his predecessors. Republican U.S. Sens. Pat Roberts, Nancy Kassebaum and Jerry Moran won reelection campaigns in the double digits. In 2014, Roberts won by 10 points, his narrowest victory. Kassebaum won reelection by 47 and 54 points. Moran’s margin of victory never fell below 30 points.
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, speaks Nov. 1, 2026, during a campaign rally in Salina featuring the second recent appearance in Kansas of President Donald Trump. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
An opening for Hamilton to enter elective politics was fashioned by Trump’s sagging approval rating and Marshall’s affinity for the president’s policies, programs and pronouncements. Hamilton, founder of a 24,000-member United Methodist church in the Kansas City metro, came along during a campaign cycle in which Kansas voters were anxious about the surging cost of living and angry about trade disruptions created by Trump that undercut farmers and ranchers.
The unexpectedly competitive U.S. Senate contest put Kansas on the national radar as Democrats sought to regain control of Congress from Republicans.
“I want to say a big thank you to everyone who’s been praying for us,” Marshall said. “I have a few people say, ‘Look, I’m just so mad. I’m mad at Washington. I’m just not going to vote.’ Your anger doesn’t count unless it’s at the ballot box. I believe its a God-given responsibility to vote. On Sundays we pray, but on Tuesday we vote.”
Marshall, who initially tied his campaign to advocacy for federal tax cuts, the immigration crackdown and investments in the military, told more than 2,000 people at the rally that Hamilton was too liberal for Kansans. The senator said Marshall mishandled a church camp abuse case in 2005, was in the pocket of Senate Democratic leaders and was fond of environmental reforms in the proposed Green New Deal.
He urged Republicans to persuade friends and relatives to cast a vote for him in Tuesday’s election because placing leadership of the U.S. Senate in the hands of Democrats would be a mistake.
“Your vote matters,” Marshall said. “Every vote matters. Don’t let anybody tell you it’s too small to count.”
Before Trump left the stage, he invited Marshall back on.
“This may be your last rally until your next reelection victory in a couple of years,” Marshall told the president.
A girl awaits President Donald Trump’s arrival Nov. 1, 2026, in Salina, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
In 2020, Marshall won his first campaign for U.S. Senate by 11.4 percentage points over Democrat Barbara Bollier. Trump, who carried Kansas in three presidential elections, carried the state in 2024 by 16.1 points.
Marshall, a former Great Bend physician, has been dogged by reports that his attorney filed lawsuits against 700 patients for unpaid bills, which resulted in the arrest of more than 80 Kansans. In response to attack ads crafted to help Hamilton, Marshall argued his debt-collection tactics were common practice and that he provided free healthcare to many patients during his career. In addition, opponents of Marshall emphasized the senator voted against release of U.S. Department of Justice documents tied to investigation of convicted child trafficker Jeffrey Epstein.
In contrast to large-format rallies favored by Trump, Hamilton worked Sunday to close out his campaign with a 20-city statewide tour based on the idea of bringing more civility and bipartisanship to national politics. While speaking this weekend to volunteers in Olathe and Kansas City, Kansas, Hamilton said voters wanted representatives in Washington, D.C., to focus on lowering consumer costs, ending the U.S. war in Iran, expanding healthcare access and rooting out government corruption.
“Our voice matters,” Hamilton said. “And now, with the election just around the corner, it’s important that we keep doing the work on the ground, talking to our neighbors, and showing up for each other to fix our broken politics.”
Marshall’s allies have accused Hamilton of improperly responding to allegations that a church volunteer groped children at a youth camp sponsored by the Church of the Resurrection. An investigation by church staff in 2005 was inconclusive, Hamilton said, but church officials shared information about the volunteer with police in 2006. Hamilton said he should have contacted authorities when the claims first surfaced.
Hamilton released a video asking for the support of Kansans who previously voted for Trump, arguing that Kansas needed a “senator for all Kansans, no matter their party.”
Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, who is nearing the end of her second term as governor, said in a video that Hamilton offered commonsense, bipartisan leadership. Kelly said Marshall’s decision to reside in Florida was contrary to what Kansans expect of their political leaders. She said Kansas needed a “frequent fighter in the U.S. Senate, not a frequent flyer to Florida.”
“I’m so proud to be a Kansan,” Kelly said. “I’ve loved living here for 40 years. Roger Marshall, on the other hand, loves living somewhere else. Ten days after become senator, Roger Marshall moved from Kansas into his million-dollar house in Florida, complete with his own boat dock. Then he fleeced taxpayers by having them pay for his flights to his new home.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Two days out from Election Day, Trump rallies for Iowa Republicans in Dubuque
description: President Donald Trump rallied with Iowa Republicans at the Five Flags Center in Dubuque Nov. 1, 2026, two days before Election Day. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)DUBUQUE — President Donald Trump urged Iowans to vote for Republicans in the midterms during a Dubuque rally Sunday, telling voters Democratic majorities would reverse work done by h[...]
text:
President Donald Trump rallied with Iowa Republicans at the Five Flags Center in Dubuque Nov. 1, 2026, two days before Election Day. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)DUBUQUE — President Donald Trump urged Iowans to vote for Republicans in the midterms during a Dubuque rally Sunday, telling voters Democratic majorities would reverse work done by his administration to lower costs and would usher in “socialism.”
“On election night, Iowa is going to prove that America does not belong to those who hate it, America belongs to those who love it,” he said.
His speech at the Five Flags Center two days before Election Day, supporting Iowa Republican candidates, is the second time the president has been to Iowa in the weeks leading up to the 2026 midterm elections. The two Iowa events come as several of the state’s races are expected to be much more competitive in 2026 than in previous election cycles — and could play a vital role in determining control of both the U.S. House and Senate.
The president’s visit comes as election forecasters and some polls show Republicans at risk of losing their congressional majorities. Trump told the crowd to unite behind GOP candidates in the upcoming election or risk allowing “extremists” to take control.
“In state after state, the Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous radicals in American history,” Trump said. “They openly are promising to abolish your borders and let millions of third-world migrants ransack, rape, and plunder your communities. They want to steal your wealth and give it to fraudsters, thieves, and stupid people like that.”
In addition to speaking about support he has provided for Iowa in office such as $12 billion in subsidies for farmers, he repeated a campaign pitch that if Republicans win both chambers of Congress, he would give $5,000 to every American, which he said was possible because the country was “taking in massive amounts (of) money through tariffs and record-setting economic success.” Even if Republicans win both chambers, there is not a guarantee that the appropriations measure would be approved by federal lawmakers.
“The Democrats love to say, ‘Well, he’ll never pull that off.’ They would say that about me, and then I pulled everything off,” Trump said.
Trump spoke in support of U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, saying if she is elected to the U.S. Senate, “we will make year-round E-15 permanent” while emphasizing laws passed over the last two years by the Republican-led Congress like the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act which he said delivered “the largest tax cuts in American history, including no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, and no tax on social security tax.”
Hinson, who currently represents Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District, is running against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for the open U.S. Senate seat currently represented by Republican Sen. Joni Ernst.
He also made a remark that he said might be “inappropriate” about her being “little bit heavier” when they first met — commenting on his own weight that he had “put on a couple of pounds.” 
Trump was interrupted by a protester who was escorted out of the event, but finished the story, saying, “Ashley knew the importance of what this was, and how important it was, and boy … She went on a regimen. She put herself in shape. She’s in perfect shape … and she did that for you.”
Trump says Iowa caucuses ‘go to the back of the pack’ if GOP loses; RPI says he was joking
He also spoke about his fondness for Iowa and being “proud” to win Iowa in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 elections — and said because of his efforts, the Iowa GOP caucuses are still leading the presidential nominating cycle while national Democrats stripped Iowa of its “first in the nation” status.
“They wanted to move you to the back of the pack. I said, ‘We’re not moving Iowa anywhere,'” Trump said. But if Republicans lose in 2026, Trump said, “I won’t have any control,” and he would not have the power to keep the Iowa Republican caucuses first.
“I don’t want to use this in any way that’s inappropriate,” Trump said. “But frankly, if we don’t win, you go into the back of the pack. If we do win, you stay first in the nation. Now, that sounds like a little tricky wording. It’s not tricky at all. You’re going to be first in the nation, because we’re going to win.”
A spokesperson for the Republican Party of Iowa said Trump’s statement was an “obvious” joke, and referenced his October speech in Sioux City where he said, “as long as I’m around in any capacity, you’re going to be number one. … I’m going to have a lot of power when I leave, and I’m going to keep you number one. It doesn’t matter.”
The Republican National Committee already approved Iowa kicking off the party’s national presidential nominating cycle for 2028, followed by the New Hampshire primary.
Trump has regularly spoken about how he has advocated for Iowa to lead the presidential nominating calendar, and Iowa has been recognized by Trump during some national Republican processes. Iowa GOP Chairman Jeff Kaufmann delivered Trump’s nominating speech at the 2024 Republican National Convention, which he said was a nod from the president on the state’s prominent role in his nomination. 
Trump continues criticism of out-of-state Democrats
When Trump held a rally in Sioux City, he urged GOP voters to go to the polls while criticizing Democrats in other states, including U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota. In Dubuque, he brought up Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his primary opponent, Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers earlier Sunday. Several Democratic officials and leaders have denounced Stevens’ endorsement and called for continued support of Al-Sayed in the election.
“I don’t know Haley,” Trump said. “I’ve never met Haley, but Haley said what few people are willing to say. … I’d love her to join the Republican Party. Actually, I think it could happen. But she showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the great people of Michigan, and that’s another important election for us. We don’t want to have a jihadist.”
He repeated several anti-Muslim remarks about El-Sayed, calling the candidate “Mohammad,” and saying, “going to have to get a special metal detector for Abdul” in the U.S. Capitol if he is elected. El-Sayed has denied ties to terrorist or extremist groups.
Full Iowa GOP delegation joins Trump for second rally
While Hinson, gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn, and congressional candidates Joe Mitchell and Chris McGowan rallied with Trump in both Sioux City and Dubuque, incumbent GOP U.S. Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn  joined only for the second rally. Both Miller-Meeks’ race in Iowa’s 1st District and Nunn’s race in the 3rd District are rated “leans Democrat” by Cook Political Report.
While the candidates in the competitive districts both told the crowd their opponents were “radical” Democrats, they presented themselves as independent and bipartisan voices rather than staunch conservatives.
U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn called for Iowans to reelect him to Congress as he spoke before President Donald Trump at the Five Flags Center in Dubuque Nov. 1, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Nunn said Iowa’s 3rd District race “will decide whether we have a majority in Congress who stands with the president, who works with the president, and candidly, who will hold the president accountable in a pragmatic way.”
Nunn and Miller-Meeks both broke ranks with Republicans and voted in favor of a war powers resolution in September that would require congressional approval for Trump to continue his war in Iran — though both had voted against similar measures in the past.
Neither of the representatives mentioned this vote at the rally, but Nunn brought up other instances where he pushed back on Trump to advocate for Iowans — and was able to find a compromise. He cited his support for year-round E-15 and calling for the suspension of Trump’s initiative to allow more foreign beef into the country.
Trump described Miller-Meeks as someone who “works so hard, and she’s really become a friend,” and Nunn as “a great guy, a great warrior.”
The Dubuque visit was one of two planned trips to Iowa before the election, but it came after some rescheduling. The president and Republican National Committee announced Thursday the rallies in Iowa and Kansas were canceled, stating Trump instead would hold telerallies. The next day, Friday, Trump announced the two rallies were back on.
Protesters lined the streets outside the entrance to the Five Flags Center in Dubuque Nov. 1, 2026 ahead of President Donald Trump’s rally. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Protesters lined the streets outside the Five Flags Convention center, holding signs calling for Trump’s impeachment, an end to the U.S.-Iran war, and highlighting the president’s relationship with Florida financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. As Hinson spoke, she asked the crowd to stand and chant “USA” for the protesters outside to hear.
She called the Dubuque rally a “real full circle moment” for her in the U.S. Senate campaign, reflecting on her first run for Congress in 2020 when she challenged former U.S. Rep. Abby Finkenauer to represent northeast Iowa.
“It was six years ago today, November 1 of 2020, that we were right here in Dubuque County rallying for President Trump and to make sure we could flip this congressional seat from blue to red,” Hinson said. “And you know what we did? We got that done in 2020, didn’t we? So we cannot let the Democrats win here in Iowa.”
She claimed U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and affiliated Democratic groups were spending significant money to support her opponent, Turek, because “Chuck Schumer knows that his path to a Democrat majority in the United States Senate runs right through Iowa” — even though, Hinson said, “Chuck Schumer could care less about Iowa … All he wants is the power.”
Outside spending has spiked in Iowa as the election nears — according to an Open Secrets analysis, outside groups had spent $59.86 million supporting Turek and $51.67 million supporting Hinson as of the Federal Election Commission report period ending Oct. 13. The largest spenders in the race during the period were $35.53 million coming from the Senate GOP-aligned SLF PAC and $28.27 million coming from the WinSenate, a Democratic super PAC.
Democrats criticize Hinson’s record, lack of public town halls
Pam Jochum, a former state lawmaker from Dubuque who served as Senate minority leader, and other Democrats who live in the 2nd Congressional District, criticized the Republican candidate’s time in office, saying she does not “listen to us and our concerns” in the district, and had not held public town halls since announcing her Senate campaign. Jochum also said Hinson’s voting record on issues like the “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act making cuts to Medicaid, as well as not voting to restrict Trump’s tariff policies or the war in Iran, shows she does not support Iowans’ best interests.
“She has been a rubber stamp for Trump, end of story,” Jochum said. “… She is responsible with her votes for all of the costs that we’re seeing rising, whether its housing or healthcare or diesel or gas, it doesn’t matter. She has to take responsibility and be held accountable for what she has done for the past six years.”
After speaking in Iowa, Trump headed to a rally in Salina, Kansas, another state hosting a crucial U.S. Senate race between incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton.

title: ‘Nearly erased’ Black patriots of the Revolution now enshrined at State House
