text:
Advance voting was underway Oct. 26, 2026, at the Lyon County Courthouse in Emporia. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)In just 48 hours, Kansans will have a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to shape history.
The opportunity is unexpected — and unexpectedly urgent.
I was thinking about that urgency the other day when I was part of a television panel discussion about politics at a public television station in Kansas. The set was quaint, as you might expect, and on a side table next to the host was a miniature wooden globe in a square stand. I wanted to pick up that globe, hold it to the camera and say we must meet the moment because this is what’s at stake.
I didn’t, but in my mind, I started writing this column.
This year’s midterm election has been called a “unicorn” for red America by a major political analyst. In Kansas, the surprisingly competitive U.S. Senate race has drawn the attention of the nation. For many, the race is a referendum on what may be the most corrupt administration in American history — and a repudiation of the phalanx of legislative quislings that keeps it in power.
While pundits have treated the dead-heat between incumbent Roger Marshall and challenger Adam Hamilton as a political singularity — after all, no Kansas Democrat has been elected to the U.S. Senate in nearly a century — the close race isn’t being held in a vacuum. It’s a sign of the growing resistance to authoritarianism, and not just in America.
In the past week, a student-led movement against corruption toppled 14 years of a repressive regime in Serbia. In Brazil, the beleaguered incumbent made a surprising political comeback against the far-right candidate who was expected to win. What happens in Europe or South America isn’t a prediction of what will happen here, but it is a semaphore of change.
We are witness to a historic political realignment in America. It’s difficult to see the outlines while being tossed about in the middle of it, but it appears to be on the same order that shook the nation over slavery in the 1850s or the Civil Rights movement of the mid-20th century. Every election is a throw of the dice, but even if the midterms don’t reshape the balance of legislative power — and two days out there is reason to believe it will — neither party will emerge from the fray unchanged. The cult of Trump is collapsing, leaving Republicans with empty sails and no rudder, while Democrats are learning again how to navigate by the brightest and most constant stars.
The ancient stain of slavery and the fight for equality are still problems Americans struggle with today. But if we do not put out the immediate fire in the kitchen of democracy, there may be no house left standing in which to debate anything other than the depth of our misery.
The American experiment, battered these last two years by a regime that has thrown away the hard-won lessons of two centuries and surrendered its humanity for a few crypto-coins to rub together, may yet be renewed.
We stand at the threshold of that renewal.
Kansas has oft been the wheel upon which American history has turned, beginning with its admission to the union as a free state in 1861, on the eve of the Civil War. It also produced one of our better presidents, Dwight D. Eisenhower, who was ranked fifth best by a C-SPAN survey of historians in 2021.
Eisenhower, whose hometown was Abilene, was the American general who commanded Allied forces in Europe during World War II. He oversaw the invasion of Normandy in 1944, a bloody but necessary assault that eventually broke the Nazi stranglehold on Europe.
In 1952, as the Republican nominee, Eisenhower was elected president. During his inauguration he offered a civic prayer for the nation. I’m not ordinarily a fan of public prayers, but my religion is democracy and our best hopes for the future are often supplications to a higher power within ourselves.
Eisenhower prayed for the ability to discern right from wrong, to be guided by the law of the land, and for the compassion to work for all Americans, regardless of “station, race or calling.”
When Eisenhower gave his farewell address in 1961, after two terms as president, it signaled the Sunflower State’s waning influence on national politics, Sens. Bob Dole and Nancy Kassebaum excepted.
You can scarcely read a history of Kansas without stumbling over the famous dictum by small-town newspaper editor William Allen White that, “When anything is going to happen in this country, it happens first in Kansas.” White, writing in 1922, was referring to movements including abolitionism, prohibition and populism.
“These things come popping out of Kansas like bats out of hell. Sooner or later other states take up these things,” he wrote.
The modern reader stumbles over this quote not only because it is now a century out of date, but was out of date just 20 years after White wrote it. As H. Edward Flentje points out in “Reform and Reaction: The Arc of Kansas Politics,” White wrote in his 1940s autobiography that his once-progressive Republican Party had become “chastened, weary, and disillusioned.”
By 1983, syndicated columnists Neal R. Peirce and Jerry Hagstrom had hammered a nail into the coffin of Kansas politics in their book, “The Story of America: Inside the Fifty States Today.” They described the Sunflower State as “scarcely the place where things happen ‘first.’ Indeed, nowhere on the American continent can the eclipse of a region or a state as a vital force — a focal point of creative change or exemplar of national life — be felt so strongly and poignantly as in Kansas.”
It has been a long time since any bats have popped.
This is not to say that Kansas is a hellish state. The recently released Kansas Speaks public opinion survey indicates that 77% of respondents believe the state is a good to excellent place to live. However, a deeper question about whether the state was on the right track resulted in a deep division, with 41% saying the state was on the “wrong track” compared with 37% of right trackers. The remaining 22% said they didn’t know.
The Peirce-Hagstrom obituary for Kansas influence is now 43 years old, and most Kansans weren’t even born when it was penned. The median age for the state is 37, according to the Kansas State Data Center at the University of Kansas. That means that our median-age Kansas voter has only been eligible to cast a ballot since 2007.
Their first presidential election would have been a year later, and if they voted for Democrat Barack Obama — as did 514,000 Kansans, 42% of the state total — their vote didn’t matter because of the winner-take-all Electoral College system. All of the state’s six Electoral College votes went to Republican nominee John McCain. That’s the way it has been for more than six decades, because the last time Kansas went for a Democrat for president was in 1964, with Lyndon B. Johnson.
For the U.S. Senate, the streak is even longer.
If you’ve paid even cursory attention, you’ve probably heard that when it comes to the Senate, Kansas Democrats have the longest political drought in American history. That’s one of the reasons that being a Democrat or an independent in Kansas can feel like being a small blue bubble tossed about on an ocean of red.
With state politics, it’s different.
Kansas is not averse to letting a Democrat take a turn at being governor, and three of those Democrats have been women, including the term-limited outgoing governor, Laura Kelly. It’s also historically different for the 3rd District of eastern Kansas, which encompasses much of the Kansas City metro area, where incumbent Democrat Sharice Davids is seeking her fifth term.
If you live in other parts of the state, voting for Democrats running for national office can seem futile. Among the state’s 2 million registered voters, 44% are registered Republicans and just 26% are Democrats, according to the Kansas Secretary of State.
But not all voters have declared a party, and about 29% are unaffiliated. Another 1% or so identify with small parties.
The more you look, the less red the state becomes.
Especially now.
The question that has been repeated over the last two years is this: When will Americans have had enough?
We may have found the limit.
The most distinctive feature of this satiety is anger.
There are plenty of targets at hand for this fury, from the price of a gallon of unleaded gasoline ($4.08 on Interstate 35 as I write) to the rising cost of food at the local grocery store. A roast for family dinner now costs $20. Whether you’re filling up the car or trying to put a meal on the table, these prices are being driven up by the ill-advised war with Iran, now in its eighth month. Things may get worse soon, because the Trump administration has warned Gulf States to prepare for a major U.S. offensive after the midterms. So far, the war has cost the U.S. government $47 billion, imposed death and human suffering on both sides, and wasted what remained of America’s global influence.
But voter anger is rooted in more than senseless war and rising prices.
There is a longing for the competence and decency that once guided America. If you are the aforementioned Kansan of median age, then you may remember that first vote you cast, in the 2008 presidential election. Never mind who you voted for. Think for a moment about the character of the candidates. Both Obama and McCain were motivated by a clearly articulated set of values. Even if you didn’t agree with them, you could understand them. Both men shared an essential decency, even though their backgrounds could hardly have been more different.
Remember how, a month before the election, McCain defended Obama as a “decent family man, citizen” when a voter at a political town hall in Minnesota brought up a worn conspiracy theory. Can you imagine that same kind of decency in national politics today from the Trump-addled Republican Party?
I long for the days of McCain. I think many of us do.
In 1961, Eisenhower gave his farewell address to the nation, and that speech is remembered today for his warning against establishing a “military industrial complex.” But the fullness of his thoughts bear repeating now.
Americans, Eisenhower said, expect their president and Congress “to find essential agreement on issues of great moment, the wise resolution of which will better shape the future of the nation.” The nation’s prestige depends not only on riches and military strength, but on how that power is used in the interests of world peace and humanity.
“As we peer into society’s future,” he said, “we — you and I, and our government — must avoid the impulse to live only for today, plundering, for our own ease and convenience, the precious resources of tomorrow. We cannot mortgage the material assets of our grandchildren without risking the loss also of their political and spiritual heritage. We want democracy to survive for all generations to come, not to become the insolvent phantom of tomorrow.”
Three days later, Democrat John F. Kennedy was sworn into office.
In that C-SPAN survey I mentioned earlier, Kennedy comes in eighth. The first spot is held by Abraham Lincoln. Trump is near the bottom, at No. 41, just above Pierce, Johnson and Buchanan. But you have to remember the survey was conducted just after Trump’s first term.
In 2024’s Presidential Greatness Project, a survey of presidential scholars, Trump came in dead last.
Trump came to Kansas on Oct. 19 in a panicky rescue. A second trip, a Halloween rally planned for Salina, was canceled and then rescheduled for Sunday.
In the Park City visit nearly two weeks ago, in a speech laden with racist tropes and vulgar language, Trump declared: “When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to ​do to America.”
It’s too bad that Eisenhower isn’t around to give Trump a history lesson about burning steeples and raging fires in France.
In February, Pete Hegseth — Trump’s secretary of defense — attempted to move the historic globe Eisenhower used during the invasion of Normandy. Hegseth wanted it for his office, but in his haste some unskilled workers dropped the globe and broke it, according to the Washington Post, smashing Antarctica and detaching it from the mounting ring that allowed it to rotate.
It is a metaphor for the Trump administration’s misuse of American power.
That Kansas is among the few states that will decide control of the U.S. Senate is reason to hope for the future, no matter the outcome of the current contest. There are signs of a return to the progressive ideals that make human freedom and dignity possible.
There may be strife to come, but that Kansas is again at the forefront of national politics is the answer to a civic prayer whispered by many conscientious and decent individuals of both parties, or of none, for the last two years.
What will the world be after Tuesday?
It’s up to us to help decide.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

text:
“Hello, darkness, my old friend, I’ve come to talk with you again”

Simon & Garfunkel 1964

Yes, daylight savings time is gone again… sooner this year than normal as November 1  is the earliest date for the change allowed by law.  
They say we’ve “gained an hour,” but it sure doesn’t feel like that.  And with the shift of clocks back an hour, we’re going to see ever-earlier sunsets and darkness… as early as 4:45 p.m. this week and 4:21 p.m. by early December. 



That means our evening commutes will be in the dark, presenting new dangers.
A 2025 study in the Journal of Safety Research found fatal pedestrian and cyclist crashes rose 13 percent after the fall time change.  And researchers at Carnegie Mellon say the pedestrian death risk at 6 p.m. in November is 11 times higher than at the same hour in April.
It’s also rutting season for deer, and about three-quarters of deer crashes with cars happen outside daylight.  Connecticut had 417 such incidents from October to December 2023.  Nothing ruins a car quite like hitting 200 pounds of amorous venison.
And don’t even get me started on the “jetlag” we all feel adjusting to the clocks this week.  And that clock on your dashboard… how long will it still think it’s daylight savings time?
As for auto accidents involving other cars, reviewing University of Connecticut data from 2020 to 2024, Connecticut crashes in the 5 p.m. hour were 35% higher in November than October.  Pedestrian crashes in that hour were up 147%!
If you must walk at night, wear white.  Or better yet, a reflectorized vest so drivers can see, and hopefully, not hit you.
For senior citizens, night driving always presents problems.  It’s both biological and psychological.
By age 60, our eyes need three times as much light as they did at age 20, because pupils shrink and don’t open as wide in the dark. A 60-year-old’s eyes also take more than twice as long as a teenager’s to adjust from light to darkness.
Seniors already reluctant to drive at night are now less likely to go out for dinner or evening events if they don’t feel safe on the roads.  You may think of the “early bird special” as a dining bargain.  Seniors think of it more like a curfew.
One of the biggest problems for drivers of any age, as I wrote about last year, is the glare of oncoming headlights.  There are several reasons that headlights appear so bright. 
The first is that the headlights may not be properly aligned, aiming too high, right into your eyes.  And with more vehicles riding higher from the road (think SUVs and trucks), their headlights shine more directly into oncoming traffic.
Most problematic are the new kinds of headlights.  The older incandescent (yellowish) lightbulbs are being replaced by LED or xenon lights, which are blue-white and more glaring to your eyes.
Oncoming headlights, especially the bluish ones, cause the pupils in your eyes to constrict rapidly, temporarily blinding you until the oncoming vehicle passes and your eyes adjust.
What can you do to stay safe? 
When bright lights come at you, don’t look into the oncoming beam.  Instead, look to the right edge line of the roadway (a.k.a. the “fog line”).  Flip your rear-view mirror to its night setting, or use an auto-dimming mirror.   Most of all, slow down!  Being blinded on darkened roads, especially if they are coated with wet slippery leaves, is dangerous.
So hang in there, fellow motorists.  It’s only about 130 days (and long nights) ‘til we change the clocks again.

(Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Millions of Florida residents who purchase their insurance policies on healthcare.gov can be[...]
text:
Open enrollment for Affordable Care Act insurance plans begins Sunday through Dec. 15 for coverage that takes effect at the start of next year. For policies that take effect Feb. 1, 2027, open enrollment is available through Jan. 15. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Millions of Florida residents who purchase their insurance policies on healthcare.gov can begin shopping Sunday for coverage to take effect next year.
Twelve companies will offer so-called Obamacare plans on the healthcare.gov marketplace, where subsidies are available to lower the costs of monthly premiums, the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation website shows. Another three are offering Obamacare-compliant plans outside of the healthcare.gov.
The OIR data show the average 2027 monthly health insurance premiums will increase by 10.4%, a  percentage that doesn’t take into consideration the potential impact of premium subsidies.
Enrollment in healthcare.gov is open through Dec. 15 for coverage that takes effect at the start of next year. For policies that take effect Feb. 1, 2027, open enrollment is available through Jan. 15.
“Our navigators are prepared to really help people understand what might best fit their needs and to support them with making important decisions about accessing care,” Xonjenese Jacobs told the Florida Phoenix.
Jacobs is director of Florida Covering Kids and Families, which receives the federal grants to support navigation services across the state. This year’s grant is $1.379 million, which mirrors what it received last year but is a 90% reduction from 2024, when it received $13.79 million.
Florida Covering Kids and Families Director Xonjenese Jacobs (Photo via University of South Florida)
Florida Covering Kids and Families has contracted with five other navigator groups across the state to ensure they are ready to assist people in need of their services.
More than 3.85 million Floridians residents enrolled in the federal health insurance exchange and paid their first month premium to effectuate their 2026 coverage. That was a 10% dip from the 4.3 million who effectuated policies on the federal exchange in 2025.
That represents 450,000 people. Whether they became uninsured, purchased individual policies outside the exchange or enrolled in an employer sponsored health insurance policy isn’t clear yet, because 2026 uninsured rates won’t be released until next year. Florida had a 13.6% uninsured rate in 2024, before elimination of the enhanced premium tax credits that helped lower the costs of the policies.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services projects that national health expenditures will exceed $6 billion in 2026 — a 6.3% jump over 2025 expenditures — and will top $6.3 billion in 2027, or $18,295 per person. Health expenditures are projected to account for 18.8% of the gross domestic product in 2027.
Jacobs maintains that people understand the importance and financial security that health insurance offers and think creatively to keep their policies, despite the rising costs.
For some people on the marketplace, that means switching from a “platinum” or “gold” plan — with higher monthly premiums but lower deductibles — to a “bronze” plan, for which premiums are lower but deductibles — amounts people must pay for care before the coverage kicks in — are higher.
Some people under 30 years old who are shopping on healthcare.gov marketplace can choose a catastrophic plan, which has the highest deductibles and the lowest monthly premiums.
“There are numerous options in the marketplace. There are many alternatives for what people have in terms of their selection,” she said. “We have grown into a culture that really understands and values the needs for access to healthcare, and I think people are willing and wanting to make a way because they simply require this.”
 Another way?

For people who cannot afford Affordable Care Act (or Obamacare) policies, Jacobs said, navigators can make referrals to federally qualified health centers and lower-cost charitable clinics.
Catalina “Cat” Jaramillo, a 43-year-old woman from Miami-Dade County who owns her home and loves her three dogs, is one of those people.
For years, she said, she went uninsured and “didn’t care.” All that changed in her late 30s, when chronic back pain drove her to a hospital, where she was diagnosed with kidney disease.
Open enrollment for Jan. 1 health insurance coverage ends Dec. 15.
She bought an Obamacare plan. 
“Thankfully, that covered my medication. I was able to see the specialist. I developed a relationship with them and I progressively got better,” she said during a Florida Voices for Health media availability last week.
But in 2026, she lost access to the enhanced tax credit that helped offset the costs of her policy. Her monthly premiums jumped from $180 a month to more than $1,000.
“The increase was just way too high. I couldn’t afford it,” she said.
Now she goes to Community Health of South Florida, a federally qualified health center where she can tap into care at a lower cost. For about $180 a month, she said, she can see her kidney disease specialists and get prescriptions to treat her ADHD and depression.
Jaramillo’s “very grateful to have this resource” but knows it’s not the same as her Obamacare plan, a health insurance policy that’s sold to qualifying individuals regardless of pre-existing medical conditions. The policies are required to cover 10 essential benefits, including emergency care, hospitalizations, maternity and newborn care, and prescription drugs. 
“The other day, I had to go to urgent care, and I’m not looking forward to that bill,” she lamented. “But you know, it’s something that was inevitable.”
 $18K in premiums annually

Dave Waalewyn is a commercial pilot who lives in Leesburg and long relied on his employer for health coverage. Waalewyn found himself without health insurance after his former employer, Spirit Airlines, ceased operations earlier this year.
For the first time, Waalewyn had to procure an individual health insurance plan and turned to a broker recommended to him by his financial adviser. They found a plan on the so-called “private” market, outside the federal healthcare exchange, that cost $800 a month. Because it doesn’t have to comply with Obamacare regulations, the policy was medically underwritten, meaning he had to answer questions about his medical history.
Waalewyn is required to pass Federal Aviation Agency screening to fly, and he has. That’s why he said disclosing the results of an abnormal stress test and a follow-up heart catheterization that showed “a trivial amount of plaque” didn’t cross his mind when he shopped for his policy.
“So, as far as I was concerned, everything was fine. So, I signed up for this $800 a month policy. About a week later, I get a letter in the mail saying, ‘Hey, what’s going on with this medical information? You know, you didn’t tell us about this,’ ” Waalewyn recalled.
Leesburg commercial airline pilot Dave Waalewyn turned to healthcare.gov for his health insurance after losing access to his employer-sponsored plan. (Screenshot Florida Voices for Health press conference Oct. 26, 2026)
Out of an abundance of caution lest the carrier deny future claims, Waalewyn said, he walked away from the non-Obamacare plan and turned to healthcare.gov. Eventually, he chose a policy that costs $1,500 a month.
“Luckily, today I start a new job and I will have medical insurance starting in December, so I don’t have to, you know, worry about that anymore until I go on Medicare at the end of the year next year in 2027,” he said.
If not for getting hired by another airline, he said, he would have paid $18,000 annually for his Obamacare policy. That doesn’t include deductibles or co-pays.
 No ACA protections

Carson Hornish is a health insurance broker in Tampa. He has clients who are enrolled in the healthcare.gov marketplace and says for those who qualify for the remaining tax subsidies (as opposed to the lapsed enhanced subsidies) that lower the costs of monthly premiums, there’s not a better plan out there.
“So, I’m never gonna push somebody away from Obamacare, especially if we’re getting a subsidy,” he said.
But he has clients who purchase what he calls “private” plans.
Carson Hornish, broker Carson Health Advising (Photo via Hornish)
Those plans are medically underwritten and not required to be issued to everyone. They aren’t required to cover mental health, substance abuse disorders, or prescription drugs. And while Obamacare plans cannot contain lifetime caps or annual limits, insurance companies can limit what they spend on policyholders’ care annually or over a lifetime. 
Those caveats have led some, including the American Lung Association, to describe them as “junk plans.” 
It’s what more of Hornish’s clients and prospective clients are looking for these days.
“I wanna say 1,000% with 100% confidence,” Hornish told the Phoenix when asked whether more people are asking him for non-ACA coverage. 
He also says that just because non-ACA-compliant plans aren’t required to meet all the requirements in the federal health care law, it doesn’t mean the plans don’t offer benefits.
“With the private marketplace, I can find whatever plan tailored for whatever person that needs coverage. So, if someone comes to me, saying, ‘Hey, I want mental health,’ well, I’m going to show them the plan that’s going to cover mental health. But it might not cover pregnancy, right?”

title: Labor groups rally for Iowa Democrats in weekend push before Election Day
description: Union members and volunteers rallied with Democratic candidates and AFL-CIO leaders Oct. 31, 2026, at the IBEW headquarters in Ankeny  for a canvassing event days before the Nov. 3, 2026 election. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)ANKENY — Iowa labor leaders and union members urged voters at a “get out the vote” event Saturday to elect Democratic [...]
text:
Union members and volunteers rallied with Democratic candidates and AFL-CIO leaders Oct. 31, 2026, at the IBEW headquarters in Ankeny  for a canvassing event days before the Nov. 3, 2026 election. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)ANKENY — Iowa labor leaders and union members urged voters at a “get out the vote” event Saturday to elect Democratic candidates in the midterms Tuesday to protect workers’ rights and Social Security.
U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek, governor candidate Rob Sand and Sarah Trone Garriott, running for the 3rd Congressional District, rallied with Iowa and national AFL-CIO leaders, union workers and volunteers at the IBEW Local 347 in Ankeny for a Halloween canvass launch.
Charlie Wishman, president of the Iowa Federation of Labor, urged the crowd to vote, knock doors and phone bank for the candidates who will support labor unions if elected.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Let’s be clear, this is not a Democrat rally,” Wishman said. “May look like one, and that’s because it seems like maybe one of them’s on our side … and one of them hasn’t been so much lately.”
The rally was held in Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, where Trone Garriott, a state senator, is set to face incumbent U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, a Republican. While Nunn has emphasized his bipartisan voting record and spoken about meeting with unions and working on legislation to tackle issues like nursing workforce shortages, Wishman said his voting record as a state lawmaker and in Congress shows he does not support union labor.
“He is not — just not — for us,” Wishman said. “He’s engaged in the biggest union-busting operation that’s ever happened in the state, which was the gutting and destroying of our public sector collective bargaining law. And then he took that playbook and he went to Washington and participated in DOGE, which was the biggest union-busting endeavor in the history of our entire country. So that bar is really, really low. But it’s not just that — Sarah Trone Garriott is with us all the time.”
Iowa Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, running for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District seat, urged union workers and volunteers to get out the vote at a rally and canvassing event with state and federal labor organizers at IBEW Local 347 in Ankeny Oct. 31, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Trone Garriott highlighted her support for the Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act — a federal proposal to expand some workers’ rights to unionization and bargaining — and to support working families by lowering fuel costs by ending the Iran war and lower healthcare costs by reversing Medicaid cuts.
“If you want things to stay the same — if you like your clinics closing and your healthcare costs going up, if you like having to pay more for everything your family needs, if you like paying over $4 a gallon for gas, over $6 a gallon for diesel, if you like the union-busting that’s happening in Washington — vote for Zach Nunn,” she said. “But if you want change, vote for me. I am so excited to get to Washington and take on the corruption that’s the heart of what is costing us so much.”
Wishman also said he did not “remember” Nunn meeting with “AFL-CIO nurses” or doing “tours of (union) halls.” Letters reviewed by Iowa Capital Dispatch showed Nunn held an Aug. 4 roundtable with Acting U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling, nurses and healthcare workers in coordination with the United Nurses of Iowa — the group organizing to form a union with Teamsters Local 90 at UnityPoint hospitals. The event was not open to press, but Nunn sent a letter to Sonderling after the meeting to discuss ways the Department of Labor was working to address concerns on high turnover rates, workplace violence and pay brought up at the event.
A Nunn campaign spokesperson emphasized Nunn’s track record in Congress, which included introducing measures like the Train More Nurses Act. The Republican also voted in support of measures like the Protect America’s Workforce Act, opposed by other House Republicans, to collective bargaining rights to federal workers.
“Zach Nunn is the third most bipartisan member of Congress because he’s one of the few Republicans willing to not only walk into a union hall for a listening session, but buck his own party to defend Iowa workers,” the spokesperson said. “He also delivers: no tax on overtime for nurses, and legislation signed into law under two presidents to defend benefits for working Iowans and their families.”
Harkin, Turek emphasize support for labor issues
Other surrogates, including national AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler and former U.S. Sen. Tom Harkin, also rallied for Democrats at the event. Harkin said he was given a lifetime score of 100% by the AFL-CIO for his support of legislation to support unions and labor during his time representing Iowa in Washington, D.C., telling the crowd, “so don’t anybody tell me that a senator from a so-called ‘right-to-work’ state can’t support organized labor.”
U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek, a state representative, urged union workers and volunteers to get out the vote at a rally and canvassing event with state and federal labor organizers and other Democratic candidates Oct. 31, 2026 at IBEW Local 347 in Ankeny. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
He said Turek would continue his work in support of Iowa labor in Congress if elected, and would “work to make sure that Social Security is there for your kids and your grandkids” in the future. Harkin also said it was important for union members and activists to reach out to their friends, families and coworkers in the final days before Nov. 3 to encourage them to vote.
“If all I did was was rely on Democrats to vote for me, I never would have made it,” Harkin said. “But I needed you as my base. I needed you as my army out there. I needed you to be out on the front lines for me, and talking about me with your friends and your neighbors. … That’s how we win. We win because you’ve taken what you believe in and the support that you want for organized labor, and you’ve reached out to friends and neighbors that probably aren’t union members to bring them across. That’s what it takes, and that’s what it’s going to take to win these races this year.”
Turek brought up his Republican opponent Ashley Hinson’s AFL-CIO voting record — which was 0% in 2025 with a lifetime score of 8% — to contrast with Harkin. The audience laughed as he said, “you would have thought at some point she would have accidentally voted on something to actually help working people.” In contrast, he criticized measures Hinson did support during her time representing Iowa’s 2nd Congressional District.
“What has she done? She has voted in a state with a healthcare crisis and a cancer crisis for 110,000 Iowans to be pulled off their healthcare, for 119,000 Iowans to see their healthcare premiums double or triple, voted for thousands of working families to lose basic food assistance, for cuts to the Social Security Administration, just to give tax breaks to billionaires,” Turek said. “It’s disgusting. All the while, five times voted in favor of these tariffs. These tariffs that have led to grocery prices going up, decimating small businesses, killing small communities, and killing our farmers.”
Voter Guide: 2026 Iowa general election

Billy Fuerst, campaign communications director for Hinson, said the Republican candidate “has a strong record of delivering for Iowa workers, including passing no tax on tips and overtime, leading legislation to expand access to affordable childcare, and making the dream of homeownership more attainable for working families.”
“But she knows there is more work to do to lower costs for Iowans and make paychecks go farther,” Fuerst said. “Josh Turek would make life harder for Iowa workers by repealing no tax on tips and overtime and raising taxes on working Iowans. Josh Turek is too liberal for Iowa.”
Turek has said he supports reversing Medicaid cuts made through the 2025 “One, Big Beautiful Bill” Act, but that he supports the law’s move to repeal taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security.
Sand cites need to raise minimum wage
Sand, the current state auditor, criticized his opponent, Republican Zach Lahn, for not committing to a simple answer on raising the minimum wage in the state during gubernatorial debates.
Democratic candidate for governor Rob Sand, joined by other Democratic candidates, urged union workers and volunteers to get out the vote at a rally and canvassing event with state and federal labor organizers at IBEW Local 347 in Ankeny Oct. 31, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
During the third gubernatorial debate, Lahn said, “I think the easy political answer to a question like this would be for somebody to say yes. But I also understand that I drove by McDonald’s just the other day that was hiring at $14 an hour.”
“I think what we need to prioritize, rather than looking at this specifically, we need to prioritize the ability for companies — that are Iowa-based companies — to expand,” Lahn said. In addition to providing more incentives to Iowa-based businesses, Lahn said he would work with the Iowa Economic Development Authority as governor to create an entrepreneurial fund.
Sand reflected on the debate, joking that as he listened to Lahn’s answer, his mind wandered and he was “starting to wonder what the weather’s going to be like on Wednesday morning after the election, because I’m going to be in a tree stand hunting.”
“I tune back in and he’s still answering the question — and he doesn’t have a number for where we should put the minimum wage,” Sand said. “And so that’s when I decided, when it’s my turn to answer, I’m just going to say, ‘Yeah, 12 bucks an hour.’ Sometimes, being a real human being is not demonstrating that you can give a long answer, but that you can give a short one, so that people know you actually think something.”

Hughes, who is seeking reelection to a fifth term representing the 135th House District of Easton, Redding and Weston, acknowledged removing lawn signs[...]
text:
Rep. Anne Hughes, D-Easton, was issued a summons Saturday for a misdemeanor larceny charge related to taking a Republican opponent’s lawn sign that he says was tracked to Hughes’ property by a hidden air tag.
Hughes, who is seeking reelection to a fifth term representing the 135th House District of Easton, Redding and Weston, acknowledged removing lawn signs that she says were improperly placed on public property.
“I apologize for removing them rather than contacting the police or my opponent’s campaign to remove them, and I take full responsibility and accountability for my actions,” Hughes said in statement.
Darrell Harris, the Republican challenger, said a volunteer frustrated by disappearing lawn signs had hidden air tags in some signs, and the campaign was able to track one Friday.
“I expected it to ping to same random person,” Harris said Saturday. “The last thing I expected was it to ping on her property.”
The signs taunted Hughes for a so-called “hot mic” moment at a press conference called by lawmakers who favor higher taxes on the wealthy. She was heard joking to colleague, “We’re not rich. But I always tell the governor to tax my people — they won’t even notice.” 
Harris’ signs said, “We noticed.”
Harris also has used the quote in advertising, including one on Facebook with the hot mic audio.

A social media ad by Republican Darrell Harris capitalizes on the hot mic moment. Credit: Darrell Harris ad

Harris said he reported the missing signs and their suspected location to Easton police. 
“The cops have to do their job,” Hughes said Saturday. “They showed up at our house at 10 p.m.”
Hughes said she had signs from several campaigns, including Gov. Ned Lamont’s, that she found either discarded or improperly placed on a public right of way.
“I brought them the whole pile,” she said.
In exchange, she was handed a summons for sixth-degree larceny, instructing her to appear in court in two weeks, she said.
“Campaigns should be about issues and differences of ideas, not yard signs,” Hughes said. “I apologize for the distraction and am committed to having civil discourse with my opponent for the duration of this campaign season.”

title: Concord Raiders stay undefeated in Class 1A District 1 with one-point victory over St. Elizabeth
description:
Concord junior Francis Willie leaps into the air to make the catch, helping the Concord Raiders defeat the St. Elizabeth Vikings, Saturday afternoon. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
The Concord Raiders (6-2, 3-0 Class 1A-D1) defeated the St. Elizabeth Vikings (2-6, 0-3 Class 1A-D1), 7-6, on October 31 and are tied with Brandywine for first place in Class 1A Distri[...]
text:
Concord junior Francis Willie leaps into the air to make the catch, helping the Concord Raiders defeat the St. Elizabeth Vikings, Saturday afternoon. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
The Concord Raiders (6-2, 3-0 Class 1A-D1) defeated the St. Elizabeth Vikings (2-6, 0-3 Class 1A-D1), 7-6, on October 31 and are tied with Brandywine for first place in Class 1A District One standings. 
 
WILMINGTON, Del. — The Raiders broke from their huddle and took their positions with the ball on the St. Elizabeth 40-yard line and less than two minutes remaining in the second quarter. Senior quarterback Declan McNulty stood alone in the backfield and took the fourth down snap, needing seven yards to continue the Raiders’ second offensive possession of the game. 
McNulty went into his drop and surveyed the field. He peaked left, but returned his eyes to the right side where the majority of his receivers were running their routes. McNulty fired a high pass toward the middle of the field for junior receiver Francis Willie and Willie rose above the defensive back in front of him. Willie secured the catch as the defender tried to swipe it out of his hands and turned toward the endzone running untouched for the Raiders first and only touchdown of the game.
Willie’s 40-yard touchdown grab and junior Derrick Hoon’s extra point were the difference in Concord’s 7-6 win over St. Elizabeth, Saturday afternoon.
“All week in practice I just do it and I haven’t been able to get an opportunity, I was out for two weeks, so to bounce back and get that touchdown that was incredible,” Willie said postgame. 
The Raiders earned an extra possession before halftime forcing a fumble on the ensuing kick-off after the touchdown, but the Vikings defense forced a turnover on downs holding Concord to the single score. Concord finished the first half with three offensive possessions after it looked like they may only get one shot on the offensive side of the ball. 
St. Elizabeth started the game with possession and held the ball for over 15 minutes of game action. The Vikings ran 20 plays on their opening drive — all of them runs — and marched 80 yards downfield for a game-opening score. Viking players Isaiah Coleman, Mi’Cah Hamilton, Ethan Valentine and Christopher Cerasari all carried the ball during the drive with the junior quarterback Cerasari leading the group with 38 rushing yards and the opening touchdown. 
Cerasari scored on a quarterback sneak and gave the Vikings a lead with a little more than nine minutes remaining in the second quarter.
Cerasari’s legs were a big part of the Vikings’ offense in the second half as well as they tried to regain the lead. Cerasari rushed for over 70 yards in the second half and helped the Vikings encroach into Raider territory, but the Raider defense held firm, never letting the Vikings enter the red zone. Cerasari finished the game with over 110 rushing yards.
“We just had to be more physical, you know,” Raider sophomore Colton Biddle said about the team’s halftime adjustments. “Coaches came in there [said] we had to be more physical, play with a higher intensity and that’s what we came out and did.” 
The Viking defense was similarly stout against the Raider offense. The Vikings held the Raiders running game to short gains and tackled well in the secondary keeping the Raiders’ passing attack in check. 
The Viking defense made a couple crucial stops late in the fourth quarter returning possession back to their offense for a chance at a game winning drive, but with little time remaining in the game the Vikings’ offense was forced into obvious passing situations. St. Elizabeth attempted seven passes in the final three minutes and all fell incomplete. Biddle broke up four of those pass attempts.
“I just knew what they were gonna do and I just stayed with my head, kept the intensity up and yeah I just had to put on for my team,” Biddle said after the game.
The Raiders have two games left to play this season and both are against district opponents. Concord will play Dickinson at home next Saturday and then travel to Brandywine High School for a Friday night matchup against the Bulldogs. Both the Raiders and Bulldogs are 3-0 in District One play this season, meaning should both teams win next week, their Week 10 matchup will determine the winner of District One. The winner of each district earns a top-seed in that class’ DIAA Tournament bracket and is guaranteed at least one home game in the tournament. 
Concord’s next game against Dickinson will start at 10:30 a.m. 
The Vikings also have two district opponents remaining on their schedule, McKean and A.I. duPont. St. Elizabeth’s next game against A.I. duPont will be on Friday, November 6, at 6:00 p.m. The game will be held at A.I. duPont High School.

title: Independent Bill Hill runs “race against time” in bid to knock off GOP U.S. Rep. Begich

text:
Independent Bill Hill poses with Nondalton residents Monday. He won 86% of votes cast in the village in the primary — but he has to build a much larger coalition to win the U.S. House seat he's seeking. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)For a minute Monday, in the small Bristol Bay village of Iliamna, it looked like U.S. House candidate Bill Hill might not get out of the local graveyard.
Hill, the independent running for Alaska’s sole House seat, had stopped to pay respects to a relative who’d recently been buried. Afterward, he jumped in the car, with his younger brother Karl at the wheel — and the rig promptly got stuck in deep sand.
Bill didn’t have time to spare: He’s on an ambitious schedule for the homestretch of his campaign, stumping from Fairbanks to Sitka as he tries to close a suddenly shrinking gap between himself and incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III. After his Iliamna visit, he was set to fly to three other villages before sundown.
“Momentum,” Bill said calmly as Karl spun the wheels. “Gotta get the momentum up first.”
The car rocked back and forth before it finally got purchase. I couldn’t detect any tension between the two brothers, and when I mentioned, once we were rolling, that the vehicular detour felt like a test of their fraternal relationship, Karl cracked a joke: He wasn’t listening to his brother anyway.

Hill stands above the shore of Iliamna Lake in the village of Kokhanok, where he grew up. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
Bill Hill’s poise and his tight family ties are both themes of his effort to knock off Begich, who’s finishing up his first term. Hill’s case on the campaign trail: Begich has prized partisan politics and wealthy allies over loyalty to Alaska constituents and he’s supported decisions by President Donald Trump that have hurt his home state, spiking the prices Alaskans pay for essentials like food, gas and health care.
The campaign started as a long shot, seeking to introduce an unfamiliar face to a statewide audience in a year when airwaves are jammed with ads for Alaska’s U.S. Senate candidates.
But the race has now tightened to what could be nearly a dead heat: Two polls released in October show Begich leading by no more than two percentage points.
Hill is not a polished politician; his vibe onstage gives more “your friend’s dad” than it does electrifying speaker. He’s faced fierce attacks over actions that predate his recent entry into politics, like a misdemeanor conviction for commercial salmon fishing outside legal boundaries — an infraction many fishermen describe as the cost of doing business. 
Opponents also say he leans farther left than he lets on, pointing to old campaign donations to Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
But what Hill lacks in conventional political experience, his supporters say, he makes up for in Alaska bona fides: He comes from an Indigenous familywith deep roots and a long history of leadership in the Bristol Bay region, and claims an understanding of the state’s rural communities that can come only with decades spent living there.
Hill’s campaign allowed me to join him on part of his final stretch — specifically, a multi-village tour through Bristol Bay, including stops at the site of his Dena’ina grandmother’s old cabin and his childhood home in the village of Kokhanok.
At every turn, supporters showed up to give Hill a hug, share news about friends and relatives, and joke about the attack ads that, as one person quipped in a text message to the candidate, make Hill out to be a drinker of “unicorn blood.”
“Fuel, groceries, electricity, airfare, it’s getting really tough,” said Jessie Wilson, a cousin of Hill’s who attended a small campaign event Monday in Iliamna. Hill “lives in it,” she added. “He gets it. He’s in the thick of it just like we are.”

Jessie Wilson, center, chats with Bill Hill in Iliamna. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
The question for Hill is not whether he has support in rural villages like Iliamna and neighboring Newhalen, where he claimed 65% of the primary vote in a single combined precinct. It’s whether his message will resonate enough in Alaska’s more urban areas to propel a first-time candidate for public office into U.S. Congress.
Hill thinks it will, telling me that “the issues that are important to rural Alaska translate directly to the rest of Alaska.” He’s pledging to work to contain gas prices and health care costs, to limit the influence of money in politics and to close tax loopholes for the wealthy.
“A lot of the work that Begich has done, through the support of the party line and what the administration wants, I don’t think reflects what Alaskans need,” Hill said.
Begich’s campaign declined my request to spend time with the candidate in the lead-up to Election Day.
But it did send a lengthy statement highlighting Begich’s legislative accomplishments, which spokesman Paul Smith described as “significant action on Alaska Native land rights, tribal health care and Alaska Native veterans.”

U.S. Rep. Nick Begich III, center, poses for a photo at a warship’s commissioning ceremony in Whittier, Alaska, earlier this month. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
Those include sponsoring bills signed into law that extend Vietnam War veterans’ opportunities to claim Native allotments and transfer federal land to a Native corporation and Native health care provider — as well as efforts to boost oil and gas lease sales and Arctic security, Smith said.
“His commitment extends well beyond Washington: He has traveled to communities throughout Alaska, from Bethel and Aniak and Chuathbaluk to Nome, Kotzebue, Anaktuvuk Pass, and Southeast Alaska, listening to the challenges facing families and local leaders,” Smith added. “Every day he serves in Congress, he is making the case for Alaska, period. His priority is Alaska, and his focus remains on delivering opportunities and results for the people he represents.”

Hill’s story, or at least one strand of it, starts in a shallow, grassy pit that once housed a cabin near the shore of Lake Clark — a bright blue expanse tucked into the mountains some 165 miles southwest of Anchorage, at the eastern reaches of the Bristol Bay watershed.
Hill’s paternal grandmother, Katie Trefon, was born there in 1919.
She lived a life that straddled the Indigenous Dena’ina subsistence traditions of trapping and fishing, and the Western commercial salmon harvesting economy that sprang up in Bristol Bay with the arrival of thousands of European immigrant fishermen in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Her first husband was Bill Hill’s grandfather Billy Hill, who came from Finland and worked as a boat builder, prospector, mechanic and winter caretaker at a fish cannery, according to a National Park Service history.

Bill Hill examines a photo of his grandmother, Katie Trefon, at left, and great grandmother, Mary Ann Trefon, from around 1929 in a book at a cousin’s house in Port Alsworth. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
Billy died suddenly in the 1940s, and Katie remarried. She raised 13 children in total, including Bill’s father.
“She was just the stalwart rock of the family,” Bill said Monday, midway through a walking tour in Port Alsworth that took him past the site of the cabin and a small burial ground. “Tough lady, but a very loving lady.”
Hill now has siblings, cousins and other relatives scattered across the region, where the Hill family members are “some of the best and brightest that Bristol Bay produced,” said John Branson, a longtime historian with the national park that encompasses Lake Clark.
Hill’s uncle Frank was one of Alaska’s first Native school superintendents. Bill’s parents were both schoolteachers and raised Hill and his siblings in the village of Kokhanok, on the south shore of the massive Lake Iliamna, just south of Lake Clark.
The kids — Hill has five siblings — grew up in what he describes as the “idealized version” of rural Alaska, chopping wood, hauling water, caring for and running the family’s several dozen sled dogs.
The Hills later moved to the Bristol Bay hub town of Naknek so that the kids could attend high school. In Kokhanok, Bill, the oldest, had just one classmate; in Naknek he had 12.

Hill speaks with children at a classroom in Kokhanok this week. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
Hill went to college for a teaching degree, then did construction and joined a trade union before getting a graduate degree and working as a teacher, principal and, ultimately, superintendent of the Naknek-based Bristol Bay Borough School District.
His service there has become a subject of attacks in recent weeks, with Begich’s campaign knocking declines in test scores that came during Hill’s tenure; Hill’s campaign says the data was cherry picked from a period when there was a statewide decline in scores tied to a change in testing methods.
Hill married and had four kids; he now has seven grandchildren. He retired from his superintendent job in 2023 and now draws a pension of some $80,000 a year, according to his financial disclosure.
Hill’s perfect retirement, he said, “would be just spending the rest of my life in Bush Alaska, not having a lot on my plate and enjoying grandchildren all over the place.”
“But we all know that sometimes those things can slip away,” he said. “They need to be preserved for the future.”

Frustrated by what he describes as “billionaires taking over our government,” Hill started having conversations with contacts he made at Alaska’s Capitol during his education career, when he’d travel to Juneau on advocacy trips. His first thought, he said, was to run for the Alaska House, but the idea of holding statewide office and “changing things at a national level” ultimately appealed more.
Hill wouldn’t identify any of the people who pushed him to run for Congress. But his conversations led him to Ship Creek Group — the Anchorage political consulting firm that’s worked with Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Republican-turned-independent former Alaska Gov. Bill Walker.
Ship Creek Group’s consultants, who now help lead Hill’s campaign, describe Hill’s biography and personality as some of the biggest selling points in their decision to work with him. And they say their polling shows that the candidate’s backstory connects with voters.
“We need to back the kinds of people who aren’t most naturally equipped to run, but who will bring a perspective and a level of decency that doesn’t exist in D.C.,” John-Henry Heckendorn, one of the group’s owners, wrote in a personal fundraising email to family and friends.
That email was sent five weeks from Election Day. At that point, Heckendorn wrote, the campaign was “no longer in a race against Nick Begich.”
“We are in a race against time,” he said. “If Alaskans learn who Bill is and what he stands for, he will win.”
Hill and his allies have also targeted Begich’s multi-million-dollar net worth, much of which is invested in software and technology companies. And the messaging seems to be working: On Tuesday, a closely watched political newsletter, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, shifted the Begich-Hill race from “likely Republican” to “leans Republican.”
What does Hill actually stand for?

Hill tapes a video in Kokhanok. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
He opposes Trump’s tariffs, the elimination of renewable energy tax credits, and the Citizens United decision that allows unlimited corporate spending in elections.
He supports expanded Medicaid coverage, abortion rights and gun rights, and natural resource extraction — except the big Pebble mine project in the Bristol Bay region, which has long been opposed by many residents and commercial fishermen for the risks it poses to the watershed’s huge salmon runs.
He’s refused to say whether he’d caucus with Democrats or Republicans if elected — though he has said he wouldn’t join a caucus headed by the current U.S. House speaker, Republican Mike Johnson.
Conservative groups have attacked him for his donations to Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez, saying they show Hill is a closet Democrat. In an interview this week, Hill said those contributions reflect “somebody that’s pissed off that billionaires are taking over our country.”
“I’ve also voted for Don Young, and (Ted) Stevens,” he added, referencing the two late, long-serving Alaska Republican politicians. “Just because you may see one segment of my politics in fundraising, it doesn’t reflect the entirety of me.”
Hill’s core message of affordability lands most urgently in rural Alaska, where gas prices in many communities now exceed $10 a gallon — driven in part by the U.S. war in Iran.

A customer at a store in Iliamna shows a receipt for a gas purchase Monday. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
But Hill and his consultants say that practical centrist positions can appeal to a broader coalition that other politicians like Peltola, Lisa Murkowski and Walker have ridden to victory in Alaska — which more often elects Republicans, even though nearly 65% of registered voters are independents.
That coalition combines Democrats with pro-development labor unions, moderate Republicans in coastal fishing communities, rural Alaska Native voters and swing voters in urban precincts.
On Tuesday, in Bristol Bay, I asked Hill why he was taking precious time in the closing stages of the campaign to visit communities with so few voters.
He acknowledged that the numbers favor him spending time in urban areas, but quickly pivoted to how more than 200 Alaska communities can only be reached by plane.
“They deserve to be represented. They deserve to have people in Washington, D.C., who understand what their lives are like — understand the power that belonging to a remote community brings and the value it brings to your life,” he said. “They should not be overlooked.”
Hill’s campaign says he’s traveled more than 25,000 miles across the state since launching his bid for House this year in his effort to build a winning majority.
But doing so is a tall order for a candidate who’s never run for elected office beyond the board of his local Native village corporation — especially without the benefit of party affiliation, according to Margaret Stock, an attorney who ran for U.S. Senate as an independent in 2016.
“A lot of people only vote based on the party label,” Stock said. “I would call people and ask for money and they would say, ‘You’re not a Democrat, I’m not giving you money.’ ‘You’re not a Republican, I’m not giving you money.’”
She added: “It’s a lot easier if you have the party infrastructure behind you.”
One key support to Hill’s campaign is a super PAC called Wheel Dog PAC, which has spent millions of dollars on his behalf.
Wheel Dog has collected six-figure contributions from groups aligned with progressive causes, including $400,000 from Sixteen Thirty Fund — an organization that Politico describes as “the left’s dark money behemoth.”
That same fund is linked to multiple other groups that have donated six-figure sums to Wheel Dog, including Contours Inc. and Government that Works PAC.

On his last-minute swing through Bristol Bay region, Hill leaned on family infrastructure, with two of his brothers, Rob and Karl, flying him in their own Bush planes.
Monday morning began in Naknek, with the three brothers, plus Rob’s wife and daughter and a pair of campaign aides, cramming into a Cessna 182 and a Piper Cherokee 180 — nearly every square inch filled with campaign signs, snacks and boxes of pizza.
They flew first to New Stuyahok, a Yup’ik village 50 miles north of Naknek on the Nushagak River, then loaded up again for the 80-mile flight to Iliamna. I met them there midday, having flown in directly from Anchorage.

Hill takes a selfie while flying with his pilot brother Karl. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
I chatted with residents at one of the village’s stores as Hill and his crew arrived. Tref Andrew, a commercial fisherman who showed up in a baseball cap that said WTF — Where’s The Fish — told me how fuel prices were so high this summer that, after setting his net, he would take the unusual step of turning off his engine while waiting for salmon to swim into it.
“How we’re going to survive here as a rural community, given the increase in the cost of living — it wasn’t too bad when I was growing up here as a child. One season of commercial fishing, you could buy everything,” Andrew said.
Today, Andrew added, he can spend $20,000 on maintenance, storage and insurance before his boat even goes into the water for the summer.
At our next stop, another store in Iliamna, the themes were similar. One shopper left with a small bag of groceries — four tomatoes, a head of iceberg lettuce, sour cream, taco seasoning and cheese — that cost $60. Another bought a $175 tank of gas at $11.98 a gallon — “like a stab in the back, every time you fill up” — while the store’s operators complained of steep prices for electricity.
Karl’s plane carried Bill onward to Port Alsworth, then to the 130-person village of Nondalton, where one Elder met him with a handwritten guide to local Dena’ina clan names.
Something like one-fourth of the village population turned out to eat the campaign’s reheated pizza and to listen to a short stump speech from Hill after a Lord’s Prayer and an introduction, in the Dena’ina language, from his sister-in-law.

Hill poses for a photo in Iliamna. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)
More chit-chatting came afterward, but daylight was dwindling; Hill and his campaign and brothers had to fly back across Lake Iliamna to Kokhanok for the night. We all clambered into a pickup truck to head back to the airport, with several of us sitting in the bed.
The next morning in Kokhanok, Rob flipped dozens of sourdough pancakes, served with sides of fried Spam and moose sausage, for residents at the old school, where the family had lived behind a partition when they first arrived in the village.
Afterward, an aide, Wil Garcia, pulled Hill outside to the shore of the lake, where he taped some video. Then Hill drove to the new school, stopped by a couple of classrooms and ate a community lunch of locally harvested caribou ribs.
One last coffee at Rob’s house, and a walk along the water, before it was time to go: The plane was heading back to the road system, and to Hill’s last week on the trail.

text:
THE REALITY OF public education in Boston is far from what Mayor Michelle Wu depicted in her recent State of the Schools address. Hiding behind the improvements she touted is a broken system with abysmal performance outcomes across every grade in the district. 
In the Boston Public Schools, seven out of every 10 third-graders can’t read or do math at grade level, which is also true for eighth-graders. The outcomes are far worse for Black and Latino students, multilingual learners, students with disabilities, and low-income students in Grades 3-8, with proficiency levels as low as 4 percent for some subgroups. 
It serves no benefit to students and families to push this truth aside or to dismiss this data point as “one number.” Our city must do better, and the first step to real improvement is acknowledging this grim reality, something Mayor Wu continues to fail to do.  
When asked head-on about these low performance outcomes, the mayor stumbled, citing “accountability metrics in the speech.” But the metrics she shared hardly show any accountability at all and fail to address the real issue: that the vast majority of the 44,000 students in BPS can’t read or do math at grade level.  
In the wake of the recent Next Chapter Boston education advocacy campaign, Mayor Wu called the group’s billboards “cynical” and “disgusting.” The billboards show a picture of a child’s eyes with the phrase “BPS IS FAILING HER,” while citing the factual data that shows why.  After the ads were pulled from the MBTA, despite prior approval, it’s clear our city’s leaders are too fearful to come to terms with the truth.  
If anything, Mayor Wu’s education speech should be described as cynical, pointing to misleading numbers and increased investment in a handful of student clubs, instead of the systemic academic overhauls that are required for improvement. In one year, the mayor announced, BPS went from six math clubs to 22 (out of 104 schools) at a time when only 33 percent of 10th-graders are doing math on grade level. For English learners, this number drops to 10 percent, and for students with disabilities it is 6 percent. 
Mayor Wu mentioned that BPS had their highest graduation rate last year, but seniors at BPS need only a D- to prove “competency” and pass core courses. Meanwhile, without MCAS as a graduation requirement, is a BPS diploma worth what it claims with standards set so low? 
The mayor also noted that Boston’s third-grade reading scores have ranked at the top of its urban school district cohort for each of the past six years. But this is disingenuous framing that makes it appear as if reading scores are actually good.  
In reality, just 29 percent of BPS students in grades 3-8 met state proficiency in reading and math on the 2026 MCAS, compared with the statewide average of 40 percent — itself a worrisome statistic.  
Our state leaders, who consistently cheerlead about Massachusetts’s number one national ranking, also need to come clean about the crisis in education that we’re experiencing. The ranking that really needs their focus is that the Commonwealth also holds the distinction of having some of the largest achievement gaps in the country. 
BPS uses its own Focus early literacy curriculum, which has been in place for more than 10 years with little results. Teachers and school administrators have voiced concerns about this curriculum and have seen no change from the district.  
The mayor spent a significant amount of time in her speech celebrating the expansion of free weekend sports, opening vocational programs at Madison Park to the community,  and expanding early college. These “nice-to-have” additions are not what BPS should be focusing on given its true state of crisis. We need real academic overhauls, acceleration academies on school breaks, and ongoing data sharing and dissemination practices to set real benchmarks for improvements across every grade.   
To continue to pretend like our schools are better than they really are is a disservice to students, teachers, families, and the city at large. The same is true of painting a picture of widespread progress when not nearly enough is being done to address our deep-rooted issues.  
The mayor also promised to set five-year targets that will improve poor performances, like attendance rates and test scores. These goals are meaningless if they don’t include concrete, measurable benchmarks. The updated 2026-2031 Strategic Roadmap for BPS, introduced at the beginning of this academic year, reads more like a roadblock. It’s vague and neglects to establish real plans or standards for needed growth.  
With years to create this plan, why are district leaders overlooking such essential details? We need to set real, achievable targets for improvements across all grades in reading, writing, math, and science, and develop a step-by-step implementation strategy to do this. 
These can’t be goals that keep getting pushed back to far-future dates. We have to create policies that make change for students now, so our city can live up to the true promise of delivering a quality public education to all students.  
With a total budget of $1.7 billion, per-pupil spending in Boston is among the highest in the nation, at roughly $37,000 per student. With such deep pockets, you would think it would be easier to integrate a concrete plan for improvement in literacy and numeracy among students. The question is not whether we invest enough money in our schools, but whether we are putting this money in the right places to achieve better results versus paying for the same mistakes year after year. 
The challenges BPS faces, whether they are academic or operational, are compounding. From literacy and math scores to chronic absenteeism to a $200 million transportation system that seems incapable of delivering students to school on time, all performance indicators are either stagnant or moving in the wrong direction.  The “fix” requires both immediate interventions and long-term policy shifts.  
This starts with true oversight and accountability standards that directly tie district funding to verifiable student benchmarks, operational efficiencies, and a guarantee that all students are safe within their school environments. Today, none of these three critical levers for change are evident.  
If the mayor is truly committed to making BPS the “best in the nation,” she and other city leaders must come to terms with the fact that we cannot achieve this without first recognizing where we are drastically falling short. And despite what Mayor Wu has stated publicly, this campaign is not aimed at families, students, or teachers; it is aimed at the people who have the power to change this. 
Mary Tamer, a former member of the Boston School Committee, is the executive director of MassPotential, a fiscally sponsored program of the Goodnation Foundation. Next Chapter Boston is an initiative of MassPotential. Vernée Wilkinson is the director of the Family Advisory Board at SchoolFacts Boston, a nonprofit working to improve education for all in Boston.

title: Canyon County judge declines to halt pro-Prop 1 ballot initiative ads amid lawsuit

text:
Volunteers pass boxes of signatures supporting a ballot initiative to end Idaho's strict ban on abortion on July 2, 2026, outside the state Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun)This story was first published by Boise State Public Radio on Oct. 30, 2026.
A Canyon County judge has rejected a request by anti-Proposition 1 campaigners to halt TV ads from airing that promote the ballot measure days before the election.
In an opinion released late Friday night, Judge Davis VanderVelde found the ads did not violate Idaho campaign finance laws and declined to keep them from being broadcast by local stations.
A Republican Party operative and three board members of Too Extreme for Idaho, which opposes restoring abortion rights under Prop 1, filed their lawsuit Tuesday morning.
They said the scheme used by Idahoans United for Women and Families (IUWF), the Idaho Democratic Party and its gubernatorial candidate, Terri Pickens, concealed the true origin of who paid for the ads.
IUWF, which qualified Prop 1 for the ballot, gave the Idaho Democratic Party more than $720,000 in recent weeks. The party then purchased advertising through Pickens’ campaign.
All political candidates receive significant discounts on ads in the 60 days leading up to an election compared to political groups.
“Ultimately, Plaintiffs’ assertion that the monies from IUWF were specifically contributed for support of Proposition 1 with the intent of concealing the original donor for such advertisements requires logical leaps that are not fully supported by the evidence,” VanderVelde wrote.
Each of these transactions is publicly available in the state’s campaign finance database, which the plaintiffs cited in the evidence presented to the judge.
VanderVelde said there’s also no evidence showing that IUWF still controlled the hundreds of thousands of dollars it donated to the state Democratic Party.
An attorney for the defendants argued in court Thursday that the party had the final say in how any of that money was spent, which VanderVelde said was not proven otherwise by the plaintiffs.
“The Court recognizes that the parties have had a short time to advance this lawsuit and that if there was additional time, additional facts may be developed by either party which could lend further credence to their claims or defenses,” he wrote.
That said, the judge found there may still be outstanding legal questions about whether the ads are truly for a candidate or a proposition and whether the lower rates should apply.
“However, without further law or authority significant questions remain as to what constitutes an appropriate advertisement under the law in order to qualify as an advertisement promoting a candidate.”
Tom Luna, one of the plaintiffs, released a statement saying he and the three other men who brought the lawsuit disagree with the decision, but that it was important voters know who paid for the ads.
“I’m sure many voters are as mad as I am about these dirty tricks. Let’s make sure we turn our frustration into action by showing up on Election Day, making our voices heard, and standing for life,” Luna said.
A request for comment from the Idaho Democratic Party wasn’t immediately returned late Friday night.

text:
By the time the three hikers called for help from a rocky face on Mount Shasta in Northern California, they’d made a series of bad decisions. They didn’t bring enough food, and they’d overestimated their fitness. Instead of turning back in late afternoon when they hadn’t yet reached the top, they summited at 7:30 p.m. and had to descend in the dark. Their lack of preparation and poor planning, as they admitted later, came partly from relying on Google’s artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. By morning, they were lost on a gnarly part of the mountain, and one hiker had banged up his knee.
“We get plenty of people who come unprepared or don’t do any research at all. To these guys’ credit, they did try,” said Nick Meyers, U.S. Forest Service program manager of the Mount Shasta Wilderness Climbing and Avalanche Center, which responded to the call. “But I think they kind of turned their brains off.”
The three 20-year-olds aren’t the only ones making missteps in wild spaces with the help of artificial intelligence. Another Mount Shasta visitor pitched her tent near a “No Camping” sign, insisting she had a right to do so because AI told her she could, Meyers said. His team also encountered a man wandering around at a trailhead with an AI-generated map that showed prominent features on the wrong side of a nearby mountain. In British Columbia, a helicopter crew rescued a 16-year-old hiker from a ledge in the Widowmaker Arete on the back of Crown Mountain. The teen had used Anthropic’s chatbot Claude to help him plan his trip. News stories focused on that fact went viral across Canada and the U.S., though the hiker said later that he also consulted Google Maps and the popular hiking app, AllTrails.
Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming has also seen a marked uptick over the past year in the percentage of visitors who report using AI for travel information, said Park Superintendent Chip Jenkins. “It went from zero to 26%. And I’m guessing that curve is not going to flatten.”
“I think they kind of turned their brains off.”Nick Meyers, U.S. Forest Service
It remains to be seen whether increasing AI use will lead to an increase in backcountry accidents and search and rescues, Meyers said. His office, which oversees a massive wilderness area in Northern California, averages a dozen rescues each year, and 2026 is shaping up to be an average year. Calls to search and rescue in Wyoming have actually gone down compared to 2025, with only 312 calls so far in 2026 compared to a total of 466 in 2025 and 377 in 2024.
Some search and rescue veterans say that AI chatbots are just the latest tools giving people new ways to get into trouble. Roughly a decade ago, when hikers, backpackers, climbers and other outdoor enthusiasts began to source their destinations, inspiration and information from Instagram and other social media sites, they faced sometimes deadly consequences. Before that, hikers and other recreationists were led astray by their reliance on Google Maps or smartphone connectivity.
“Over the last two decades, there’s been a phenomenal push in the media to get more people outdoors, and consequently we have more people outdoors and recreating,” said Jim Moss, a Colorado-based recreation attorney and search and rescue volunteer. It’s still unclear how questionable advice from a robot will influence all those people, he added.
Turning to an AI chatbot for guidance does come with unique risks. Not only can chatbots “hallucinate,” persuasively presenting misinformation as real, but their use can lead to a phenomenon called “cognitive surrender,” said Chris Flathmann, a human-centered computing professor at Clemson University in South Carolina who has studied AI and search and rescue.
“When humans work with AI systems, they can get so deep into it they give up thinking critically for themselves,” he explained. When AI pretends to be an expert on an unfamiliar topic, “you can’t call BS on that, because you don’t have the expertise.” And once you stop thinking critically, it can be hard to start again, especially in a stressful backcountry situation.
Chatbots also tend to tell users what they want to hear, and to do so with authority regardless of whether the sources they’re consulting are reliable, Flathmann and others said. Claude or ChatGPT might answer a query with extensive directions and advice that sound credible but are actually scraped from Reddit threads and out-of-date YouTube videos — and might even be entirely fabricated.

Access to public land? There’s an app for that

TikTok and Instagram may offer a viewer inspiration, but AI tends to offer instructions — right or wrong — as well as encouragement, Flathmann said. “AI isn’t trying to trick people into going up mountains, but I think it’s the natural evolution of what happens when you get a tool like this.”
Regardless of the resources recreators use, experts have the same advice: When you’re headed to a new place, make sure you double-check your information against reliable, authoritative sources like up-to-date public-land agency maps and websites, trail association websites or guidebooks. Even better, talk to a real-live guide, a national forest official or a park ranger.
“If you’re going to go into places that will kill you,” Meyers said, “you should take your planning seriously.”

Rep. Dan Goddard, shown here at a Jan. 11, 2023, committee hearing, died Oct. 29, 2026, just days before his 79th birthday. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Rep. Dan Goddard, who served in the Kansas House since 2023, died Thursday. He was 78.
Goddard was a Parsons Republican who served in the Kansas Senate from 2017 to 2021 and was elected in 2022 to the House.
In an interview with Kansas Reflector after announcing he would not run for reelection this year, Goddard said he had never dreamed of being a politician. Instead, he joined the U.S. Air Force, becoming a pilot and serving for 24 years. After that, he worked to support economic development at closed military bases.
“I came to Kansas without a political thought in my mind,” Goddard said as his final session in the Legislature came to a close. “There are some great, great people in this chamber on both sides of the aisle. I’ve made friends that I will never, ever, ever forget.”
Those friends went online to mourn his passing. Senate Minority Leader Dynah Sykes, a Lenexa Democrat who is running for state insurance commissioner, wrote in a Facebook post that she was grateful for his kindness and friendship.
“Dan was always willing to work together and support good policies, despite us coming from different sides of the aisle,” she said.
