title: Opinion: Thank goodness President Trump will return to Kansas. Now he can check out all our hot GOP men!
description:
From left, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt attend a Topeka rally featuring Vice President JD Vance on Oct. 26, 2026, in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)We know that President Donald Trump appreciates the finer points of a masculine physique.
He’s told rally audiences repeatedly in recent[...]
text:
From left, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt attend a Topeka rally featuring Vice President JD Vance on Oct. 26, 2026, in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)We know that President Donald Trump appreciates the finer points of a masculine physique.
He’s told rally audiences repeatedly in recent weeks about the primo posteriors of Republicans running for office. He’s praised their good looks, straight from “central casting.”
“I looked at his ass and then I looked at his legs,” Trump said of U.S. Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio. “I said his ass — it’s like a pile of muscle.”
“Rick Jackson’s a very handsome, distinguished, beautiful-looking guy,” he opined about the Florida gubernatorial candidate. 
I was concerned when news came Thursday that Trump had canceled a Saturday rally in Salina. Think of all the missed opportunities to ogle the glorious glutes of Kansas candidates! Surely they had good looks to spare.
But my worries were assuaged when Trump reconsidered and decided to visit Kansas on Sunday instead. Hopefully, we can hear his tributes to the macho men of the Sunflower State’s GOP. Allow me to offer a few pointers. As a gay man, I obviously have opinions about the attractiveness of various menfolk, but I have made a practice of keeping such opinions to myself.
The president has shown me a new way. (And thanks to photographer Thad Allton for capturing these stunning shots of top Republicans at Vice President JD Vance’s recent Topeka appearance.)
 
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall points into the crowd at an Oct. 26, 2026, rally featuring Vice President JD Vance in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
Look at this silver fox! U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall has a beautifully blended mane, mixing light and dark shades. Move lower on his face and you’ll glimpse blindingly white choppers. Some might say they’re a bit too much, but just as Marshall took a bite out of all the low-income Kansans he sued for not paying their medical bills, he’ll take a bite out of liberal priorities in Washington, D.C.
You might want to watch for his skin tone, though. In a recent Fox News appearance, Marshall appeared to be emulating the president’s pumpkin-hued face. We all know how attractive that is, of course, but we don’t want Marshall to just be a copycat.
 
U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt raises his arms in enthusiasm at the Oct. 26, 2026, rally featuring Vice President JD Vance in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
What a meaty mountain of a man!
U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt‘s campaign website declares that he’s “standing tall for Kansans,” and the towering 2nd District congressman has the height to spare. Schmidt served three terms as Kansas attorney general, but he fell short in challenging Gov. Laura Kelly’s reelection bid four years ago. No worries — the prettiest face doesn’t always win in the popularity contest.
Schmidt faces a surprisingly competitive race this year from Democrat Don Coover, but perhaps he has the standing to persuade voters.
 
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach gestures to the crowd at the Oct. 26, 2026, rally featuring Vice President JD Vance in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
Just look at that jawline! Kris Kobach might have lost his bid for U.S. Senate against Marshall back in 2020. He might have lost his bid for the Kansas governor’s race against Kelly back in 2018. But he hasn’t lost his bid for the squarest face of any Kansas politician.
If any single Kansas Republican could be described as being built out of LEGO bricks, that politician is Kris Kobach. Those sharp edges complement his sharp approach to immigration and crime. They don’t necessarily reflect the sharpest legal mind, though.
He also really likes guns, so look for his pin-up calendar any day now.
 
Kansas gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson speaks at the Oct. 26, 2026, rally featuring Vice President JD Vance in Topeka. (Photo by Thad Allton for Kansas Reflector)
We’ve saved the dreamiest for last.
Republican Senate President Ty Masterson is a vision of well-oiled brilliance. First off, look at that pompadour. It’s a pompadour that says: “It doesn’t matter how much I do at my Wichita State University ‘GoCreate’ director job, my style sense gets me through.”
Second, look at that snazzy suit. Always well-tailored, Masterson has been a vision on two legs at the Kansas Statehouse for years. If the polling is to be believed, he might soon bring that incendiary hotness to Cedar Crest.
I kid, of course.
Trump, 80, may enjoy verbally caressing the highs and lows of younger candidates’ bodies (as well as the derriere of Trinidad-born rapper Nicki Minaj). Kansas has been blessed with a bountiful harvest of buff hopefuls. But does any of that really serve our cities and towns and farms? Do external qualities represent who’s best to guide us all into the future?
I think we all know the answer.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Maryland Matters
title: Frederick GOP wants investigation of Baltimore campaign consultant
description: Frederick County Republicans are asking state election officials to investigate a high-profile Maryland political fundraiser who they say violated state laws barring coordination between a super PAC and a candidate. (File photo by Danielle Gaines/Maryland Matters)Frederick Republicans say a high-profile Maryland political fundraiser violated state laws barri[...]
text:
Frederick County Republicans are asking state election officials to investigate a high-profile Maryland political fundraiser who they say violated state laws barring coordination between a super PAC and a candidate. (File photo by Danielle Gaines/Maryland Matters)Frederick Republicans say a high-profile Maryland political fundraiser violated state laws barring coordination between candidates and a super PAC.
The complaint, filed this week with the state Board of Elections by the Frederick County Republican Party, alleges that Baltimore-based consultant Sophia Silbergeld was paid last fall to work on a fundraising effort for Frederick County Executive Jessica Fitzwater, a Democrat.
Silbergeld now serves as treasurer of United Frederick, a political action committee that had spent nearly $500,000 as of Friday on mailings and online advertising attacking Jeff Holtzinger, Fitzwater’s Republican opponent for county executive. That constitutes an illegal coordination of campaigns, the Republicans charge.
“A consultant cannot work for a candidate and also run the Super PAC supporting that candidate,” said a statement from Justin Wages, chairman of the Frederick County Republican Central Committee.
“The law presumes coordination in exactly this situation,” the statement said. “Voters deserve to know whether it happened, and whether the people spending … to influence this election are legally separate from the campaign.”
The two events occurred within the state’s 18-month exclusion window meant to prevent coordination between candidates and independent groups.
Lierman seeks another term, Dunn just wants an ear in subdued comptroller’s race

“None of these facts alone proves coordination,” the county Republicans said in their statement. “Together, they raise questions the Board should answer. The Committee has filed a complaint with the Board asking it to investigate.”
Silbergeld is president of Baltimore-based Adeo Advocacy’s political division, which counts a number of high-profile clients, including Comptroller Brooke Lierman and Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City). She said Fitzwater “is not a client,” but declined to speak about the complaint.
She said she has not yet received a copy or formal inquiry from state elections officials. “When I receive a complaint, I plan to respond to it,” Silbergeld said.
In a statement, the Fitzwater campaign said Adeo Advocacy was hired “to manage a standalone event” roughly nine months before the formation of United Frederick. The campaign said Adeo had no access to “proprietary information.” Adeo has not worked for Fitzwater since, according to campaign and state records.
“The campaign does not coordinate or communicate with PACs such as United Frederick,” the campaign said.
The Republican complaint is the latest twist in a Frederick County executive race that appears tighter than expected.
Silbergeld’s website links to a Baltimore Banner story listing Fitzwater as a client, but in comments to the Frederick News-Post she said the reference in the Banner was an error. She said she organized a single campaign event for Fitzwater at the behest of David Trone, the former congressman and a Fitzwater supporter.
Trone is one of three donors who has helped pump $550,000 into the United Frederick PAC, along with the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees and the Maryland State Education Association.
Reports filed in January by the Fitzwater campaign show a $5,000 payment in November 2025 to Paul Fulcher as a reimbursement for fundraising expenses. Fulcher is the treasurer for the Fitzwater campaign.
The payment notes Silbergeld’s firm as the ultimate recipient of the payment. Maryland Matters asked the campaign how it reported the payment and was told Fulcher was reimbursed after he “used his personal credit card to pay” Silbergeld.
Maryland has one of the toughest independent expenditure laws in the country, requiring an 18-month separation period to ensure consultants and staffers are not enabling coordination between a candidate and super PAC activities.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
So-called independent expenditure groups can raise and spend almost unlimited amounts. Maryland law sets 48-hour reporting deadlines to provide transparency. Other provisions are meant to ensure candidates and those outside entities are not coordinating.
“The whole point of this law is to protect the political process,” said Jared DeMarinis, state election director.“We want to make sure that when we say that they’re independent, they truly are independent from the candidate.”
DeMarinis said the law is an attempt to balance concerns about the flood of money in campaigns with constitutionally protected political speech.
“What you can protect is the integrity,” he said. “Maryland has taken a very hard line in saying, when we say independent spending, you are independent and you will be spending this money without coordination or without any sort of consultation with a benefiting candidate.”
DeMarinis confirmed receipt of the Republican complaint. He declined to discuss any specifics.
Complaints related to campaign coordination are rare. The one involving Silbergeld is just the second. Elections officials were also asked to issue a “declaratory ruling” for a Republican consultant looking to ensure they were not violating the law.
Violations of election law related to coordination are considered misdemeanors. The accused carries the burden of proving they are false.
One way to do that is to show there was a firewall between the “insider information” and the consultant.
DeMarinis said it is possible for candidates and independent expenditure groups to have shared vendors — even consultants — “as long as there is a firewall established restricting the sharing of strategic campaign information between those individuals.”
The Republicans, in their letter to state elections official, acknowledge the possibility of a firewall or a declaratory ruling from elections officials sanctioning the shared vendor.
“We have seen no indication that ether exists,” they said in their letter.

text:

TUPELO — Former President Bill Clinton campaigned for Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom on Friday, casting Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith as out of touch with Mississippians struggling with surging consumer prices and lack of healthcare.
Clinton, joined by longtime adviser James Carville, argued that Colom, a district attorney in northern Mississippi, would work across party lines and put “Mississippi first,” while accusing Hyde-Smith of putting President Donald Trump first and rubber-stamping his agenda.
“I’m supporting Scott because he will honestly give you his opinion, and if you disagree, he’ll have a conversation with you. And if you can change his mind, he’ll change his mind,” Clinton said. “You can’t put MAGA first. You have to put Mississippi first.”

The crowd of roughly 400 people broke out with chants of “We want Scott” and “If we vote, we win,” mirroring other Colom rallies in Columbus and Biloxi. 
Colom’s campaign has drawn national attention to Mississippi, prompting pundits to ask whether a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982 could flip to blue. 
Former President Bill Clinton speaks to a crowd of Scott Colom supporters in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodayFormer President Bill Clinton speaks to a crowd of Scott Colom supporters in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodayFormer President Bill Clinton greets the crowd in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodayDesoto county residents Kelly Jacobs, left, and Betty Sheffield-Fargo, right, hold signs welcoming former President Bill Clinton in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026.Democratic candidate for US Senate Scott Colom speaks to a crowd of supporters in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodaySupporters stand in line before a Scott Colom rally featuring former President Bill Clinton in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodaySupporters stand in line before a Scott Colom rally featuring former President Bill Clinton in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi TodayFormer President Bill Clinton speaks to a crowd of Scott Colom supporters in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi Today
If elected, Colom would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction and the first elected by popular vote, in a state with a history of some of the nation’s most brutal racial violence.
The former president panned a Hyde-Smith interview on WLOX, where she said “you know, you have so many proteins to choose from” when asked about high beef prices. 
Clinton said that was “a shopping tip, not a policy.” 
“I don’t believe we need a senator to explain the existence of chicken,” Clinton said. 
Larry Lambert, a Booneville resident, stands in line for a Scott Colom rally featuring former President Bill Clinton in Tupelo on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Credit: Richard Lake/Mississippi Today
Colom has repeatedly hammered Hyde-Smith for supporting Trump’s tariffs because he believes they’ve hurt farmers in Mississippi, a state where agriculture is the top industry. Clinton also criticized tariffs and gave a nod to how much they’ve impacted the furniture manufacturing industry in Tupelo. 
“Because you make so much furniture, you not only pay more for the food, you pay more to sit down at the table and eat it,” Clinton said. 
Clinton said Mississippians are smart enough to decide what the government should spend money on, contrasting affordable health care with Trump’s Rose Garden renovation at the White House, which he said looks like ‘the entrance to Liberace’s bedroom.” 
Hyde-Smith’s campaign has tried to use the steady string of national politicians such as Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg stumping for Colom as a liability, and label him as part of the far-left faction of the Democratic Party. 
If Colom were to pull off an upset in ruby-red Mississippi, it would be a stunning defeat for President Donald Trump in the Deep South and make the incumbent Republican a casualty of the president’s sinking popularity. 
Colom’s campaign has homed in on issues of affordability, access to health care and a rejection of Trump’s tariffs in the home stretch of his campaign. He has pledged to tackle the cuts to Medicaid that the Republican-majority Congress passed as part of the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill. 
At a Thursday night Jackson rally alongside U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina, Colom said his pitch to Republicans who may be on the fence about his campaign is to deliver what Trump originally promised to deliver for them in 2024. 
“They were promised lower grocery prices. That’s what I’m going to fight for,” Colom said. “That’s my message to them. I’m going to give you what you were promised in 2024. You were promised no more endless wars. I’m going to give you no more endless wars.”
Colom told reporters he wants to end partisan gerrymandering by largely taking redistricting out of state lawmakers’ hands. He also said he would advocate for the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, which would restore federal oversight of voting changes in states with a history of discrimination.
“We cannot allow people like Gov. Reeves to draw lines in ways where they get to pick the voters that matter. We have to make sure that independent commissions draw lines that empower the voters to pick the leaders.” 
Clyburn told a crowd of roughly 100 people they should elect Colom because he is interested in being a public servant and “not interested in being a partisan.”
Clyburn said he has encountered people who have grown dissatisfied with politics and don’t plan to vote because they believe one vote won’t make enough of a difference. He pushed back on that idea.
“The most critical things that happened to fairness in this country were each decided by one vote,” Clyburn said.
He pointed to the 1876 presidential election, when no candidate won a majority of Electoral College votes amid disputed results in several states. Congress formed a 15-member commission to settle it, and the commission voted 8-7 to award the presidency to Rutherford B. Hayes. Hayes later withdrew federal troops from the South, effectively ending Reconstruction. 
Like Clyburn, Colom has urged the crowd to “write a new chapter” in Mississippi’s history that lifts the state as a whole and depart from the chapters stained with divisive history. 
“There is nothing wrong with Mississippi that can’t be fixed with what’s right about Mississippi,” Colom said.

text:
Democratic state Rep. Amy Walen is running for reelection and faces a tough challenge from Jessica Forsythe, a fellow Democrat. (Walen Campaign photo)Tiffany knows fashion. Lita opines on the outdoors. Their online content creations draw thousands of views from those seeking their advice and recommendations.
Recently Tiffany and Lita veered into politics, posting Instagram videos urging their followers to back the re-election of Democratic state Rep. Amy Walen of Kirkland over Jessica Forsythe, a Democratic challenger.
Neither influencer lives in the 48th Legislative District in King County that Walen represents.
Both creators — and a handful of others — got paid for their pitch from the resources of Washington Needs to Compete, a political committee with a huge treasury and savvy leaders betting this approach, used increasingly in campaigns across the country, will pay dividends in the smaller battleground of a legislative district.
“Working with creators is simply another way to reach voters and share information about the issues that matter to them,” said Nick Streuli, an officer with the political committee who worked as a top policy adviser to Washington’s Democratic former Gov. Jay Inslee.
“Campaigns have long used a variety of channels to communicate with voters, and social media is increasingly part of that mix. This effort is no different,” said Streuli, managing partner of Sundial Advocacy.
Jessica Forsythe, a Democrat, is challenging Democratic state Rep. Amy Walen in Tuesday’s election. (Forsythe Campaign photo)
The tactic drew fire from the leader of a political committee funded by statewide unions and Democratic legislative caucuses that is spending a small warchest to unseat Walen.
“Amy Walen’s campaign is so uninspiring that her corporate special interest backers needed to pay a firm in Wyoming $105,000 to buy phony influencer support from people who don’t even live in the 48th District,” said Kurt Fritts, director of New Direction PAC.
High Stakes
Walen, a moderate Democrat, is a business owner and former Kirkland City Council member. She won her House seat in 2018 and is seeking a fifth term. Last year, in a special election, she lost to Sen. Vandana Slatter, a Democrat to her political left. 
This year, she’s locked in a fierce battle with Forsythe, a two-term Redmond City Council member who is a progressive Democrat. She enjoys backing of Slatter and former governor Jay Inslee.
Forsythe won the primary by 17 votes, setting the stage for a potential nail-biter in Tuesday’s election.
A major policy on which they diverge is the state’s new income tax, a 9.9% levy on households with earnings of more than $1 million a year.
Walen voted against the income tax bill that her Democratic colleagues passed and Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson signed. In this election, she said she is voting for Initiative 645 to repeal the tax. Even so, Ferguson has endorsed her reelection. So too have former governors Gary Locke and Christine Gregoire, both Democrats.
Forsythe said she supports the tax  and will vote to keep it in place. She’s said she’ll work “really hard to ensure that it stays at the million-dollar threshold.”
Big money
Entering the weekend, Walen had reported spending roughly $382,000 to Forsythe’s  $128,000. The combined total of the candidates pales in comparison to the nearly $2 million spent by political committees boosting and attacking each of them.
Leading the way is Washington Needs to Compete, the brainchild and political vehicle of Microsoft president Brad Smith. Of the $13.8 million it has raised, nearly $5.1 million is from Microsoft, followed by T-Mobile at $1 million, according to filings with the state Public Disclosure Commission. 
The PAC had shelled out close to $3.2 million as of Wednesday, with $700,068 worth of independent expenditures aimed at boosting support for Walen.
New Direction PAC is keeping pace with money from its largest donors, including the Washington Education Association, Washington Federation of State Employees, SEIU and the Kennedy Fund, which is the political arm of the state Senate Democratic Caucus. That fund has contributed $950,000 since June.
In this race, New Direction has spent close to $690,000, based on state campaign finance records. Roughly $400,000 has gone to support Forsythe and the remainder trying to bring down the incumbent.
The Influencers entered the fray earlier this month when Washington Needs to Compete paid $105,000 to Ryegrass LLC in Wyoming for what is described in campaign finance records as social media management and posting. Ryegrass describes itself as the “leading influencer agency” with access to more than 17,000 creators and influencers in Washington.
“In a time of trust & efficacy erosion in digital media, Ryegrass engineers virality that earns votes, creates conversations, and impacts policy and elections,” reads its website.
At least six influencers posted Instagram videos endorsing Walen. Each video notes that they are paid for their post by Washington Needs to Compete.
How much those videos influence voters is uncertain. More clear is that with two Democrats on the ballot, the district’s independent and Republican-aligned voters could swing the outcome.
At a recent forum, each was asked to make their best pitch to win over a Republican voter.
“I guess what I would say is I have demonstrated my independence in the Legislature,” Walen said. “I listen to everyone. I’ve demonstrated my willingness to get into the nuance, consider the unintended consequences, and to partner with my friends, offer amendments, and stand up to my caucus.”
Forsythe said she has had “a long history of working with a variety of folks. I’m not afraid to get into difficult conversations and find common ground. I believe that if we move past talking points, we can all find common threads and common realities that we want to work on and we want to fix.”
The winner of Tuesday’s election will serve a two-year term in the district that takes in Hunts Point and Medina and portions of Redmond, Bellevue and Kirkland.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Voters have questions on Question 3, the congressional redistricting amendment
description: Signs for and against Question 3, the proposed constitutional amendment on congressional redistricting, on display outside a voting center in Calvert County on Thursday, the last day of early voting. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)If approved by voters, Question 3 would amend the Maryland Constitution to change the rules applying to the ways cong[...]
text:
Signs for and against Question 3, the proposed constitutional amendment on congressional redistricting, on display outside a voting center in Calvert County on Thursday, the last day of early voting. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)If approved by voters, Question 3 would amend the Maryland Constitution to change the rules applying to the ways congressional districts are drawn, making it easier for the party in control to draw a map that favors it, and limiting court challenges.
Got that? Not all voters do.
The ballot question was the product of a two-day rushed special legislative session in August and it was subsequently rewritten a month later by the Supreme Court of Maryland after a two-hour hearing in which the justices found the question “misleading.” The rewrite came on the same day ballots had to go to the printer.
The rewritten version still leaves some voters, such as Linda Frazier, a Democrat from Prince George’s County, had having to read the question “two or three times” to comprehend it.


 










View this post on Instagram






















 
A post shared by Maryland Matters (@marylandmatters)



For Frazier, the deciding factor was the support of Gov. Wes Moore (D), a vocal supporter of Question 3.
The measure was a response to President Donald Trump’s push get Republican-led states to redistrict this year, ahead of schedule, in an effort to gain a partisan advantage in this fall’s elections. It’s being championed by Moore and many other Maryland’s Democratic leaders with a simple message: It’s needed to combat Trump’s push in GOP-controlled state legislatures redraw maps and decrease voter representation.
For Frazier, hearing from Moore was enough. And Frazier, who voted Tuesday, said the Trump administration’s “not for the greater good.”
If passed, the bill would have no effect this year, but could affect elections in 2028, as Trump is scheduled to leave office. And the best Maryland Democrats could do is pick up one seat: Currently, seven of Maryland’s eight congressional districts are held by Democrats, with eight-term Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st) holding the only GOP seat.
Maryland’s Republican leaders are saying “partisan gerrymandering” and eliminating of their voices would be the result of Question 3 passing.
“It’s intentionally written to be confusing to the average person,” said Jason Scaggs, a Republican who’s seeking an at-large seat on the Board of County Commissioners in Calvert County.
“It gives ultimate control for all of the laws and tax and everything to one central power, and that’s not how our government was designed to work,” Suggs said on the last day of early voting Thursday. “Two [political] parties that fight and bicker back and forth … it kind of keeps everybody honest.”
Voters interviewed during the eight-day early voting period acknowledged they were confused and had to read and research the question several times. A Calvert County voter, who declined to be identified, called it a “reluctant vote” in favor of Question 3.
Even an expert in Maryland politics needed to conduct some research to understand Question 3.
“I’ve said it several times. I have a freaking Ph.D. in political science and American politics, and if I didn’t know what that amendment was about, I would have no idea what that amendment was about,” Todd Eberly, political science professor at St. Mary’s College, said in an interview this month.
“For the folks that will see it for the very first time in the voting booth, where they can’t even pull out their phone and try to Google, ‘What the heck does this mean?’” he said.



Questioning Question 3
Rather than reject the “misleading” ballot question on congressional redistricting this fall, the Supreme Court of Maryland decided to rewrite the question. This is what voters see on their ballots:
FOR the purpose of clarifying that certain requirements apply only to districts for the election of members of the Senate of Maryland and the House of Delegates; authorizing the General Assembly to grant original jurisdiction to the Supreme Court of Maryland to review the congressional districting plan of the State; and providing that nothing in the Maryland Constitution provides applicable criteria for the boundaries of a congressional districting plan.

title: Data center developers sue county in Arkansas over new regulations
description: Wendell Griffen, the Democratic nominee for Pulaski County judge, speaks to the quorum court on proposed data center regulations as the proposals sponsor, Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood, listens on May 12, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)The Connecticut-based company behind a data center planned in Arkansas sued local officials in feder[...]
text:
Wendell Griffen, the Democratic nominee for Pulaski County judge, speaks to the quorum court on proposed data center regulations as the proposals sponsor, Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood, listens on May 12, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)The Connecticut-based company behind a data center planned in Arkansas sued local officials in federal court Thursday over regulations targeting projects like it, claiming the county didn’t have the authority to enact such limits and that the state’s open meetings law was circumvented. 
The 38-page lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court of Eastern Arkansas, accused Pulaski County of enacting regulations targeting AVAIO Digital’s planned data center that infringe on the federal government’s authority to regulate interstate electrical transmission and commerce.
AVAIO asked the court for an injunction preventing the regulations from being applied to its project, monetary damages and for the disclosure of public records it said had been withheld from them.
It marks the second lawsuit filed in federal court this year connected to data center projects that have appeared in the state over the last two years. 
Judge denies effort to block Arkansas outlets from publishing details about data center agreement

Entergy Arkansas unsuccessfully sued the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, one of its reporters and a local resident in September over the publication of details of the utility’s power agreement for Google’s West Memphis data center that the resident obtained through a public records request. 
The regulations AVAIO is contesting went into effect earlier this week after the quorum court overrode Democratic Judge Barry Hyde’s veto of them, and were drafted in response to community anger over AVAIO’s project located just off 145th Street.
The regulations create uncertainty and threaten AVAIO’s “existing business, financial, and investment arrangements,” the company wrote in the complaint.
The lawsuit  also accused Democratic nominee for county judge, Wendell Griffen, of having “unlawful control over the Pulaski County Quorum Court,” pointing to his role authoring and advocating for the regulations.
Griffen told the Arkansas Advocate that the lawsuit was expected, and said it was the county’s “constitutional power” to regulate data centers within its boundaries. A spokesperson for Pulaski County did not immediately respond to a request for comment Friday evening.
The company said Griffen and several members of the quorum court engaged in polling and deliberations that violated the Arkansas Freedom of Information Act. The lawsuit also named Democratic Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood, who was the lead legislative sponsor of the regulations.
Griffen also disputed AVAIO’s characterizations of his communications with quorum court members
“If they contend that a private citizen exercising his First Amendment right to approach members of the legislative body of the county about a matter of public interest is unlawful authority, then they need to reread the First Amendment to the Constitution of the United States,” Griffen said.
The ordinance “is without effect because it is an obstacle to the full exercise of the federal government’s authorities under the Federal Power Act to regulate the transmission of electricity,” AVAIO wrote in its complaint.
The alleged polling, the company said, also makes the passed ordinance invalid.
Judge Lee Rudofsky, who oversaw Entergy’s lawsuit against the Democrat-Gazette, is the assigned judge on the case.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: DOJ again warns election officials of potential criminal prosecution, days before midterm elections
description:
A Lancaster County ballot drop box at Lancaster County Election Commission office on April 24,  2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access.
The Justice Department has sent yet another round of letters to state election offic[...]
text:
A Lancaster County ballot drop box at Lancaster County Election Commission office on April 24,  2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access.
The Justice Department has sent yet another round of letters to state election officials warning them that they could face criminal prosecution for violating federal election laws, this time reminding them that they must preserve ballots, voter-registration records, and other election materials for 22 months after a federal election.




The Nebraska context
Like the other 49 states, Nebraska’s top election official received the letter Thursday.
As Nebraska Public Media first reported, the DOJ is also sending two election monitors to Omaha-area polling places on Election Day. Nebraska voters will choose a new secretary of state from Scott Petersen, Sarah Slattery, Bob Krist, and Paul Rumbaugh.
Current Secretary of State Bob Evnen lost the GOP primary to Petersen, a challenger from Evnen’s  right. Petersen has previously described his GOP primary victory as a referendum on election integrity issues raised by President Donald Trump and others. Another factor, he said, is people’s lack of confidence in state leaders.
Robert Evnen_261029_175128




Multiple state election offices confirmed to Votebeat that they received identical letters dated Oct. 29 and signed by acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. Officials familiar with the correspondence said the letters appear to have been sent to all 50 states.
“It is a crime to willfully fail to comply with Section 20701,” the letter said, according to a copy provided to Votebeat. Votebeat also viewed letters sent to other states, which were identical. “Such a failure is punishable by up to a year in prison and a $1,000 fine.” The letter also warns that it is unlawful to willfully steal, destroy, conceal, mutilate, or alter election records.
The letters, dated Thursday, Oct. 29, came two days after a federal judge in California verbally admonished the Trump administration for threatening election officials with criminal prosecution in a separate dispute over ballots cast by suspected noncitizens.
“This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately,” U.S. District Judge David O. Carter said during Tuesday’s hearing.
In a written ruling Wednesday, Carter rejected the DOJ’s attempt to force California to set aside ballots from roughly 20,000 voters and reiterated his warning: “These threats must stop.”
Justin Levitt, a former Justice Department official and White House voting rights adviser under President Joe Biden, said he was unaware of any precedent for sending such a reminder to election officials nationwide.
“Election officials know that they have an obligation to comply with this law — they know that real, real well — and this certainly looks like it’s meant to intimidate rather than to inform,” Levitt said.
Votebeat asked the Justice Department why the letters were sent just days before Election Day, why McCotter personally signed them, and whether similar reminders had been issued before previous federal elections. The department had not responded as of publication.
Another round of DOJ warnings
Several states did not immediately see the letters. As it has before, the DOJ sent some of the letters to general or incorrect inboxes. Texas’s letter, which was delivered to the correct location, was addressed to “Sec. Jane Nelson.” Nelson left office in July.
Connecticut Secretary of State Stephanie Thomas, a Democrat, told Votebeat in a statement that her office remains focused on carrying out the Nov. 3 election.
“While I hope the decision to emphasize criminal penalties was intended simply as a reminder of the law, it could have been handled differently,” she said, adding that her office complies with the law as a matter of course, and did not need the reminder.
“This work is not something we do just because we receive a letter,” she said.
The letters are the latest in a series of warnings from the Trump administration to state election officials. A July mailing warned officials they could face prosecution for knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote, while September letters threatened civil or criminal penalties for failing to preserve records from the 2024 election.
The July letters were signed by Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general overseeing the Justice Department’s civil rights division. The September letters, signed by Eric Neff, the acting chief of the division’s voting section, directed 29 states and Washington, D.C., to preserve records in connection with ongoing litigation over access to voter-registration data. Dhillon described those notices at the time as standard litigation practice rather than threats.
The October letters, by contrast, cite an existing preservation requirement dating to 1960 without identifying a particular violation or pending investigation. They were also signed by a more senior official: McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general and the department’s second-highest-ranking official, who assumed the role in August.
McCotter has recently played a direct role in the Justice Department’s election-related litigation. Earlier this month, he signed letters to California officials, including Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, demanding that they investigate a federal list of suspected noncitizens who had received mail ballots. He gave officials 48 hours to review the list and instructed them to set aside ballots from voters whose citizenship could not be confirmed, warning that the Justice Department would seek emergency court intervention.
The Justice Department subsequently sued California, asking a judge to bar the state from counting the ballots of voters on the list. State and county officials disputed the accuracy of the federal government’s data, saying it included U.S. citizens and people who were not registered to vote. Carter rejected the department’s request Wednesday, finding that the proposed intervention could disrupt voting and prevent eligible citizens from having their ballots counted. The Justice Department appealed, and has since issued grand jury subpoenas to California election officials.
Experts question the timing and purpose
Levitt said there was nothing inherently improper about the Justice Department reminding officials of their legal obligations, but such reminders are typically prompted by concerns about compliance or understanding of the law.
“It is not itself improper,” Levitt said. “But it’s super weird that the deputy sent this letter, and it’s super weird he sent the letter to everybody.”
Joshua Douglas, an election law professor at the University of Kentucky, also questioned the timing, particularly when election officials are occupied with preparations for Election Day.
“I have never seen the DOJ send this kind of letter across the country in the days before the election,” Douglas said.
The letters impose no new legal requirements, Douglas said, but create another issue for election officials to deal with during an already demanding period.
“At least they aren’t targeting based on politics, but it feels very unnecessary and creates confusion,” he said.
The nationwide mailing also comes as federal courts scrutinize other Justice Department demands to states. On Thursday, a federal judge in Washington ordered the department by noon today to disclose which states had received letters demanding that ballots from suspected noncitizens be set aside.
Votebeat reporters Natalia Contreras, Carter Walker, Alexander Shur, Dion Nissenbaum, Hayley Harding, and Sasha Hupka contributed.
Jessica Huseman is Votebeat’s editorial director and is based in Dallas. Contact Jessica at jhuseman@votebeat.org.
Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization covering local election integrity and voting access. Sign up for their newsletters here.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: As Alaskans vote, state’s top federal prosecutor confirms criminal investigation of Dem groups
description: U.S. Attorney Michael J. Heyman for the District of Alaska speaks at an Oct. 30, 2026, news conference about U.S. Justice Department investigations into the Alaska U.S. Senate race. Next to him is Col. Maurice Hughes of the Alaska State Troopers. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The U.S. Department of Justice has launched criminal and civil investigation[...]
text:
U.S. Attorney Michael J. Heyman for the District of Alaska speaks at an Oct. 30, 2026, news conference about U.S. Justice Department investigations into the Alaska U.S. Senate race. Next to him is Col. Maurice Hughes of the Alaska State Troopers. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The U.S. Department of Justice has launched criminal and civil investigations into groups affiliated with the U.S. Senate campaign of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, Alaska’s top federal prosecutor confirmed Friday during a news conference with reporters.
Michael Heyman, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska, said there has been “a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska” since the New York Times published an article describing how Democratic campaigners sought to recruit spoiler candidates who could siphon votes away from incumbent U.S. Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, who is running for re-election.
Heyman said the investigation has been ongoing for months but the Times article gave it new momentum.
One of the people allegedly recruited by the campaigners was independent Dan J. Sullivan, who is on the election ballot alongside the incumbent, Peltola and Republican Gerald Heikes.
Despite repeated questions, Heyman did not say what law the Peltola-affiliated groups are being accused of breaking. 
Recruiting a spoiler candidate isn’t against the law unless accompanied by some other violation, such as lying to a court or offering a bribe to a candidate.
“I mean, you’re assuming that there is a crime being committed. It’s a criminal investigation, right? And that’s what we do — we investigate whether a crime has been committed under several theories, so I’m not going to comment on what those theories are, and I’m also not going to put the cart before the horse,” he said.
U.S. Attorney Michael J. Heyman for the District of Alaska speaks at an Oct. 30 , 2026, news conference about U.S. Justice Department investigations into the Alaska U.S. Senate race. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
Heyman also declined to say who is being investigated by federal officials.
Speaking Thursday night in Juneau, Peltola said she was unaware of the recruitment effort, denying one element of the Times reporting. 
Peltola’s campaign organization, Alaskans for Mary, has also denied involvement, but the Times article describes events before that group’s creation and also said an intermediary did much of the recruiting.
Separately from the federal criminal investigation, Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a state-level criminal investigation by the Alaska Department of Public Safety. That agency also declined to say who is being investigated and what law might have been broken.
In civil court, the Department of Justice has sued the Alaska Division of Elections and has asked U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason — an appointee of President Barack Obama — to prevent the state from declaring anyone but Dan S. Sullivan the winner of the U.S. Senate election.
That could allow time for further investigation, federal attorneys argued, and on Friday, they filed a motion asking a judge to order the Division of Elections to preserve all ballots cast for Dan S. Sullivan.
The Division of Elections promptly responded that it already preserves federal ballots for 22 months. 
The federal government also asked Gleason to order the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee — two groups linked by the New York Times to the recruitment effort — to turn over related text messages and other communications.
The Times relied on text messages provided by a former Peltola campaign manager when reporting its article.
That request may not matter — Gleason is expected to first rule on whether or not the Department of Justice is allowed to bring its lawsuit at all. The U.S. Constitution prescribes that states, not the federal government, are in charge of elections except where provided by Congress.
The federal government has offered a legally tenuous argument stating that the introduction to the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 gives the federal government a general interest in elections, but that argument has been opposed by the Division of Elections, Democratic groups, nonpartisan groups that have intervened in the lawsuit, the NAACP and other experts offering legal advice to the court.
Gleason has indicated that she will rule no later than Monday on whether or not the federal government has standing.
Some outside experts believe the legal actions in Alaska are part of a broader campaign by the administration of President Donald Trump to disrupt a possible Democratic wave in the ongoing general election.
National polling indicates Democratic candidates may perform significantly better than normal in races across the country during this year’s midterm elections. 
Alaska’s Senate race is one of a handful that may decide whether Democrats or Republicans control the U.S. Senate. If control of the Senate comes down to Alaska and Peltola wins but is denied the opportunity to take office, it could preserve Republican control for weeks or months longer than normal.
This week, Dunleavy declined to say whether he would certify Peltola the winner of the election if she received the most votes. 
Last week, Trump said he had ordered the Department of Justice to file the civil complaint against the Division of Elections.
Anchorage reporter Nat Herz, among a crowd of state and national journalists, asks a question at an Oct. 30, 2026, news conference held by U.S. Attorney Michael J. Heyman for the District of Alaska. The news conference was on U.S. Department of Justice investigations into the U.S. Senate race in Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
On Friday, a CNN reporter asked Heyman if he had spoken with the White House about the criminal or civil investigation.
“I have not had any discussions with the White House about those complaints,” Heyman said.
Speaking Oct. 13 at a rally in Wasilla, Trump told a crowd that he had just met with Heyman.
“I told him — I just shook his hand, took a picture — I said I hope you’re going to make sure there’s no cheating, because any place you have rank(ed) choice, you have damn bad cheating. And we can’t let that happen. So, we’re going to defend the integrity of Alaska’s elections,” Trump said.
Speaking to reporters on Friday in Anchorage, Heyman said, “This is all about election integrity. I want to encourage everyone with information on whether it be the information that we know about the Dan Sullivan issue or any other election integrity issue, to contact the FBI.”

text:
Presidents, civil rights leaders and America’s favorite humorists disagreed about plenty. On the importance of citizens showing up, their message was remarkably similar.
By George D. Rotsch, Publisher of Delaware LIVE
WILMINGTON, Del. — Americans have never needed much encouragement to complain about politics.
Will Rogers made a career out of it.
“I don’t make jokes. I just watch the government and report the facts,” the beloved humorist famously observed. The line, attributed to Rogers in a later Saturday Review quotation, still sounds surprisingly current.
But behind the jokes, arguments, campaign signs and partisan disagreements is a responsibility Americans across generations have repeatedly been reminded not to ignore:
Vote.
Not because everyone agrees.
Not because every voter loves every candidate.
And certainly not because politics suddenly becomes pleasant.
Americans vote because choosing the people who govern them is one of the fundamental privileges — and responsibilities — of citizenship.
The future is in voters’ hands
Dwight D. Eisenhower put it simply in 1949:
“The future of this Republic is in the hands of the American voter.”
Eisenhower, the general who commanded Allied forces in Europe during World War II before becoming president, went further in that speech. Americans, he argued, should stop treating politics as something that belongs only to politicians and stop assuming one vote does not matter.
His point was straightforward: Self-government requires citizens to participate in governing themselves.
Franklin D. Roosevelt delivered a similar warning during a 1944 radio address.
Roosevelt argued that Americans were unlikely to lose the right to vote because someone simply took it away. The greater danger, he said, was Americans surrendering its power by choosing not to use it.
That idea may be especially relevant in an era when political frustration sometimes becomes an excuse for staying home.
Not voting is also a choice.
It simply leaves the decision to everyone who does vote.
A powerful instrument
For millions of Americans, the right to vote was not always guaranteed in practice.
That history was central to President Lyndon B. Johnson when he signed the Voting Rights Act in 1965.
Johnson called the vote “the most powerful instrument ever devised by man” for confronting injustice.
His message was directed particularly toward Black Americans who had been systematically denied access to the ballot, but the broader lesson survives: A legal right acquires its political power only when citizens exercise it.
Martin Luther King Jr. made much the same argument during the civil rights movement, repeatedly linking voting with the ability of ordinary citizens to turn demands for change into political action.
The ballot is different from almost every other tool available to citizens.
You can complain about your taxes.
You can yell at the television.
You can argue with your neighbor.
You can post something online.
But voting is the moment when opinion becomes a decision.
A ‘crown jewel’
Republican President Ronald Reagan approached the question from another direction.
“The right to vote is the crown jewel of American liberties,” Reagan said while advocating an extension of the Voting Rights Act in 1981.
That sentiment helps demonstrate how deeply the principle crosses ideological lines.
Roosevelt was a Democrat.
Eisenhower and Reagan were Republicans.
Johnson was a Democrat.
King challenged leaders in both parties.
Yet all recognized essentially the same principle: The legitimacy of representative government ultimately rests with the people who choose it.
And there is something wonderfully American about that.
A president’s vote counts once.
A billionaire’s vote counts once.
The person standing beside you in line whose political opinions drive you absolutely crazy gets one, too.
So do you.
You don’t have to love politics
Perhaps one reason Americans sometimes tune out elections is that politics can feel exhausting.
The advertisements are relentless. The arguments are predictable. Candidates sometimes seem more interested in explaining why the other person is terrible than why they themselves deserve the job.
Will Rogers would probably have found plenty of material.
Another old political saying captures the problem neatly: “Bad officials are elected by good citizens who do not vote.”
The phrase has long been attributed to critic George Jean Nathan, although research suggests its precise origin is uncertain, and versions of it were circulating by the 1920s.
The authorship matters less than the point.
Choosing not to participate does not remove politics from your life.
Elected officials will still make decisions about schools, roads, taxes, public safety, business regulations, energy, health care and countless other issues.
The only question is whether you participate in choosing them.
Your neighbor doesn’t have to be wrong
There is another reason to vote that sometimes gets overlooked.
Voting does not require believing that everyone who disagrees with you is ignorant, dishonest or dangerous.
In fact, the American system was built around the assumption that citizens would disagree.
Sometimes loudly.
An election gives Americans a peaceful way to settle those disagreements for the moment and then return later and reconsider the decision.
The winner governs.
The loser gets another opportunity.
Citizens continue arguing.
And the country continues.
That process is imperfect, frequently frustrating and occasionally messy.
It is also extraordinary.
The simplest argument
So why vote?
Roosevelt might say because a right unused can lose its meaning.
Eisenhower might say because the future of the republic belongs to the voter.
Johnson might remind us that the ballot can change society.
Reagan might call it one of our most precious liberties.
And Will Rogers would probably make us laugh about whichever candidates we elected.
Different generations. Different political philosophies. Different ways of saying essentially the same thing.
You don’t have to agree with your neighbor.
You don’t have to belong to a political party.
You don’t have to believe your candidate is perfect.
You don’t even have to enjoy politics.
Learn about the people asking to represent you. Make your own decision.
Then participate.
Because democracy ultimately depends on ordinary Americans deciding that their voice is worth using.
TO GO
What: Learn more about the history and importance of voting in America
Why it matters: Voting allows citizens to choose their representatives, hold government accountable and peacefully decide the direction of their communities and country.
Learn more: The Eisenhower Presidential Library, Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library, Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Lyndon Baines Johnson Presidential Library maintain speeches and historical materials documenting presidents’ views on voting, citizenship and representative government.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Trump officials travel to St. Cloud to announce arrests of allegedly fraudulent Medicaid providers
description: Scott Bessent, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, speaks, flanked by Dr. Mehmet Oz, Administrator of the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, and Kash Patel, FBI Director, and other members of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud during a press conference discussing advancements in what the department calls the War on Fraud Friday, Oct. 30, 2[...]
text:
Scott Bessent, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, speaks, flanked by Dr. Mehmet Oz, Administrator of the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, and Kash Patel, FBI Director, and other members of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud during a press conference discussing advancements in what the department calls the War on Fraud Friday, Oct. 30, 2026 in St. Cloud, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Top Trump administration officials announced the arrests of four Medicaid providers at St. Cloud’s police headquarters Wednesday, alleging they fraudulently billed for services. The announcement came a day after federal and state agents raided childcare centers and early autism therapy centers.
The arrests and press conference landing just a few days before the Nov. 3 elections appeared aimed at drawing more attention to the long-running fraud crisis in the state’s safety net programs that has bedeviled the administration of Democratic-Farmer-Labor Gov. Tim Walz.
Although Republicans have sought to seize on the fraud charges as evidence of the failures of Walz and his fellow Democrats, President Donald Trump has undercut the message repeatedly by pardoning healthcare executives who have been convicted of Medicaid and Medicare fraud schemes.
Former clients of one of the defendants arrested Thursday, Jama Mohamod of American Home Health Care, have told local news outlets, including the Reformer, for over a year that Mohamod and his organization provided shoddy services. Mohamod was billing in a program called Integrated Community Supports, a state-run Medicaid-funded disability service intended to give people support to live more independently in apartments instead of institutions.
According to multiple former clients, Mohamod charged Medicaid hundreds of dollars for services that weren’t provided, created a threatening atmosphere, and — when the state’s human services department began withholding payments from ICS providers for “credible allegations of fraud” last year — effectively evicted his clients from the apartments for which he was supposed to be paying rent.
He also billed Medicaid for services that could not have been provided, due to clients being on vacation or at an out-of-town funeral, according to the indictment, unsealed Thursday.
U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel, Center for Medicaid, Medicare Services Administrator Mehmet Oz and other Trump administration officials provided a laundry list of federal initiatives on fraud in the administration’s “War on Fraud.” The effort has also led to significant funding uncertainty for legitimate Medicaid providers trying to care for Minnesota’s most vulnerable populations.
Dr. Mehmet Oz, Administrator of the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, speaks while Kash Patel, FBI Director, holds up a sign depicting a screengrab of the website of Sharmaine Meadows, who was convicted of fraud in a housing stabilization program, during a press conference discussing advancements in what the department calls the War on Fraud Friday, Oct. 30, 2026 in St. Cloud, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Oz’s Friday appearance signaled continued conflict between Minnesota and the federal government when it comes to Medicaid, which is the state-federal healthcare program for low-income and disabled people and seniors receiving long-term care. The Trump administration has threatened to cut $2 billion annually in Medicaid funding over program integrity, and has withheld hundreds of millions more.
At times, the officials gave misleading statements about the extent of fraud in Minnesota, claiming, for instance, that Minnesota disenrolling Medicaid providers was a sign of widespread fraud.
In fact, the state’s Department of Human Services, in a rush to respond to a federal deadline to re-screen and re-validate most providers, disenrolled 60% of them in  13 Medicaid services deemed high risk for fraud, waste and abuse.
Several providers reported being disenrolled because the state agency failed to process their revalidation or for bureaucratic paperwork issues, and not for suspicions of fraud.
Still, Oz, in the press conference, cited the mass disenrollment as a “degree of fraud” that “you have to purposely be averting your glance to allow to happen.”
Oz has previously misrepresented the results of the rushed re-screening process, known as revalidation. Minnesota Department of Human Services Temporary Commissioner John Connolly, in an Oct. 2 letter, asked Oz specifically to be more accurate on that front: “Providers may be disenrolled for administrative or enrollment issues that do not establish fraud, waste or abuse. … Minnesota requests that future public communications clearly and accurately distinguish suspected or established fraud, waste or abuse from administrative or funding actions.”
CMS deferred around $153 million of Medicaid claims — i.e., retroactively withdrew payment for services that were already given earlier this year — from providers because they were disenrolled in the administrative revalidation process, without specifying what concerns it had around those providers.
Connolly, in the letter, sought clarification on why those providers would constitute a fraud risk.
While the state agency struggles to get clear responses from the federal administration, service providers for Minnesota’s elderly and disabled people in turn have complained about a lack of clear communication from the state, especially around the mass revalidation process and an abrupt two-week delay in payments over the winter.
Oz did not address the domino effects of the administration’s repeated threats to Minnesota’s Medicaid funding, instead focusing on providers who defrauded Medicaid services such as the shuttered Housing Stabilization Services program.
“This housing stabilization program, which everyone on the stage thinks has merit, was shut down because of fraudsters like Sharmaine Meadows,” he said, referencing a provider convicted of a $3.6 million fraud scheme.
Walz shut the program down last year when evidence emerged that the program was riddled with fraudulent providers.
During the press conference, KARE 11’s Lou Raguse asked about the station’s recent reporting on a lucrative deal secured by CoreCivic, the private prison company, which sold its Appleton, Minn., facility to the federal government for hundreds of millions more than what the company had hoped to get from the state.
“If the administration has declared war on waste and fraud, could you explain the $420 million overpayment for a prison in Appleton, Minnesota when the company offered it to the state of Minnesota for $75 million?”
Bessent: “Yeah, I don’t know anything about that. What we are here to do is to prosecute criminal fraud. And any question like that that deflects away from it, I think is a waste of our time.”
Scott Bessent, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, listens while other members of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud speak during a press conference discussing advancements in what the department calls the War on Fraud Friday, Oct. 30, 2026 in St. Cloud, Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)

title: WA mobilizes National Guard for added security for ballot drop boxes
description: A voter deposits their ballot in a drop box in Tacoma, Washington on Oct. 29, 2026.  Washington has a mail-in voting system and election officials are urging people to use the boxes to return their ballots. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)In a precedent-setting move, members of the Washington National Guard are being deployed in seven cou[...]
text:
A voter deposits their ballot in a drop box in Tacoma, Washington on Oct. 29, 2026.  Washington has a mail-in voting system and election officials are urging people to use the boxes to return their ballots. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)In a precedent-setting move, members of the Washington National Guard are being deployed in seven counties to help protect ballot drop boxes in the final days of the election.
The mission, dubbed Election Neighborhood Watch by Gov. Bob Ferguson, appears to be the first large-scale activation of National Guard members to provide greater security of ballots cast in the state’s mail-in system. Nearly 70% of ballots returned so far arrived from a drop box.
As of Friday afternoon, National Guard members were headed to King, Pierce, Snohomish, Thurston, Clark, Lewis and Island counties. Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, who is also a National Guard member, said this “has not been done before.”
Auditors say they had not detected any credible threats to drop boxes that would prompt a request for the National Guard’s presence. But when the governor offered to provide assistance, several accepted, seizing on the opportunity to amplify their efforts at no cost to their local taxpayers.
“There’s a lot of noise about elections right now,” said Linda Kent, Pierce County’s deputy auditor. “Looking at the broader context, out of an abundance of caution additional resources is not a bad idea.”
Pierce County Auditor Linda Farmer said elections officials whose biggest worry was once power outages are now dealing with “threats against the people who work here and the actual ballots.”
Historically, the Washington National Guard has had different roles related to the election.
Cybersecurity professionals from the guard have been activated to assist with cybersecurity tasks for every election since 2016, according to the governor’s office. 
In 2024, Gov. Jay Inslee activated the guard after a drop box was set on fire in Clark County in southwest Washington. More recently white powder has been sent to offices of numerous elected officials in the state and across the country.
Election workers empty a ballot drop box in Tacoma, Washington on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
“Amid these recent developments and the highly charged atmosphere of this election, my administration is taking every precaution to ensure that every vote counts and that counties have the resources they need to monitor and respond to potential threats,” Ferguson wrote auditors.
Ferguson signed the activation order Oct. 21. It directs the guard members “to provide public safety and ballot security support” to bolster participating counties’ efforts “to ensure free and fair elections.” Election Neighborhood Watch began Monday and will end at 12:01 a.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 10.
National Guard personnel are to be unarmed and in plainclothes, not their uniforms. They are not to interact with voters or have a conspicuous presence at drop boxes, voting centers or other locations where ballots are getting cast. Their role is to observe. If they see someone trying to tamper with a box or other unusual activity, they are to call 911 or notify local authorities.
In Pierce County, they will be doing a “roving survey” of boxes. There, and in other counties, that will likely mean driving around at night and overnight, making visual checks
“We don’t want anybody camped out,” Farmer said. On election night there will be trained observers on hand to lock up and empty boxes when voting ends at 8 p.m.
King County is taking a similar approach.
“They will simply be additional eyes and ears at drop boxes and Vote Centers, and supplement our existing security plans,” emailed Halei Watkins, communications manager for King County Elections. “This is not intended to be a visible presence, but more folks to say something if they see something.”
Meanwhile, the U.S. Department of Justice is sending eight monitors to King County. Watkins said they are interested in observing ballot counting, vote centers, and some of the county’s 101 drop boxes. The last time federal monitors were sent to the county was 2008.
Elections Director Julie Wise said they’ll have “the same level of access as the public does. Nothing more, nothing less.”
Yakima County will also have a couple federal monitors. They won’t be coming inside the election center, and will only interact with people who engage with them, said county Auditor Charles Ross. Yakima hosted court-authorized observers in 2004 under a consent decree related to Spanish language election access, but they weren’t staff from the Justice Department. 
“We regularly welcome observers of all kinds, and are confident in our team and processes,” wrote Watkins, of King County. “We are expecting smooth sailing.”
Reporter Jake Goldstein-Street contributed to this report.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Kenis Lopez Gonzalez to be freed, returned to U.S. from Central African Republic
description:
Kenis Lopez Gonzalez. Courtesy photo. A federal judge has ordered the federal government to immediately return Kenis Lopez Gonzalez to the U.S. from the Central African Republic, where he has been detained since August despite having no ties to the country. 
Lopez, who has no criminal record, arrived in the U.S. in 2022 from Nicaragua and turned himself in t[...]
text:
Kenis Lopez Gonzalez. Courtesy photo. A federal judge has ordered the federal government to immediately return Kenis Lopez Gonzalez to the U.S. from the Central African Republic, where he has been detained since August despite having no ties to the country. 
Lopez, who has no criminal record, arrived in the U.S. in 2022 from Nicaragua and turned himself in to immigration authorities at the border. In 2024, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to his home country because he was at risk of torture. 
After he was arrested outside his Shakopee home in January, Immigration and Customs Enforcement held him in various detention centers before deporting him to the Central African Republic in August. Lopez is among more than 25,000 people deported to countries that aren’t their home country since President Donald Trump took office in 2025.  
Following oral arguments on Friday afternoon, U.S. District Judge Jeffrey M. Bryan ordered that ICE return Lopez to Minnesota expeditiously, where he will — at least for now — return to the same immigration status he held before he was arrested in January. 
During Friday’s hearing, Justice Department attorneys indicated they would file a motion requesting that Bryan extend the timeline for Lopez’s return, so that they have time to appeal the order.
Bryan, in a strongly-worded opinion, found that Lopez risked irreparable harm if allowed to remain in the Central African Republic; that his case against the government was likely to succeed; and that it was in the public’s best interest that ICE follow its own policies and return Lopez. 
ICE has not always followed court orders. During the two-and-a-half months of Operation Metro Surge, the agency violated 210 court orders. In some cases like Lopez’s, the federal government has dragged its feet returning people. On Oct. 7, for instance, a judge ordered the Department of Homeland Security to bring  Ahmed Soliman back from Equitoreal Guinea. He still has not arrived in the U.S.  
Seemingly aware of such cases, Bryan mandated a nine-step process, with deadlines, for immigration officials to facilitate Lopez’s return.  
Much of Bryan’s questioning in the hearing centered on Lopez’s expression of fear of removal to the Central African Republic. Immigrants who fear persecution in their home countries are entitled to hearings to determine whether those fears are justified and warrant a cancellation of deportation — exactly what happened in Lopez’s prior immigration case, when a judge found that his fear of return to Nicaragua was justified, and blocked his deportation. 
When Lopez learned he was about to board a plane to Central African Republic, he expressed fear to the staff. But he was not permitted a hearing on the subject. Instead, agents used projectiles — either rubber bullets or pepper balls — to force him and others off of the bus. They wrapped him in a full body restraint and carried him onto the plane. 
“The threat of irreparable harm to Lopez of remaining in the Central African Republic while his claims are pending is self-evident and was known to Defendants well before they ever forced Lopez (with quickly developing bruises and welts) onto a flight to the Central African Republic,” Bryan wrote. 
The government’s argument that Lopez does not face the risk of harm in the Central African Republic, Bryan wrote, is “plainly disingenuous.”
‘Diplomatic assurances’
David Fuller, assistant U.S. attorney for the District of Minnesota, argued that Lopez was not entitled to a hearing on his fear of removal to Central African Republic because it was not the country — Nicaragua — named in his immigration case for the threat of torture. 
Fuller and Bryan have met before: In early March, Bryan summoned Fuller and his boss, U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen, to his courtroom to explain why they should not be held in contempt for failure to comply with court orders.
Fuller’s argument also relied on “diplomatic assurances” from the government of the Central African Republic that detainees would be treated humanely in accordance with international law. 
The Central African Republic has been mired in political violence for years, especially since rebels took power in 2013. The State Department website, updated in January, warns Americans not to travel to the country due to risks of unrest, crime, kidnapping, health, terrorism and more. Corruption is a “significant concern,” the State Department warns, and armed groups control large areas of the country. 
“It’s a little difficult to juxtapose what the Department of State tells people about living in the Central African Republic — even the existence of a government there — and a statement that some government officials have provided ‘diplomatic assurances’ of something,” Bryan told Fuller. 
And, later in oral arguments: “I’m sure you’ve seen the Department of State reports about the Central African Republic,” Bryan said. 
“I must admit I have not, and I don’t know what it says, but that would fall into the purview and the province of the Department of State,” Fuller replied. 
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is a defendant in the lawsuit. 
In his order, Bryan extensively cited the State Department’s report on the Central African Republic to demonstrate the risks Lopez faces there.  
Little is known about the terms of the deal between the U.S. government and the Central African Republic. The federal government began sending deportees to the country after paying $85 million to the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration in the Central African Republic. That organization is overseeing the detention center in the capital city of Bangui, where Lopez is held. 
Christopher Landau, the deputy secretary of state, sent a letter to interim ICE director Todd Lyons in May stating that the government of the Central African Republic assured the U.S. that “it would treat any third-country nationals transferred from the United States to CAR in a manner that is in accordance with its international legal obligations and that the third-country nationals removed to CAR would not be subjected to persecution.”
“It is the Department of State’s view that the assurances received from the CAR government are credible and reliable,” Landau wrote. 
He ended the letter by asking the Department of Homeland Security to “refrain from publicly discussing our cooperation with CAR on this matter.” 
The letter was submitted by U.S. attorneys as evidence in Lopez’s case. 
“The Court is left to presume the reason for asking DHS to refrain from making the arrangement public; perhaps it is because they do not want the general public to know that they have agreed to forcibly relocate prisoners to a country in which foreign nationals will be subject to the known and serious danger,” Bryan wrote in his order. 
As an exclamation point, Bryan’s final point in the order prohibits the government from shooting Lopez with rubber bullets or any other projectiles, at close range or otherwise.

title: Para que conste: El hombre de Fresno deportado por ICE tenía antecedentes de cruces ilegales
description:
