text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Un inmigrante deportado, cuyo perfil fue publicado en un artículo de CalMatters a principios de esta semana, no reveló sus antecedentes penales ni su historial de deportaciones a nuestro medio de comunicación.
 CalMatters se enteró de sus antecedentes a través de una publicación en redes sociales del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas de Estados Unidos que atacaba a la organización de noticias el jueves.
La cuenta en X (Twitter) de ICE afirmó que Luis Arreguin había sido deportado cinco veces y que tenía “antecedentes penales que incluían agresión con agravantes con arma, delitos con armas de fuego y conducir bajo los efectos del alcohol”, y señaló que CalMatters no incluyó ese contexto en su artículo publicado el miércoles.
 La editora en jefe de CalMatters, Kristen Go, declaró que la reportera de este medio de comunicación sin fines de lucro intentó comunicarse dos veces con el equipo de prensa de ICE durante un período de seis días, sin obtener respuesta. La reportera también consultó los antecedentes de Arreguin en una base de datos judicial y en una base de datos de registros públicos, pero en ninguna de ellas se encontraron los registros que ICE describió.
 “Siempre queremos creer lo que nos dicen nuestras fuentes, pero como periodistas, también tomamos medidas para verificar esa información”, dijo Go. “En este caso, hicimos una verificación de antecedentes y nos comunicamos con ICE en dos ocasiones. No fue sino hasta después de que se publicó nuestro artículo que ICE decidió proporcionarnos la información que habíamos solicitado”.
 “Creemos en la transparencia por parte de las personas sobre las que informamos y extendemos ese mismo estándar a nuestros reportajes.”
 Arreguin fue arrestado hace un año en el condado de Fresno por un cargo de agresión. La Fiscalía decidió no procesarlo y no presentó cargos, según informó un portavoz.
 La reportera Wendy Fry envió al equipo de prensa del ICE siete preguntas sobre el historial migratorio de Arreguin la noche del 21 de octubre, solicitando la base legal para la deportación de Arreguin y los hechos básicos de su detención.
 «No encontramos antecedentes penales recientes del Sr. Arreguin. ¿Acaso el ICE o el gobierno federal lo consideraron una amenaza para la seguridad pública? De ser así, ¿por qué?», preguntó Fry en el correo electrónico.
 El resto de las preguntas buscaban confirmar algunos elementos del relato de Arreguin sobre su detención y su huida para ser deportado.
Fry envió un correo electrónico de seguimiento a ICE el martes siguiente: “Volvemos a traer a colación esto. Nuestra historia se publicará mañana”.
 Go afirmó que Fry no recibió respuesta a esas preguntas.
En su artículo, Fry citó a miembros de la familia Arreguin, quienes repitieron la versión del hombre. CalMatters se ha puesto en contacto con ellos y con Arreguin para obtener sus comentarios, pero no ha recibido respuesta.
Contactada el jueves, la hija de Arreguin dijo que su padre estaba centrado en describir su terrible experiencia en su entrevista con la periodista y que no tenía intención de ocultar su deportación ni sus antecedentes penales.
 El jueves, un día después de la publicación del artículo de Fry, un reportero de Fox News escribió en las redes sociales que fuentes del gobierno federal le habían dicho que Arreguin había sido deportado cinco veces.
 Exactamente 30 minutos después, el ICE citó el mensaje del reportero de Fox News en una publicación en sus redes sociales.
 “Nos gustaría creer que las agencias gubernamentales actúan de buena fe, pero cabe preguntarse por qué el ICE esperó hasta después de la publicación y, aun así, no se puso en contacto directamente con el periodista”, dijo Go.
 ICE no respondió de inmediato a las preguntas de CalMatters sobre su respuesta, ni sobre si el equipo de redes sociales tiene acceso a registros que no están disponibles para el equipo de prensa que responde a las solicitudes de los periodistas.
 La agencia aún no ha respondido a las preguntas iniciales de Fry.
 Edward Wasserman, profesor de periodismo y ex decano de la Escuela de Periodismo de la Universidad de California en Berkeley, afirmó que es imposible saber si una agencia tan grande como ICE “obstaculizó deliberadamente la investigación”.
 “Es peligroso especular sobre si tenían algún motivo”, dijo Wasserman.
 Desde una perspectiva de relaciones públicas pragmática, dijo Wasserman, la estrategia de divulgar información después de que se haya publicado una noticia no ayuda a la causa de una agencia.
 “En realidad no les conviene”, dijo.

title: Matos campaign asks RI elections board to investigate Loughlin’s financial reports, TV buys
description: NBC 10 moderator Gene Valicenti speaks with Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos, center, and Republican challenger John Loughlin after Wednesday’s lieutenant governor debate at the Providence Performing Arts Center on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)With just days to go before Tuesday’s general election, Democratic Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos’ camp[...]
text:
NBC 10 moderator Gene Valicenti speaks with Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos, center, and Republican challenger John Loughlin after Wednesday’s lieutenant governor debate at the Providence Performing Arts Center on Oct. 7, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)With just days to go before Tuesday’s general election, Democratic Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos’ campaign filed a complaint with state elections officials against her Republican opponent John Loughlin Thursday alleging Loughlin’s campaign manager improperly reported and benefited from taxpayer-funded campaign money.
Loughlin denies the allegations. 
“The Matos campaign’s letter is a textbook example of either a fundamental misunderstanding of how media is purchased or a deliberate attempt to invent a scandal where none exists,” Loughlin wrote in a letter to the Board of Elections that he also shared with Rhode Island Current Friday.
The Board of Elections declined to say Friday whether or not the issue was being investigated.
Loughlin filed his campaign spending report by the Oct. 27 deadline, listing $659 in expenses. The next morning, he amended his final pre-election campaign finance report twice, with both totaling $3,641 in expenses.
The next day, the Matos campaign asked the Rhode Island Board of Elections to investigate whether Loughlin’s campaign manager improperly benefited from taxpayer-funded campaign money, a practice the Matos team has characterized as “skimming.” 
After the Matos campaign filed the complaint Thursday morning, Loughlin amended the report a third time, listing $58,651 in campaign expenditures for the period ending Oct. 26. The newly added expenses total $55,010, including two $25,000 expenditures for TV ads — one each for WJAR and WPRI — plus $5,010 in radio ads.
Loughlin’s refiled paperwork followed a $25 late fee levied Wednesday by the Rhode Island Board of Elections, because the changes made were significant enough that they made the submission count as a late filing. State election regulations define a material amendment as one which “shall mean to add, delete, or alter more than $500, or 10%, whichever is larger, of the total fiscal sum or either the contributions or expenditures on any campaign finance report,” and Loughlin’s changes fell into this category. 
Board of Elections spokesperson Christopher Hunter did not confirm or deny whether an investigation had begun. He said that campaign finance investigations remain confidential until a violation is believed to have occurred. The person being investigated can also waive confidentiality. 
The Matos campaign’s complaint accused Chris Mueller, Loughlin’s campaign manager, of ultimately deriving financial benefit from publicly matched campaign funds. Matos’ campaign manager Mark Gray alleged in the complaint that Mueller used his advertising business to collect commissions on the television ads purchased by the Loughlin campaign.
“The report failed to reflect over $80,000 in matching public funds and $3000 in payments by his campaign, both vastly exceeding the 10% threshold for a substantially complete report,” Gray wrote of Loughlin’s original Oct. 27 filing.
Gray’s complaint distinguishes the campaign’s radio advertisements from its TV spots, claiming that the radio ads were purchased directly and without commission. He noted that Federal Communications Commission forms show the TV ads were purchased through Chris Mueller Campaigns, and cite a 15% commission for the agency. 
Gray argues that Mueller’s business and the Loughlin campaign headquarters share an address, and that Mueller filled out the required candidate advertising agreements for both the radio and TV orders. Gray concluded that this amounted to routing the television purchases through Mueller’s business, thereby allowing him to profit from publicly matched funds via the commission fees. 
Candidates who participate in Rhode Island’s public matching funds program are permitted to use the money for specified campaign expenses, including radio and television advertising. But in his letter, Gray accused Mueller’s agency of rerouting the funds and violating the law’s intent to “prevent politicians from… funneling public funds into the pockets of vendors and campaign staff.”
“It is not possible that the Loughlin campaign is not aware of these expenditures, given that all of the ads were bought directly by the campaign or by a campaign employee,” Gray wrote. “It is our belief that the Loughlin campaign, as managed by Mr. Mueller, is deliberately hiding these costs and flaunting the state’s disclosure laws in an attempt to hide their use of matching public funds from the voters.” 
A Rhode Island Current analysis of Loughlin’s FCC filings identified $58,605 in TV orders, which included $28,375 at WPRI, $26,600 at WJAR and $3,630 at WNAC. The campaign also purchased $9,790 in radio spots on WPRO, bringing the total to $68,395.
Those figures include spots scheduled to air beyond the Oct. 26 campaign finance reporting period. The television contracts also show Chris Mueller Campaigns as the buying agency and note a 15% agency commission, although these forms don’t establish that Mueller received this money, or exactly when expenses were incurred or paid.
‘No public matching funds were diverted to any individual’
Rhode Island Current contacted Loughlin and Mueller Friday with several questions. Loughlin responded by emailing the letter he sent to election officials, arguing the allegations are inaccurate and reflect a lack of insight into purchasing mores. 
“The core of their allegation rests on the difference between gross and net rates — a distinction every experienced media buyer, station salesperson, and campaign understands,” Loughlin wrote.
Loughlin said his campaign was charged a gross rate by the television stations, a standard practice. The net price, meanwhile, is calculated after removing the commission.
“When a campaign or its media buyer is billed the gross rate, the station retains the option to issue a refund or credit for the commission portion (the difference between gross and net),” Loughlin wrote. “That is standard industry practice, not a scheme.” 
So, Loughlin wrote, when the TV stations then told his campaign that a refund was available for the commission portion, the campaign told the stations to reinvest that money into more ads, rather than refund the cash.
“No public matching funds were diverted to any individual,” Loughlin wrote. “The money stayed in advertising.”
Neither Loughlin’s letter nor his revised forms have convinced the Matos campaign. 
Gray wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current Friday that, despite the Loughlin campaign’s multiple amendments, “There are still major differences between what the campaign is reporting and the FCC files.” 
Gray’s complaint is asking the elections board to revisit Loughlin’s Oct. 27 report and examine whether its multiple amendments have made it remain delinquent, and assess any penalties as necessary. 
A poll released Oct. 20 by Salve Regina University’s Pell Center found the lieutenant governor’s race was statistically tied with 44% of likely voters supporting Loughlin and 43% backing Matos. Matos performed well among women and Hispanic voters while Loughlin has stronger support among men and white voters, the poll found.
Reporter Christopher Shea contributed to this story.

description: New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Oct. 29, 2026, criticized President Donald Trump’s administration for failing to approve federal reimbursement for costs local and tribal governments are incurring as they respond to widespread flooding, including in Bloomfield, pictured above. (Photo courtesy Elmer Ignacio)New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on T[...]
text:
New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Oct. 29, 2026, criticized President Donald Trump’s administration for failing to approve federal reimbursement for costs local and tribal governments are incurring as they respond to widespread flooding, including in Bloomfield, pictured above. (Photo courtesy Elmer Ignacio)New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Thursday urged President Donald Trump’s administration to authorize additional federal assistance to northern New Mexico communities recovering from widespread flooding.
Trump earlier this week declared a presidential disaster following floods that damaged thousands of homes in San Juan County and elsewhere, a declaration that authorized assistance from various federal agencies including debris removal from the U.S. Army Corp of Engineers, flood monitoring from the U.S. Geological Survey and drinking water testing from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. 
The federal assistance is directed to four counties and four pueblos that have endured widespread flooding since Oct. 22. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
At least 10,000 homes remained “underwater” following flooding along the San Juan and Animas rivers in San Juan County, according to a disaster declaration request state emergency officials sent to Trump on Oct. 24, and dozens of homes in the Laguna, Jicarilla Apache, Zia and San Ildefonso Pueblos also incurred damage. 
Water levels were so high along some of the rivers that flood gauges broke, according to the declaration request, and levels broke records last set more than a century ago. 
But Trump’s declaration does not include assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency that the governor’s office and members of the state’s congressional declaration specifically requested. Funding from FEMA’s public assistance program, which reimburses local and tribal governments for up to 75% of costs they incur for debris cleanup and emergency protection, is absent from the list of approved assistance.  
“The president has recognized what families in San Juan County already know: This is a disaster,” Gov. Lujan Grisham said in a statement. “What hasn’t come yet is the federal commitment to help pay for the response. FEMA should already be on the ground in New Mexico, and we can’t sit and wait for them with more storms on the way. New Mexico is now forced to cover these costs while pressing our case to Washington.”
Forecasters with the National Weather Service are predicting more flooding potential, including in some of the affected areas, beginning late Saturday through Monday morning. 
In a statement, the governor’s office contends that the public assistance program approval happened automatically in other federally declared disasters in New Mexico. As a result of the lack of FEMA funding, counties and tribal governments are footing the bill for costs that they cannot afford, Lujan Grisham said.
FEMA has authorized more than $422 million in public assistance funding to local governments following the 2022 Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire in northern New Mexico, according to a Source NM review, as well as nearly $60 million in that funding following the South Fork and Salt Fires in the Ruidoso area. 
FEMA officials have not responded to Source NM’s requests for comment about the state’s request for public assistance funding, including an emailed request for comment Friday. The governor’s office’s statement Thursday said that state officials have received “indications that its request for federal financial assistance and personnel remains under consideration.”
The flooding in New Mexico this year could ultimately cost state and local governments at least $200 million, Lujan Grisham has said. 
‘A terrible crisis’: San Juan County officials describe widespread flooding impacts

In total, the governor has approved more than $55 million in state funding to address the emergency, including an additional round of $42.75 million she authorized Thursday through emergency executive orders.
Lujan Grisham concluded her statement Thursday by thanking first responders, including those who pulled families out of swift-moving water and off rooftops. At least 30 swiftwater rescues occurred in the hours following the flooding. 
“Our road crews cleared debris around the clock, and our counties and Tribal nations spent money they don’t have to keep people safe,” she said. “We’re planning now for the next storm, and we’ll keep working with our federal partners until that reimbursement is approved.”

text:
Guest Commentary written by

Christian Paiz
Christian Paiz is an associate professor of ethnic studies at UC Berkeley. He is the author of “The Strikers of Coachella: A Rank-and-File History of the UFW Movement.”


The only time I have been arrested was with Dolores Huerta in 2004.
I was 21 and an intern with the Hotel Employees and Restaurant Employees union, or HERE, which was leading a campaign to unionize workers in the Agua Caliente Casino and Resort in Palm Springs. 
The workers’ demands spoke of everyday concerns and needs, and of the marginal conditions in their absence: livable wages, for instance, for a decent home; healthcare and retirement benefits; protection from sexual harassment and assault, whether from bosses or costumers; grievance procedures to curtail abusive supervisors; employer guarantees to respect employee choices.
Facing typical hostility, HERE responded with civil disobedience. The union rallied a crowd and invited local reporters, whose stories it hoped to leverage. Twenty-five people walked into the street facing the casino and sat down to block traffic and provoke arrests.
At the center was a 74-year-old Dolores Huerta, cross-legged on desert-hot asphalt, singing, “We Shall Overcome.”
By then, Huerta, who died this week at her home in Bakersfield, had spent half a century fighting for labor rights in California. Born in 1930, she earned a college degree when few Mexican Americans graduated from high school, most being funneled into labor as children. In the 1950s, she was a leader of the Community Service Organization, a critical force in California’s civil and political rights history. And then, in 1962, she moved to Delano, where she was co-founder of the National Farm Worker Association, a precursor to the United Farm Worker movement of the 1960s and 1970s. 
In the next three decades, Huerta played a range of leadership roles — from contract negotiator to boycott organizer; from strategist to fundraiser; from media speaker to grower antagonist.
Like HERE, the UFW fought to improve worker life — from the viscerally mundane, like clean toilets and cold water in work fields, to the existential: For many, the union inspired a new sense of possibility. And like most unions, the UFW drew strength from its many members and allies.
This was certainly the case in the Coachella Valley, where Palm Springs is located. Amalia Uribe Deaztlan, for instance, joined the UFW in 1968 when she was not yet 20, picketing fields, traveling to boycott rallies and suing growers for their poisoning pesticides. Similarly, Lupe Crespo moved from Los Angeles to the UFW headquarters, where she found an eclectic group of organizers. In the late 1970s, she moved to the Coachella Valley, where she and her husband continued to unionize farmworkers and support progressive forces. 
For both women, Huerta was an inspirational role model, a militant who named and shaped our world. In turn, both contributed to the movement that made Huerta a household name. 
I do not know what Huerta in 2004 remembered of my previous home, though I can imagine that she was aware of the region’s stark geographic inequalities: an eastern half of poor, immigrant and Mexican farmworker families and a western half of wealthy white families living on a resort-based economy. Whatever her thoughts, she was there, on that asphalt, using her body to help workers gain what was rightfully theirs — as she had done in the 1950s, 1960s, 1970s, 1980s, 1990s, and 2000s. 
A lifetime of labor, in short, and a lifetime of vision.
It seemed fitting to me, then, that during the UFW’s 2024 National Convention in Bakersfield, hotel workers from Los Angeles’s UNITE-HERE Local 11 came to share their gratitude for the UFW’s aid in recent contract battles. Some spoke of a future when hotel unions demand union produce for their hotel kitchens, and when workers in California — a state that flatters itself with progressive politics while a quarter of its children remain hungry — can say their labor is respected by employers and consumers alike. 
I remember Dolores Huerta as a labor organizer who spanned nearly a century of mobilizations and, without exaggeration, helped build the largest farmworker movement in U.S. history. That movement, with all its shortcomings, inspired and sprouted organizers across the country and helped keep unions alive when their existence (like today) was in question. 
I also remember Dolores Huerta as a Latina leader, who, in her last months of life, spoke of her sexual assault by Cesar Chavez, thereby bulwarking the testimonies of other survivors and compelling an overdue confrontation with widespread male impunity. 
Lastly, I remember her as a political thinker of steely resoluteness. The ‘Si Se Puede’ chant credited to her is less a reassurance — as it is often understood — and more a cutting demand for action: You cannot hide your passivity, it says, under the claim of pessimism. 
May Ms. Huerta rest in peace, may her movement continue, and may we one day see the world you envisioned so long ago.

description:

text:
Brewers staff take in the parade crowd. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)Thousands of Brewer fans packed into downtown Milwaukee and the city’s Summerfest grounds Friday to celebrate the Milwaukee Brewers winning the first World Series in franchise history. 
As the buses and cars drove past carrying the team, its staff and local dignitaries — including Gov. Tony Evers, Milwaukee Mayor Cavalier Johnson and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic nominee for governor — roars echoed through the streets celebrating the end of more than a half century of waiting for a championship team. 
Parents lifted kids on shoulders and fans stood on every possible elevated surface, including Milwaukee Police Department vehicles, to get a glimpse of the world champion Brewers — who defeated the Tampa Bay Rays in game five of the series on Wednesday. 
On Milwaukee’s Summerfest grounds, the official team rally celebrating the win was held at the American Family Insurance Amphitheater while fans packed in to watch the video of the celebration at every stage in the sprawling festival venue. 





 








 

Fans hang from a parking garage to see the Milwaukee Brewers World Series parade. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

Fans climb on cars to see the Brewers parade go by. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

The Brewers team bus through the legs of a young fan. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

Fans watch the Brewers World Series parade. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

Fans watch the Brewers championship parade from a parking garage. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

Milwaukee celebrates the Brewers World Series victory (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

Fans in a 3rd Ward apartment building watch the Brewers championship parade pass by. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

Fans watch the Brewers championship parade. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

Fans in a 3rd Ward apartment watch the Brewers championship parade. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

Fans watch the Brewers championship rally at Summerfest grounds. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

Fans line up for Miller High Life after the Brewers championship parade. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)







 

The Office in Milwaukee serves fans downtown for the Brewers championship parade. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)






While players and coaches spoke from the stage, they repeatedly credited the fan support for carrying them through the playoffs. 
“We couldn’t have done it without these people,” Brewers Manager Pat Murphy said from the rally stage.
Days before the midterm elections, after a campaign season in which Wisconsin’s 50-50 political divide has been laid bare, Brewer fans celebrated the common ground the team offered the state. But politics was not entirely absent from the celebration. While the parade moved through the city, a plane trailed a banner noting that “David Crowley helped keep the Brewers in Milwaukee.” 
“It means everything, the whole state,” Milwaukee resident Mario Williams told the Wisconsin Examiner, adding that the celebration was for fans in “La Crosse, Wausau and Marinette.” 
“We get a bad rep,” he said of Milwaukee. “We’re a great city, multi-cultural, it’s not just all violence.” Thomas Carson, a graduate of Milwaukee’s Casimir Pulaski High School, said that Friday’s celebration was a “spontaneous combustion” of energy in the city. 
“I’ve been waiting on this day,” he said. 
Laura Toburen, who drove down from the city of Greenwood in Clark County to see the parade with her Milwaukee resident daughter and grandkids, said that after 57 years of waiting she was happy to celebrate the team and its city. 
“I love it, to feel it together and just enjoy,” Toburen said.

title: Gates stolen from Montana’s oldest Jewish cemetery
description:
The stone archway at Home of Peace Cemetery is seen on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026 in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)The gates of a 159-year old Jewish cemetery in Helena were stolen sometime this week, likely on Tuesday evening, according to Home of Peace Cemetery.
The gates, which were attached to a stone archway, were removed from their hinges and [...]
text:
The stone archway at Home of Peace Cemetery is seen on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026 in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)The gates of a 159-year old Jewish cemetery in Helena were stolen sometime this week, likely on Tuesday evening, according to Home of Peace Cemetery.
The gates, which were attached to a stone archway, were removed from their hinges and taken, and Phil Grossberg, president of the cemetery’s board, said a report has been filed with the Helena Police Department. The department could not be reached for comment by press time Friday.
Pieces of the gate’s hinges were still on the ground Friday, and a metal that used to hold the gate into the stone is bent and twisted.
“It’s bizarre,” Grossberg said. “And it’s more that it’s very unsettling because it’s more than just gates. It’s a sacred place, of course, and there’s a lot of history there.”
The reasoning for the theft was difficult to determine, he said, and it was still early in the police investigation.
“It’s hard to figure out what their intent was, other than try and benefit from it in a monetary way,” Grossberg said.
The cemetery was established in 1867, and the gates were added in 1910, according to Home of Peace Cemetery. It’s also on the National Register of Historic Places. The fence around the cemetery is original to its 1867 establishment, according to Department of Interior documents.
I gate pin is seen laying on the ground at Home of Peace Cemetery on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026 in Helena, MT. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)
“Many of the first Jews who came to Bannack and Virginia City moved on to Helena to establish businesses and families,” the register documents say. “Many of these pioneers are buried in the Home of Peace.” 
The cemetery is still active and holds burials, Grossberg said. It’s located adjacent to Capital High School and is also often used by people with dogs, which the cemetery allows, so long as people clean up after them, he added.
There’s a water tower and shed on the property, along with large, shady trees and numerous headstones.
The cemetery is offering a reward for the return of the gates and anyone with knowledge of the theft should reach out to the Helena Police department at 406-442-3233 or email Homeofpeacehelena@proton.me.

text:
(Photo by simpson33 via iStock / Getty Images Plus)
A nonprofit organization that helps refugees and immigrants in Iowa is being sued for allegedly discriminating against clients who are African, Muslim or disabled.
Alaa Elqatary-Reelitz is suing the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa. The committee is a nongovernmental, nonprofit organization dedicated to addressing the needs of refugees and immigrants. It is headquartered in Viriginia, but has an office in Des Moines.
In her lawsuit, Elqatary-Reelitz, an African-Egyptian Muslim, alleges that in September 2023 she began working in the organization’s Des Moines office as a program coordinator. She was later passed over for promotion to the positions of field office director, refugee services manager, child and youth support officer and development associate, she alleges.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Azizullah Azam, a male from Afghanistan, was hired as a case manager assistant in January 2024, the lawsuit alleges. Later, when Elqatary-Reelitz complained of what she perceived to be Azam’s aggressive and harassing conduct toward her, Azam allegedly responded by telling her he treated his wife the same way when she aggravated him.
On one occasion, the lawsuit alleges, Elqatary-Reelitz was walking through the organization’s parking lot where Azam was “waiting in his car.” According to the lawsuit, Azam threw his car into reverse, almost striking Elqatary-Reelitz, and then began “yelling at screaming” at her.
According to the lawsuit, Elqatary-Reelitz then took medical leave for treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder and later reported ongoing discrimination and retaliation to the organization’s CEO. After she was cleared to return to work, the lawsuit alleges, she was terminated by the organization.
In her lawsuit, Elqatary-Reelitz alleges that not only was she subject to discrimination, harassment and retaliation at work, but that U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants employees engaged in “biased decision-making, including against persons who were African, Muslim, Middle Eastern or disabled.”
As an example, the lawsuit alleges Elqatary-Reelitz once asked why disabled refugee clients were excluded from a program and was told it was because the program was focused on rapid job placement, which meant prioritizing young and healthy individuals.
The U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants has yet to file a response to the lawsuit, and the Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach anyone Friday at the organization’s offices in Des Moines for comment.

title: Peltola denies knowledge of spoiler candidate plan at Juneau rally
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks to supporters at a campaign event in Juneau on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola opened her remarks to a packed crowd at a Juneau campaign stop Thursday night by denying she had any knowledge of an alleged Democratic effort to recruit [...]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks to supporters at a campaign event in Juneau on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola opened her remarks to a packed crowd at a Juneau campaign stop Thursday night by denying she had any knowledge of an alleged Democratic effort to recruit spoiler candidates in the race for the U.S. Senate.
“I just want to clear the air. I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about,” she said. “I am not interested in tricking voters. I know I can beat Dan Sullivan. We know we can win this.”
The allegations stem from reporting by the New York Times, which said Peltola’s former staff members worked with a Democratic intermediary to recruit candidates who could peel votes away from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in the U.S. Senate race. That recruitment effort allegedly includes Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg, an independent running alongside Peltola and Dan S. Sullivan. Republican Gerald Heikes is also in the race.     

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks at a campaign event in Juneau on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Peltola defended her campaign: “This isn’t about me. This is about every single person in this room, every single person in this state, and this campaign has felt amazing. This is the best campaign I’ve ever been involved in, let alone be the candidate for. In 2024, we had 1,000 Alaskan volunteers,” she said, referring to her unsuccessful U.S. House re-election campaign. “In 2026, we’ve got over 15,000.”
Peltola did not directly address the civil and criminal investigations launched by the U.S. Department of Justice and the Alaska Department of Public Safety this week. At a press conference on Friday, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Alaska, Michael Heyman, declined to say what criminal laws may have been violated with the recruitment effort. 
Alaska law does not prohibit the recruitment of spoiler candidates, and the strategy has been used by both Republicans and Democrats in statewide races. 
Peltola only indirectly addressed the scrutiny from the New York Times.  
“I just feel like I’m dodging bullets left and right, you know, just with all the nonsense. And when did the New York Times become the National Enquirer?” she joked, to laughs from the crowd. “Inquiring minds want to know.”
Peltola also reassured the crowd that a recent car accident where she was rear-ended in Anchorage was not deliberate. “She was very legitimately very very drunk,” she said, to laughs from the crowd. “And so that was not a political conspiracy, in my opinion.”
She focused on her run for the U.S. Senate seat, describing it as crucial for addressing skyrocketing costs, protecting public assistance programs like Social Security and Medicaid and opposing the Trump administration’s agenda, including tariffs and the U.S. war in Iran.
“This war in Iran has to stop,” she said, to cheers from the crowd. “It is uncalled for.” 
“It is a war of choice, and we should not be there jacking up everybody’s prices,” she continued. “Freight costs have gone through the roof. Groceries are through the roof. We have a Congress that’s half millionaires and billionaires, working on a millionaire-billionaire agenda, not our agenda, not affordability agenda.” 
Peltola criticized the money flooding the midterm elections. This year’s races are the most expensive election cycle on record, with roughly $2.86 billion spent on U.S. Senate and House races so far. 
In Alaska alone, more than $40 million had been spent through the end of September, according to an accounting by AdImpact. 
She criticized attack ads as being a result of uncapped third-party campaign spending allowed by the 2010 Citizens United decision by the U.S. Supreme Court.     

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola poses for a photo with a supporter at a campaign event in Juneau on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

“We have got to put an end to Citizens United, she said. “These attack ads have just been nasty all the way around on all sides, and this is completely not the way Alaskans do things.”
Several Juneau residents in attendance told the Alaska Beacon their support for Peltola was unchanged by the Times article, and dismissed the reporting as unfounded. That included Sharon Love.
“I came to hear what she had to say about it, and I feel that she’s telling the truth. It’s dirty politics at the end of this race — I think Republicans are desperate,” she said.
Love said Alaska needs a change in representation in Congress. “I don’t think Dan has been representing Alaska very well,” she said, referring to the incumbent, who was elected to office in 2014. 
She said she was disappointed in a vote against releasing the files related to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and by reports that Sullivan’s personal wealth has grown through stock trades while in Congress. 
“He’s getting rich while he’s in Washington,” she said. 
Love also dismissed the criminal investigations related to the Peltola campaign and alleged recruitment of spoiler candidates, calling them baseless. 
“I think they’re just trying to scare voters, or change voters at the last minute,” she said. “I haven’t heard of anybody, any of my friends saying they’re going to change their vote in any way.”
Last week, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections, seeking to have a federal judge order that no one but Dan S. Sullivan can be declared the winner of the U.S. Senate election because voters might be confused by the fact that two Dan Sullivans are on the ballot.
Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee subsequently filed to intervene on behalf of the defense and told the court they couldn’t say whether Dan J. Sullivan was a candidate for the sole purpose of confusing voters.
In an amended legal complaint published after the Times article, the DOJ cited the Times article and said the Democratic groups had lied to the court.
“Nonsense,” attorneys for the campaign and DSCC wrote on Thursday. “The only one who could possibly know Daniel J. Sullivan’s true reasons for filing as a candidate is Daniel J. Sullivan, and Alaskans for Mary and DSCC’s statement that they could not admit or deny that allegation was entirely proper.”
Earlier this year, the Alaska Division of Elections removed Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg from the ballot alleging he was a sham candidate, but the Alaska Supreme Court struck down the decision saying the division did not have the authority to do so and he was eligible to run.

text:
An adult Carolina mantis is pictured on a plant. Oklahoma lawmakers have made the Carolina mantis the state predator insect. (Photo by Grandbrothers/Getty Images)OKLAHOMA CITY – More than 200 new laws take effect Sunday following a legislative session that ended in May.
Oklahoma’s newest laws run the gamut from ones designed to protect children to requiring GPS monitoring for some domestic violence defendants to new state symbols.
Here’s a few of them: 
Ban on all childhood marriage 
Senate Bill 504 sets the marital age at 18.
The measure repeals all exceptions for minors getting married, including allowing matrimony with parental permission or with a court’s permission. Existing law allowed children 16 or under to be married with a judge’s permission.
The measure passed the state House by a single vote.
“It is one more thing we can do to protect children from predators,” said Sen. Warren Hamilton, R-McCurtain.
Sen. Warren Hamilton, R-McCurtain, listens to the governor’s State of the State Address on Feb. 3, 2025, in the House chamber of the state Capitol. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
He said the measure will help preserve the dignity of marriage.
“Marriage is the biggest decision a lot of people will make,” Hamilton said.
Oklahoma becomes the 17th state to ban child marriage. 
Visitation changes
Senate Bill 2170 adds sexual abuse to the list of reasons why supervised visitation shall be required.
Under the new law, anyone who has had
substantiated findings by the Department of Human Services of  of sexualabuse of a child will be required to have a third party present when having visitation with a child.
New state symbols
Some new laws add to the state’s growing list of symbols.
Senate Bill 2159 designates wheat as the state crop.
Meanwhile, Senate Bill 2065, dubbed the “Lucile Morehouse Pollinator Act,” designates the European honeybee as the agricultural pollinator, the American bumblebee the native insect, the Carolina mantis as the predator insect, and the rainbow scarab, a dung beetle, as the soil conservation insect.
Morehouse and her mother started the Lucile’s Pollinator Project after learning that pollinators were in decline. The project provides free seeds.
Weakening the governor’s appointment powers 
Senate Bill 1327 restores the Oklahoma Tourism and Recreation Commission’s power to appoint the head of the Oklahoma Department of Tourism and Recreation.
It removes the governor’s power to make the appointment.
The action comes after the agency was embroiled in a scandal in which a restaurant vendor was convicted of defrauding the state of millions by submitting inflated invoices.
The agency head will serve at the pleasure of the commission instead of the governor, according to the measure.
Tracking domestic violence offenders
Senate Bill 1325 requires certain defendants charged with domestic violence offenses, who are released on bond, to wear a global positioning device that can be tracked by the victim.
Sen. Bill Coleman, R-Ponca City, is the author. Coleman said he talked to a number of judges who thought the measure could save lives.
Sen. Bill Coleman, R-Ponca City, sits at his desk on the Senate floor on May 21, 2025 ahead of the swearing in ceremony for a newly elected senator. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
If a victim were able to have advance warning that the defendant was approaching their home or business, it would allow the victim to get to a safe location, Coleman said.
Marijuana packaging changes
House Bill 4454 prohibits edible marijuana packaging from being attractive to people under 18. It prohibits the use of cartoons, toys, animals and food to sell the product. It also bars the product from being shaped like commercially available candy.
Jed Green, director for Oklahomans for Responsible Cannabis Action, said laws like the one created by HB 4454 can be a little subjective.
“I would urge folks in the industry to err on the side of caution,” Green said. 
Rep. Carl Newton, R-Cherokee, said the measure also requires the products to list the content of Tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the psychoactive element of marijuana, to help prevent over medication.
Adoptions and gender-affirming care
House Bill 3586 prohibits the denial of adoption based on the parents’ refusal to enable the child to accessgender-affirming care.
Raising the child consistent with the child’s biological sex does not constitute abuse, according to the measure.
A new bridge
House Bill 2123 allows the Oklahoma Turnpike Authority to build a new bridge crossing the Arkansas River in the Bixby area.
Rep. Mark Tedford, R-Tulsa, said the measure empowers the agency to start surveying and evaluating locations for their portion of the project.
Rep. Mark Tedford, R-Tulsa, front, and Sen. Adam Pugh, R-Edmond, back, wait in line for candidate filing on April 1, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Additional roads would need to be built by local entities, he said.
“It is going to be a team effort to get the proper funding and get the whole project done,” Tedford said.
‘True Grit Trail’
House Bill 1411 establishes the True Grit Trail in southeast Oklahoma.
“True Grit” is a novel written by Arkansas-born author Charles Portis that depicts 14-year-old Mattie Ross’ efforts to avenge her father’s murder. It was made into a 1969 movie featuring the late John Wayne who plays U.S. Marshall Reuben J. “Rooster” Cogburn.
Much of the story was set in Oklahoma, said Rep. Jim Grego, R-Wilburton, in a statement.
“This new trail will give us a way to show off the places made popular in the story and  hopefully will draw new visitors to this area of the state,” Grego said. “This could positively impact our local hotels, restaurants and other businesses.”
Towns and places of interest along the trail include: Sallisaw, Spiro, Bokoshe, McCurtain, Kinta, Quinton, Krebs, McAlester, Hartshorne, Wilburton, Red Oak, Bengal, Talihina, Robbers Cave State Park and the Talimena National Scenic Byway.

text:
The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals as photographed on June 12, 2017, in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)A federal appeals court panel ruled on Friday that Idaho’s abortion ban may continue to be fully enforced, including against a Boise doctor who challenged the ban’s lack of health exemption. 
A U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit panel ruled 2-1 to continue to block a lower court’s decision that would have prevented prosecution of maternal-fetal medicine specialist Dr. Stacy Seyb if he performed abortions in which he determined there were serious risks to the mother’s health or mental health. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Idaho’s laws prohibit most abortions, except in cases to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors face felony penalties and civil lawsuits of a minimum of $20,000 if they perform the procedure outside those exemptions.
Seyb’s challenge, which argued Idaho’s abortion ban’s lack of exemptions to prevent serious harm to the mother’s health or death from self-harm were unconstitutional, will continue to be litigated in court. 
Ninth Circuit Judges Kim McLane Wardlaw and Consuelo Callahan said in the majority opinion that Seyb’s argument for a constitutional right to abortion as a health-saving measure or in cases of risk of self-harm were unlikely to align with the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2022 Dobbs decision, which overturned Roe v. Wade. 
“We think it unlikely that Dr. Seyb will be able to square the district court’s perspective on the history and tradition concerning abortions with the Supreme Court’s perspective in Dobbs,” Callahan wrote. “… Idaho has a strong interest in limiting abortions to those allowed under its law. This interest clearly outweighs the potential harm to Dr. Seyb of having to abide by Idaho’s law pending the resolution of this appeal.” 
Judge Marsha S. Berzon disagreed, writing that the high court’s decision only applied to elective abortions, and not when the procedure may be medically necessary or indicated. 
Berzon agreed with district court Judge B. Lynn Winmill, whose previous order argued there was likely a “fundamental right” to abortions to preserve the mother’s health. Berzon also argued that the risk of harm for Seyb’s patients was greater than that of the state’s. 
“… with the stay imposed by the majority in place, some women with serious pregnancy complications will during the pendency of this appeal be required to continue their pregnancies at serious, permanent risk to their health,” Berzon wrote. “The risk, absent the injunction, to Dr. Seyb’s pregnant patients of serious and lasting harm short of death is definitionally a risk of irreparable injury.” 
The conservative Christian advocacy group the Idaho Family Policy Center, which helped author Idaho’s abortion ban allowing civil lawsuits against doctors, celebrated Friday’s decision in a press release. 
“Pregnant mothers don’t have a constitutional right to abortion merely because they threaten to harm themselves,” Idaho Family Policy Center Blaine Conzatti said in the release. “Women in mental health crises need treatment, not abortion. This decision ensures that our pro-life laws here in Idaho will continue protecting both mother and baby.”

text:
Sen. Pete Ricketts (left) and Dan Osborn (Right) are in a bitter Senate race.  (Photos were taken by Zach Wendling and Juan Salinas II) LINCOLN — The U.S. Senate race between one of Nebraska’s wealthiest elected officials and a former labor union leader is one of the most expensive the state has seen in direct fundraising, according to an Examiner analysis of campaign finance reports. 
Incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts, registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn and the other candidates on the ballot have raised more than $25.6 million combined. 
Osborn raised $10 million this cycle while Ricketts raised $14 million. The race has been heavy on mudslinging, with most campaign ads attacking each other. 
The former union leader spent roughly $9 million. Ricketts spent $13 million.  
The $25 million figure comes from official campaign accounts, not including outside spending from PACs. According to Open Secrets, the combined outside spending for Ricketts and Osborn is about $55 million.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Osborn had about $24 million spent against him and $10 million in support through various political action committees. Ricketts had $18 million spent against him and $1 million for him.
On the official campaign accounts side, the second-most expensive Nebraska federal race was Osborn’s bid against U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024, with a combined $21.7 million raised. 
This year’s Senate race lags behind the 2022 gubernatorial GOP primary between Charles Herbster, Gov. Jim Pillen and former State Sen. Brett Lindstrom — which brought in $26 million. The 2022 gubernatorial race brought in $28.3 million in total. 
Ricketts raised nearly $5.9 million in his successful 2024 special Senate election to finish out the remainder of Ben Sasse’s term. 
Ricketts has donated roughly $7 million to his own campaign this cycle, according to campaign finance reports. In 2006, when he lost his bid challenging U.S. Sen. Ben Nelson, Ricketts donated $12 million to his campaign. 
According to Politico, independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont disclosed he donated $25,000 to Osborn’s campaign. Both Osborn and Ricketts received most of their contributions from out of state — roughly 81% of Osborn’s funding is out of state, while Ricketts’ funding is roughly 65% out of state, according to Open Secrets.  
Early voting has already begun. The general election is Nov. 3.
Examiner Reporter Zach Wendling contributed to this report.

title: Commentary: Symbols of fascism and genocide don’t have a place in Alaska

(Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)When I was in ninth grade, my parents sent me to counseling. The reasons were twofold. One was severe depression, the other standard teenaged snootiness about how[...]
text:
Protestors hold signs outside of the Fairbanks hangar where Vice President JD Vance delivered a speech at a campaign rally for U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)When I was in ninth grade, my parents sent me to counseling. The reasons were twofold. One was severe depression, the other standard teenaged snootiness about how unfairly I believed that the world was treating me. 
The depression was something I could only be offered tools for managing, but the snootiness was more easily resolved. 
You see, the counselor was a Holocaust survivor. So after I rattled off my list of petty grievances, he calmly began telling me of his own teen years. Of the horrors he lived through and witnessed in the camps. And of his many family members who simply did not live. 
It’s too long ago for me to recall the details now, but the impression remains. It was my first direct encounter with what Adolph Hitler and his Nazi Party had done. It would take time for the lessons to fully sink in, but they did.
These lessons were bolstered by my mother, whose father and brother were career Navy men who served in the Atlantic during World War II. I never met my grandfather, but I knew my uncle well. Both he and my mother stressed to me that my job was to speak out any time I was confronted with Naziism. 
As my adult life proceeded I met others who were irreparably tied to the Holocaust. Who lost family members. Had parents and grandparents who were imprisoned. The occasional survivor. It’s something I have known about since childhood. And there is but one conclusion I have ever drawn. That there is nothing more evil than Nazis and their flag.
Thus we come to the recent Fairbanks No Kings Protest and the two men who arrived with swastika bands on their arms, waving that flag. I was not present, but video of what occurred can be found online. Both individuals have been identified. One is quite young, something clearly visible from footage of him being chased off by two women dressed, quite appropriately, in chicken costumes. The other is old enough to have no excuse. 
On one hand, the pair were fully within their constitutional rights to make the statement that they did. In the video it appears that someone took a swing at the younger one. It’s unclear if the fist connected, but in the absence of violence being committed by the man, it was an emotionally understandable but nonetheless improper response. Hitting people for their political positions is not a precedent we want. It’s a reaction too easily returned. 
On the other hand, condemning the two is not simply acceptable, but by all standards of basic morality, an absolute necessity. What they did crosses any line that a civilized society aware of history will abide. 
I’m old enough to have had parents who lived through the era of the Nazis. The two men aren’t. Time and distance have caused our culture to lose touch with the gravity of the worst crime ever committed by and against humanity. One unfortunate result is that younger people are now being seduced into embracing the ideology, often by online provocateurs. Nazi symbolism is now appearing on American streets. 
This should horrify us all. Regardless of where any of us fall on the political spectrum, this cannot be normalized. 
Our democratic society has long condemned the extreme fascism and genocide the Nazi flag and emblem stand for, and they are not welcome in Fairbanks or anyplace else in Alaska or America.
I’m sorry to have to write this. But I owe it to Dr. Reicher, who shared with me his story when I was 15, to insist 47 years later that we never forget the Holocaust and the unforgivable evils of the Nazis. And that we never, ever, turn a blind eye to those who act as if we should.

text:
President Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Kalispell on Oct 14, 2026. (Micah Drew/Daily Montanan)President Donald Trump’s campaign rally in Kalispell earlier this month cost Flathead County and nearby municipalities more than $107,000 for emergency services personnel, and local taxpayers are on the hook for the costs. 
Flathead County identified approximately $58,000 in costs from supporting security operations during Trump’s visit, where he stumped for Republican candidates in Montana’s federal elections. 
In a press release this week, county officials said they would not seek reimbursement from the federal government for the expenses, “consistent with precedent” established during visits by former vice presidents to the area. 
“We have a duty to assist with security efforts during any presidential visit of this scale,” said Flathead County Commission Chairman Brad Abell. “It was also an honor for Flathead County to host a sitting president of the United States.”
The county’s expenses primarily consisted of overtime wages for members of the Sheriff’s Office. 
Flathead County Sheriff Brian Heino told KPAX that around 200 local personnel helped with security operations and traffic control during the visit. 
“Securing an event of this size requires an extraordinary team effort, and our Sheriff’s Office personnel and partner agencies rose to the occasion with complete professionalism,” said Heino in a statement. “Whenever a high-profile leader visits the Flathead Valley, our duty is clear: Provide maximum security, and protect everyone involved. I could not be prouder of how our entire team performed.”
The City of Kalispell reported a bill of $45,781 for mobilization of city personnel, and Mayor Ryan Hunter has said he would like to seek reimbursement. 
“The kind of security that goes around with the president — quite, quite expensive as people can imagine,” Hunter said at a council work session following the president’s visit. “And it was a campaign event, not necessarily like an official federal government event, which makes it kind of unique as well. So certainly, hopefully we can find some grants to pay for some of our time and effort into that as a city.”
Hunter added that other cities have billed the president for expenses, and he would like to see that happen, though he is “not super hopeful” that the city would be reimbursed. 
The Daily Montanan earlier reported that the president did not fully pay for the costs of his visits to Missoula and Billings in 2018.
In 2024, Trump held a campaign stop in Bozeman, where Gallatin County footed the more than $62,000 bill. 
The Kalispell City Council is expected to discuss the issue at its Nov. 2 meeting. 
Up in Whitefish, the city manager told the Daily Montanan that five Whitefish police officers provided support to the Sheriff’s Office during the visit, incurring approximately $3,755 in overtime. The city council has not directed staff to seek reimbursement.
Columbia Falls is not seeking reimbursement for costs with the event, which also primarily included overtime. The city manager told the Daily Montanan that operational schedules were adjusted to minimize the impact to the city. 
Montana Highway Patrol did not respond to a request for any costs incurred at the state level related to Trump’s visit and Vice President JD Vance’s subsequent stop in Belgrade this week.

text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more Connecticut political news, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
PURA approves new solar tariffs
The Public Utilities Regulatory Authority on Wednesday approved new compensation rates, or tariffs, for owners of residential rooftop solar systems.
Beginning next year, most Eversource customers who participate in the state’s residential renewable energy solutions, or RRES, program will pay 3.25 cents for every kilowatt-hour of electricity produced by their solar panels. UI customers will pay 6.57 cents per kWh. Those “netting” charges are deducted from the excess electricity that solar customers sell back to the utility. In 2026, PURA set the rate for both utilities at 4.02 cents per kWh.
As part of a bipartisan bill passed last year to address utility costs, lawmakers ordered a steep increase in netting tariffs to lower the cost of solar incentives that are passed on to other customers. 
— John Moritz, Energy & Environment Reporter
Murphy talks Middle East policy
Following his trip to the Middle East, U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., continues to raise concerns about the Trump administration’s plans regarding Iran.
Murphy said he sat in on a briefing to learn what the plan may look like if the U.S. restarts military operations. “It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of the law,” Murphy said during a Wednesday discussion at the Middle East Institute.
Recent reports show the administration is weighing more attacks against Iran following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
Briefs filed in support of CT’s assault weapons ban
As the Supreme Court weighs assault weapons bans in Connecticut and Illinois, gun violence prevention groups and Democratic lawmakers are filing amicus briefs in support of those laws.
Some of the groups include Sandy Hook Promise and Teachers Unify to End Gun Violence. The latter was co-founded by Abbey Clements, a teacher who survived the Sandy Hook school shooting. Clements said “it’s critical that teachers and school staff have a voice in these cases.”
Connecticut’s congressional delegation and Attorney General William Tong filed briefs to defend the constitutionality of Connecticut’s ban, which was updated in 2013. The court will hear oral arguments on Dec. 2 about whether bans in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, violate the Second Amendment.
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
CT to receive $6M in GM data privacy settlement
Connecticut will receive part of a $220 million multistate deal with General Motors to settle allegations that the automotive manufacturer improperly sold drivers’ private data, Attorney General William Tong announced this week.
In 2024, The New York Times reported that GM’s now-defunct Smart Driver program, which was pitched as a way to promote safer driving habits, was sharing users’ driving data with third party brokers. Brokers passed the data to insurance companies, who often hiked rates for Smart Driver participants.
An investigation into the program’s use in Connecticut was one of the first launched under the Connecticut Data Privacy Act. According to Tong’s office, some 123,000 residents were affected. 
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
Danbury legislator supports call for statewide moratorium
Residents in Danbury shared their concerns over a proposal to redevelop part of the former Union Carbide world headquarters into a data center this week.
As in other parts of the state, residents said they are anxious about noise, environmental impacts and property values. The developer behind the proposal intends to conduct a sound study to determine how a potential data center could impact the area. A formal application for a data center has not been submitted at this time.
Earlier this week, Rep. Raghib Allie-Brennan, who represents part of Danbury, said that he does not support data centers in the city, adding that he plans to introduce legislation to repeal the state’s tax incentives for data centers. The lawmaker also said that he would support passing a temporary statewide moratorium on large-scale data centers.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
Judge strikes down “medical frailty” rule
A federal judge in Boston struck down an interim final rule from the Trump administration that critics warned would have made it more difficult for people with certain disabilities to qualify for an exemption to Medicaid work requirements going into effect on Jan. 1.
The interim rule would have required people claiming an eligibility through “medical frailty” to not only prove their diagnoses, but also demonstrate that their conditions would “significantly impair” their ability to comply with work requirements. Attorney General William Tong called the decision a victory over the federal government’s attempt “to deny millions of Americans access to healthcare.”
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter
CT veteran files new legal action over VA claim denial
Ron Christoforo, a Connecticut Vietnam veteran, and his daughter Michele filed a new legal action in the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims over the denial of her claim.
They’re challenging a federal statute that says children who have certain birth defects are eligible for VA benefits if their mother served in Vietnam. Michele was born with a genetic disorder that causes dwarfism, but she doesn’t qualify since her father was the one who served.
The Christoforos previously filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court in April. But the case has been on hold because of a pending case before the U.S. Supreme Court.
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
Lamont scores endorsement from climate group
Gov. Ned Lamont earned a reelection endorsement on Monday from one of the state’s largest environmental groups, the Connecticut League of Conservation Voters.
“These next four years will require our state leaders to make difficult decisions not only to meet our climate and clean energy goals, but to deliver the affordable, local and reliable energy that Connecticut voters deserve,” the group’s executive director, Lori Brown, said in a statement. “We have no question that Governor Lamont is prepared to deliver for our state and continue making progress in moving Connecticut towards a cleaner and more sustainable future.”
The CTLVC endorsed Lamont in each of his prior two general election campaigns, in 2018 and 2022. However, the group and its members have also clashed with Lamont over some of his policies, most notably his support for an expansion of natural gas infrastructure.
— John Moritz, Energy & Environment Reporter

text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Eight Jackson State University positions are being eliminated at the end of the year as federal funding for the roles dry up, possibly affecting the institution’s ability to secure donations and other private financial support. 
The news, confirmed in a letter obtained Friday by Mississippi Today, comes as the university expects to lose millions of dollars from the U.S. Department of Education.
In 2022, JSU received $8.2 million in Title III funds, according to the federal agency’s website. University officials did not disclose how much money they are expected to lose.
Anthony Howard, a spokesperson for JSU, denied in an email that the university is losing Title III funding. 
“Jackson State University has not lost any Title III grant funding,” Howard said.
He confirmed that eight positions would be affected by the layoffs, characterizing the move as part of a reallocation of federal money.
The letter obtained by Mississippi Today describes the positions being cut as being funded by Title III money. At least a handful of staff members in the university’s Division of Institutional Advancement were notified this week that their roles would be eliminated Dec. 31. 
The letter specifically mentioned funding for “JSU’s Activity Six, Title III, Part B. Historically Black Colleges and Universities Program,” which the university’s website describes as “elevating contributions from alumni and private donors.” This is one of 21 projects under the university’s HBCU Title III grant which the federal government awarded for the 2022-27 cycle. 
Employees affected by the layoff were encouraged to apply for vacancies, officials said. 
In his statement, Howard said the university would reallocate the funds to other Title III activities. The university did not disclose how much money nor where it would go. 
Title III was created in 1965 under the Higher Education Act, and it was established to help historically Black colleges and universities overcome past underfunding and provide students with equal opportunity to a quality education, according to the federal education department’s website. 
The aid can help eligible institutions build infrastructure, develop academic programs and training, and raise endowments. 
It remains unclear whether JSU or Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning, the state’s college board, will seek alternative funding to retain these positions. 
IHL declined to comment to Mississippi Today. 
It is unclear how much of the lost funding is directly to blame for the layoffs. It is also unclear why the university’s funding is being terminated by the federal government. 
JSU’s Division of Institutional Advancement oversees fundraising efforts, including securing major gifts, maintaining relationships with alumni and private donors, fundraising campaigns and growing the university’s endowment. The office also works with the JSU’s Development Foundation to secure financial support for scholarships, academic programs and other institutional needs.

title: Pamela Atkinson, Utah’s champion for the homeless, remembered as ‘larger than life’

(Photo courtesy of the Utah Governor's Office)In a church full of people who came to honor Pamela Atkinson’s memory at her funeral Friday — a crowd that inclu[...]
text:
Pamela Atkinson, a longtime advocate for people experiencing homelessness in Utah, is honored at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City after Gov. Spencer Cox declared Pamela Atkinson Day on Feb. 24, 2023. (Photo courtesy of the Utah Governor's Office)In a church full of people who came to honor Pamela Atkinson’s memory at her funeral Friday — a crowd that included Utah Gov. Spencer Cox and other prominent dignitaries — Ed Snoddy said he had “many stories” from the more than 30 years he spent alongside her helping Utah’s most vulnerable. 
“But this one has stayed with me a long, long time,” he said. 
Atkinson, he said, invited then-Utah Gov. Mike Leavitt to come with the Volunteers of America’s outreach team to check in on people experiencing homelessness. That day, “we went to see our homeless friend, Chuck,” Snoddy said. Chuck and Leavitt chatted for about 20 minutes before parting ways. 
But the next day, Snoddy said, when he and Atkinson went to check on Chuck again, “he said he was in a lot of pain.” They took him to the hospital, where he was admitted for liver cancer and diagnosed as terminally ill.
“Pamela called the governor and told him … how much Chuck enjoyed meeting him,” Snoddy said. 
Leavitt then went to the hospital to spend more time with him. 
“This whole time, the doctors, the nurses were going, ‘Who is this homeless person and why is the governor in here?’” he said.
Atkinson died Oct. 10 at the age of 93. 



“Her body finally wore out from her continual love and service to so many, particularly the vulnerable in society, but her lasting impact will live on through the footprints of all she has left behind,” her obituary says. 
During her funeral service at the First Presbyterian Church of Salt Lake City on Friday, Atkinson was remembered as a pillar in Utah’s homeless and humanitarian community who was as politically savvy and influential as she was selfless. 
Atkinson advised four Utah governors, including Cox, on homeless services and policies. Several facilities and programs have been named after her, including the Pamela Atkinson Resource Center, a 300-bed emergency shelter in South Salt Lake, and the Pamela Atkinson Homeless Trust Fund, a state account that supports homeless services across Utah.  
Snoddy recalled that while Chuck was hospitalized, Atkinson — “being a wee bit cheeky at times” — hid his dog, Lucy, in her jacket to sneak her in to see him, Snoddy said. 
“I said, ‘Are you sure?’ She said: ‘Yes. Just follow me and don’t tell anyone,’” he recalled, to laughs from the crowd. “So we went into his room, and Chuck’s reaction was, ‘First, the governor and now my dog Lucy? That’s the best medicine ever.’ I can see his face right now.” 
When Chuck later died while on hospice at a friend’s house, Atkinson held his hand. 
Pamela Atkinson a longtime advocate for people experiencing homelessness in Utah, is honored at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City after Gov. Spencer Cox declared Pamela Atkinson Day on Feb. 24, 2023. (Photo courtesy of the Utah Governor’s Office)
She was there for countless others, Snoddy recalled, and also spent Thanksgiving and Christmas trudging through snow handing out presents and warm turkey or roast beef dinners to people sleeping in tents or nothing but a sleeping bag. 
“Often you’d see a little tear come out of their eyes, and it was common to hear, ‘Thank you for not forgetting about me,’” he said. “And that was Pamela. She did not forget.” 
Utah’s current governor, Cox, spoke at Atkinson’s funeral. At times his voice shook with emotion as some wiped tears from their cheeks. 
Cox said when he first learned of her death, he looked through photos to reminisce. He had pictures of her during vigils honoring people who had died homeless, others that showed her introducing him to Utah’s former Sen. “Mitt Romney, the Dalai Lama, and apostles of my own faith.” 
“Such was the life of Pamela Atkinson,” he said. “For more than 20 years, she served as an adviser and confidant to Utah’s most powerful politicians. And for longer than that she served as an angel to thousands of Utah’s most vulnerable.” 
He and other speakers acknowledged that she was often called the “Mother Teresa” of Utah, but she “hated that comparison” because it painted her as someone rare and remarkable when she continually urged that anyone — through small acts of kindness alone — could do what she did. 
“Pamela was constantly asking us to ask ourselves, ‘What would Jesus do?’ … However, I never had to ask what would Jesus do. I would only have to look at what Pamela was actually doing,” Cox said. “For years she taught me and all of us how to live and how to serve and how to love.” 
Pamela Atkinson a longtime advocate for people experiencing homelessness in Utah, is honored at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City after Gov. Spencer Cox declared Pamela Atkinson Day on Feb. 24, 2023. (Photo courtesy of the Utah Governor’s Office)
Born in Bromley, Kent, England in 1933, Atkinson herself experienced a childhood “marked by poverty and hardship,” her obituary says. 
“She lived through the air raids of World War II, watched her father gamble away the family’s income, and experienced his eventual abandonment,” according to her obituary. “She knew firsthand what it meant to go without food, stable housing, or even the clothing needed to fit in at school.” 
Atkinson poured herself into her education, which her obituary says “was the key to breaking the poverty cycle.” She later traveled the world and earned multiple academic degrees before she became a nurse, worked in hospital administration, and eventually came to Salt Lake City, where she stayed. 
Rev. Jamie White, the senior pastor of the First Presbyterian Church of Salt Lake City, said Atkinson was an “incredible, larger-than-life force” that she compared to Hyperion, the world’s tallest living tree that towers 380 feet tall in California’s Redwood National Park. 
White said it’s easy to “stare up at her, her stature, and feel insecure about our inadequate, maybe meager efforts to answer life’s big question for ourselves. We might think to ourselves, we could never do what she did.” 
But White noted that Hyperion’s pinecones, its seeds, are as small as a thumbnail. 
“Do you think that Pamela, sleeping in the cold as a teenager in the U.K., often hungry at night and unsure if she’d ever make it out of poverty, much less become a nurse and do all she was able to accomplish — do you think she could possibly imagine the influence she would have?” White said. “No. Absolutely not. She started as a tiny pinecone, like we all do. She simply gave her tiny self over to Jesus and made a conscious decision to listen to what she called God’s ‘holy nudges’ in her life.” 
The governor said when he asked Atkinson before she died what her final message was to Utahns, she said: “Just follow Jesus. It’s so easy to do.’” 
Pamela Atkinson a longtime advocate for people experiencing homelessness in Utah, is honored at the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City after Gov. Spencer Cox declared Pamela Atkinson Day on Feb. 24, 2023. (Photo courtesy of the Utah Governor’s Office)
