name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida Republicans say they’re not sweating early voter turnout — not yet, anyway
description: Signs outside of a polling location in St. Petersburg on Oct 21, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Although Gov. Ron DeSantis sounded the alarm about Republican voter turnout earlier this week, other Florida GOP officials insist they’ve little to worry about as Democrats turned out in bigger numbers than they did four years ago in early in-person a[...]
text:
Signs outside of a polling location in St. Petersburg on Oct 21, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)Although Gov. Ron DeSantis sounded the alarm about Republican voter turnout earlier this week, other Florida GOP officials insist they’ve little to worry about as Democrats turned out in bigger numbers than they did four years ago in early in-person and mail voting.
Little to worry about yet, anyway.
Anthony Pedicini, a Republican strategist, predicts the Republicans will dominate on Election Day and that everything will turn out just fine for the party in power.
Democrats have already cashed their chips,” he said in an email to the Phoenix. “Their most reliable voters have voted. Ours haven’t yet, because Republican super-voters show up on Election Day. Anyone calling this race before Tuesday is reading half a tea leaf.”
He added: “We’ve heard it at the door, on the phone, and in the surveys: ‘I’m voting Tuesday.’ No one should be celebrating anything in Florida until 7 p.m. Tuesday.”
(Getty Images)
Early voting in Florida ends on Saturday in many counties. Some counties will extend early voting until Sunday, Nov. 1.
In traditionally red Polk County, as of Friday morning, registered Republicans had cast just 468 more votes than registered Democrats. That’s in a county where Republicans have a 13-point registration advantage.
“We’re doing a campaign of trying to get people to go out and vote early because a lot of people, they’re just used to doing it on Election Day, so that’s why the numbers look like they do right now,” said Kat Gates-Skipper, a Polk County GOP state committeewoman. “So, we’re contacting people and telling them, ‘Don’t wait until Tuesday.’”
 Banking on Election Day
Hillsborough County was one of the bluest spots on the map for Democrats during the 2010s, but Republicans overtook them in party registration there in early 2025. The GOP has nearly 20,000 more registered Republicans than Democrats in the county, but Democrats held an 18,312-vote lead as of Thursday afternoon.
“What I’m seeing on the ground, it appears that the Democrats have been able to create or develop more enthusiasm for their top of the ticket than what we’re seeing from Republicans,” said Hillsborough County state GOP committeewoman April Schiff. “I’m not sure why that is, but it is what it is.”
Republicans in recent election cycles have voted in greater numbers than Democrats on Election Day in Florida, and that is what the GOP is counting on. In the August primary, Republican election day turnout was double the number for Democrats (60%-30%).
More than 4.4 million Floridians had voted as of Friday afternoon. Registered Republicans had cast 40.4% of all votes. Democrats had cast 38.4% of votes, a 2% margin. Non-party-affiliated and third-party voters made up 21.2% of the vote. That’s according to the University of Florida Election Lab tracker.
“We have seen Republicans turn out in force on Election Day in the last couple of cycles,” Democratic strategist Jackson McMillan acknowledged. “However, I’m confident at this point that they need to increase their turn-out lead to around R + 25 to be comfortable. And right now we’re in an R+2 environment. So, they need to dramatically increase their lead to be comfortable.”
“Republicans are clearly counting on Election Day to save them, but if I were them I’d be concerned about the combination of increased Democratic turnout and NPAs appearing to break heavily our way,” added Democratic strategist Chris Mitchell. “The enthusiasm is clearly on our side, but this is far from over.”
 Enthusiasm gap
Some Republicans acknowledge dissatisfaction with the Iran war and the attendant high gas prices have hurt the economy and their popularity. They also attribute the sluggish early turnout to the fact that it’s a midterm election.
“It’s just more the traditional reduction in enthusiasm during an off-year election, I think,” said John Roberts, chair of the Escambia County Republican Party. “A presidential election is just going to draw in more people.”
Jack Brill, chair of the Republican Executive Committee in Sarasota County, predicts this year’s midterm elections in Florida will see closer margins than the past two election cycles.
“This will be a closer race like 2018 versus 2022, the governor’s race, where you’re seeing the same polling we’re all seeing,” he said. “It’s going to be a tight race, and it’s going to be a race where Byron [Donalds] will win, but it’s going to be much closer to 2018 than 2022.”
In 2018, the margin of victory for DeSantis, Scott, and Democratic Agriculture Commissioner Nikki Fried were all within 0.5 percent, triggering statutorily required-machine recounts.
By contrast, DeSantis defeated Democrat Charlie Crist in the 2022 gubernatorial race by 19 points and Republican Marco Rubio won the U.S. Senate seat by 16 points over Democrat Val Demings.
“In ’22, when I was running four years ago, I mean like, you could put hot coals in front of the polling place and our people were going to walk over those barefoot. They wanted to vote, right?” DeSantis said this week during a press conference in Crystal River. “Just a different time.”
Kevin J. Cooper, chair of the Miami-Dade County Republican Party, is confident Trump’s appeal to Republican voters has not waned. The president was the first Republican to carry Miami-Dade in more than three decades when he won there in 2024.
 Toxic’

Cooper believes the Democrats caused themselves a big problem by nominating Angie Nixon as their standard-bearer for Senate, noting her affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America.
Any association with socialism can be toxic in Hispanic precincts in South Florida, home to hundreds of thousands of immigrants, refugees, and exiles from authoritarian governments in Cuba, Venezuela, and Nicaragua.
That taints all Democrats running in Miami-Dade, Cooper said, noting the kerfuffle that took place last week when Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries appeared with Democratic Congressional District 27 candidate Eliott Rodriguez at a Cuban bakery in Miami.
While both Democrats have denounced socialism, some social media users criticized the bakery for hosting the two men, accusing it of association with that ideology.
“They go in there, they chitchat, they do whatever they do, and then everyone has to condemn socialism,” Cooper said.
“It just shows you that it’s a great case study as to the way that people are thinking and the way that people are feeling, that these folks go to a Cuban bakery and the bakery has to condemn socialism. When socialism wasn’t even discussed at the event,” he said.
“That just shows you how toxic this issue is from a leadership perspective from the top, that they come to South Florida with this message, and everyone recoils at it. There is no difference between the Democratic Party and the Democratic Socialists Party. They’ve basically merged.”
Some observers warn the governor’s race, at least, could prove more competitive than was expected at the beginning of this year. Matt Towery, a pollster with InsiderAdvantage, said his team had been analyzing the early vote in Florida and “it is entirely possible that the race for governor will be very close.”
“While the GOP has a slight advantage in the early vote, there is a large segment of independent voters in the mix … and in our surveys they are breaking more for Democrats this cycle,” he wrote on X.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Lawsuit seeks to block TN from denying driver’s licenses to immigrants legally allowed to work
description: An immigrant advocacy organization has filed a legal challenge to new state rules denying licenses to immigrants authorized to live and work in the United States, placing them at risk for losing jobs without transportation or for arrest, detention and deportation for driving without a license. Pictured: a Tennessee Highway Patrol officer and a Homeland Secur[...]
text:
An immigrant advocacy organization has filed a legal challenge to new state rules denying licenses to immigrants authorized to live and work in the United States, placing them at risk for losing jobs without transportation or for arrest, detention and deportation for driving without a license. Pictured: a Tennessee Highway Patrol officer and a Homeland Security Investigations officer searched a vehicle during a traffic stop in Memphis, Tennessee on Oct. 7, 2025. (Photograph by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)An immigrant advocacy organization filed a legal challenge on Friday to new Tennessee rules that deny driver’s licenses to immigrants who are legally authorized to work in the United States, arguing the state failed to follow its own rules by abruptly shifting long-standing license requirements.
The Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition is seeking an immediate court order to temporarily block the state from denying licenses to immigrants authorized to live and work in Tennessee, among them thousands of state residents who have been able to legally hold and renew state licenses for nearly two decades.
The organization is joined in filing suit by six individuals, identified only by their initials, who were recently denied licenses and license renewals, or face being denied a license or license renewal in the future.
The legal challenge, filed in Davidson County Chancery Court, also seeks a finding that new rules, implemented in recent weeks without public input, are invalid. 
Tennessee Gov. Lee questions state rules denying licenses to immigrants legally able to work in U.S.

“Tennessee’s denial of driver’s licenses to immigrants is unlawful and infringes on Tennesseans’ right to have a say in matters affecting their communities,” said Peter McGraw, legal deputy director of the National Immigration Law Center, among the groups representing the plaintiffs. 
Tennessee “issued its new driver’s license policies without first seeking community input or approval, and a state agency must consult the public before implementing extreme policies that affect all of us. Tennesseans should be able to drive safely and freely, and we look forward to putting driver’s licenses back in the hands of people who depend on them.”  
For many years, the Tennessee Department of Safety & Homeland Security routinely accepted an “employment authorization document” issued by the federal government to immigrants legally allowed to work and live in the United States as sufficient proof of immigration status for the purposes of obtaining a license.
In recent weeks, the department began rejecting individuals seeking new or renewed licenses who presented the federal work permit. For many immigrants who are not permanent residents — such as asylum seekers and so-called Dreamers who were brought to the U.S. as children and are now protected from deportation — the document is among the only valid proof they have of their immigration status. 
On Wednesday, Gov. Bill Lee said he had just learned of the rule change and was in the process of determining “ what impact it actually does have and are there changes we need to make.” 
A spokesperson for the state Department of Safety and Homeland Security on Friday cited longstanding practice in declining to comment on pending litigation.
Tennessee blocks driver’s licenses for Dreamers, other immigrants with U.S. work permits

Immigrant advocates said the denial of licenses could impact potentially thousands of Tennessee immigrants with legal authorization to be in the country. Without a valid license, they said, immigrants face an impossible choice: stop driving and risk losing their jobs or risk driving and be subject to arrest, detention and subsequent deportation if caught.
Among those recently denied a license is an East Tennessee registered nurse who asked to be identified only by his initials, L.R., who is not a party to the lawsuit.
Speaking at a virtual news conference on Friday, L.R. said he is legally allowed to work and live in the United States as a recipient of DACA, or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals. DACA recipients were brought to the United States without legal authorization as children and have since been granted the right to legally live and work in the country.
He went to multiple county driver’s centers earlier this month to renew the temporary license that has previously been made available to DACA recipients who are able to produce the credit-card-sized federal work permit cards. He was turned away at each one, he said.
After 20 years in Tennessee, he is considering leaving despite an acute statewide nursing shortage. There is no public transportation in the rural community where he lives, and finding a ride to his job at a Level 1 trauma center at 4 a.m. to begin his shift is impractical, he said.  
“I hate the idea of having to uproot my entire life due to being gatekept (by) a piece of plastic just to survive,” he said. “I’m holding strong to the belief that change can be made, but if I have no other choice then I will relocate and put my knowledge and skills to use in a new place.”
The legal challenge argues the Department of Safety & Homeland Security is violating its own regulations and state law in imposing new rules that limit acceptable forms of immigration status. 
It also challenges the decision as exceeding the department’s authority. 
“Under its new rules, the Department is determining — in place of the federal government — who is authorized to be present in the United States, for what purpose, and for how long,” in violation of state law. 
The lawsuit alleges that in addition to rejecting work permits, the department is no longer verifying license applicants’ status through the federal S.A.V.E. system, an online system administered by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services that states use to verify immigration and citizenship status for those seeking “benefits or licenses.”
No court date has yet been set in the legal challenge, which was brought by attorneys with the Tennessee Coalition for Immigrant & Refugee Rights, Nashville law firm Bass, Berry & Simms and the National Immigration Law Center.

title: New Mexico Dem governor nominee Haaland adds $1.5M to historic fundraising haul in final push
description: New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland received approximately $1.5 million in recent weeks, according to New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office filings. (Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland ended a historic campaign fundraising haul with an additional $1.5 million in recent weeks, accord[...]
text:
New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland received approximately $1.5 million in recent weeks, according to New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office filings. (Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland ended a historic campaign fundraising haul with an additional $1.5 million in recent weeks, according to the latest campaign finance filings with the New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office.
Haaland has national name recognition as the nation’s first-ever Indigenous female U.S. Interior Department secretary and has received more than $20 million over course of the 2026 primary and general elections.
Between Oct. 6 and Oct. 27, Haaland received a little more than $1.5 million across nearly 30,000 donations. Her Republican opponent Gregg Hull, a former Rio Rancho mayor, received a little over $350,000 from approximately 1,200 donations in the same time period. Hull has received approximately $2.8 million this election season. 
A campaign haul of $20 million dwarfs recent gubernatorial campaigns, including that of incumbent Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan who is finishing her second and final term in office. She received approximately $13.8 million for her 2022 re-election campaign, according to Secretary of State’s Office records. 
Contributions to Haaland’s campaign alone make up more than more than 80% of more than 36,000 donations in the latest filing period to all candidates running for election or re-election this cycle. 
Like in previous campaign finance reports, Haaland received small-dollar donations from every state and territory in the country, as well as from military members serving overseas. The largest percentage of her donations came from California, followed closely by New Mexico. 
During the primary campaign against Bernalillo County District Attorney Sam Bregman, Haaland’s haul of donations contained in filings numbering in the thousands of pages temporarily broke the Secretary of State’s website. 
Also like previous campaign filings, Hull’s donations came almost entirely from New Mexico donors, with all but 11 of his 1,186 donations being listed as in-state. 
Hull has previously pointed to his in-state support as proof that his campaign is geared toward New Mexicans. Haaland has cited the sheer number of small donations from across the country as evidence of her wide, grassroots support.
The latest filings, due to the Secretary of State’s Office on Thursday, mark the final glimpse into campaign fundraising activity before the general election concludes Tuesday.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Portland, Bangor, Augusta courts to stay open late Tuesday in case of emergency election filings
description: Several Maine state courts will stay open late on Election Day to accept and act on emergency filings related to elections. (Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)Maine courthouses in Portland, Bangor and Augusta will stay open until 9 p.m. Tuesday to accept emergency filings related to the election, according to a release from the Maine Judicial Branch. [...]
text:
Several Maine state courts will stay open late on Election Day to accept and act on emergency filings related to elections. (Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)Maine courthouses in Portland, Bangor and Augusta will stay open until 9 p.m. Tuesday to accept emergency filings related to the election, according to a release from the Maine Judicial Branch. 
The announcement comes as several Maine cities expect federal election monitors at the polls and numerous lawsuits in federal court across the country continue to develop in the final few days before the midterms. 
The Maine Judicial Branch said a judge, clerk and marshal will be on duty at each courthouse to accept and act on any emergency filings. 
Maine Superior Court Chief Justice Robert Mullen and Maine District Court Chief Judge Brent Davis also issued an order Thursday that all filings pertaining to the election must be filed with paper documents at a clerk’s office, not through the state’s electronic filing system. 
Paper filings will be immediately reviewed by the clerk and directed to the appropriate judge for timely review. The judicial branch is also urging filers to include cell phone numbers on any filings, so that they can be reached after hours. 
All public documents related to election filings will then be posted on the judicial branch’s high-profile cases webpage, as soon as possible. 
A spokesperson for the Maine Secretary of State’s Office said the courts have always been open and available to the office until polls close on Election Day.
“We appreciate the partnership with the courts to ensure that every voter’s constitutional right to vote is protected,” the spokesperson said in an email.
The state court plans come as federal courts across the country continue to consider a bevy of lawsuits related to the Trump administration’s sweeping efforts to combat noncitizen voting and assert authority over elections, as Democrats and voting rights groups allege federal election interference.
Election monitors 
The U.S. Department of Justice will also send election monitors to South Portland, the Secretary of State’s Office confirmed Friday. 
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said last week that election monitors will also be in Portland and Lewiston. 
The Department of Justice has in recent years sent observers to other states on a smaller scale, usually in response to a civil rights violation. But this comes amid the Trump administration’s efforts to assert authority over the election and following an attempt to force Maine, among other states, to hand over voter information.
“Any monitors are subject to the same laws and rules as any other observer at the poll,” Bellows told Maine Morning Star last week. “That means they can observe what’s taking place, but they may not interact with voters, handle ballots or equipment, or disrupt voting in any way.” 
“We will monitor the monitors very carefully to ensure that they don’t cross any lines,” Bellows added.
South Portland mayor Elyse Tipton told Maine Morning Star about a meeting held Thursday where the city learned that election observers would be at their polling places from 7 a.m. until polls close.
The Department of Justice let city staff know the observers would be in plainclothes, she said, but she did not know why South Portland had been chosen in addition to the state’s two largest cities.
It’s a small piece of the federal agency’s plan to send 1,000 monitors to locations in all 50 states, DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels told States Newsroom on Monday. 
The Justice Department for decades has deployed monitors across the country to watch the voting process. During President Joe Biden’s administration, the DOJ sent monitors to 64 jurisdictions across 24 states for the 2022 midterm elections.
Maine Morning Star Senior Reporter Eesha Pendharkar contributed to this report.

title: Santee Cooper approves rate increase, including early expenses for new gas plant
description:
Santee Cooper CEO Jimmy Stanton pictured at a legislative hearing in the state House office building. (Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Customers of South Carolina’s state-owned utility will see their bills go up 9% over the next two years under a rate hike unanimously approved by the company’s governing board Friday.
Under the new rates, Santee Cooper resid[...]
text:
Santee Cooper CEO Jimmy Stanton pictured at a legislative hearing in the state House office building. (Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)Customers of South Carolina’s state-owned utility will see their bills go up 9% over the next two years under a rate hike unanimously approved by the company’s governing board Friday.
Under the new rates, Santee Cooper residential customers’ rates will increase 4.7% starting Feb. 1 of next year and another 4.6% in 2028. That comes to about $13 more per month for the standard residential customer by the time the new rates take full effect.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The governing board voted unanimously to enact the increased rates for the utility’s more than 220,000 direct customers, located in Berkeley, Georgetown and Horry counties.
These rates do not apply to the roughly 800,000 customers of the state’s rural power cooperatives, which buy electricity from Santee Cooper through a separate contract.
“Nobody wants to make changes to our rates, but the board went through an incredibly thorough process,” CEO Jimmy Staton told the board Friday. “These rates will enable us to improve the grid, to bring much-needed capacity to the state and provide reliable service while balancing that against affordability. And our rates remain very affordable.”
Industrial and commercial customers will see rate increases between 2.1% and 2.9% each of the two years.
Critics of the plan, including South Carolina’s consumer advocacy agency and environmental groups, argued the changes put a greater burden of costs on residential customers. The state’s utility watchdog and an outside consultant hired by Santee Cooper to evaluate the plan said that wasn’t the case.
What’s included
Utility regulators permit $5B natural gas plant proposed in SC Lowcountry

Within the expenses included in the rate hike is about $120 million worth of parts needed for a new 2,200-megawatt natural gas power plant.
In May, utility regulators signed off on the gas plant, which is being built in cooperation with Dominion Energy on the site of a former coal plant along the Edisto River, near Canadys, in the Lowcountry.
To stay on track to open the gas plant in mid-2033, Santee Cooper and Dominion paid deposits to save their spot in line to receive some of the hard-to-get components, such as turbines.
“There are so many folks that want to build generating assets, so many people that want to construct generating facilities, that what we’re seeing is a little bit of a time lag associated with building those resources,” Bryan Lewis, director of retail customer service, told the board. “So, we’re trying to purchase them a little bit earlier.
“Many utilities are spending earlier in order to minimize the impacts of inflation and also minimize the impacts of receiving some components later than they would like to,” Lewis added.
However, this rate increase won’t cover the total cost of the gas plant, for which the total price estimates doubled — to $5 billion — up from a $2.5 billion told to senators last August.
That early estimate was based on historical costs to build similar units. But prices have increased dramatically since then as utility companies globally rush to build similar plants, Staton said last December.
Until the Canadys plant can be built, Santee Cooper also has had to buy power from other producers “to bridge the gap,” Chief Financial Officer Tami Wilson told the board earlier this year.
That power is expensive, Wilson said, and the utility expects to spend nearly $90 million more on the open market in 2027.
Other expenses the company has taken on include $300 million for a pair of natural gas turbines on the site of an existing coal plant near Georgetown and $270 million for the expansion of an existing natural gas plant in Anderson County. That spending is part of what’s driving the rate increase, along with higher prices across the board for operations and maintenance, spokeswoman Mollie Gore previously told the Daily Gazette.
Energy efficiency
To help those customers Santee Cooper has deemed “energy burdened,” the utility plans to spend $400,000 in its upcoming budget to expand its energy efficiency program.
Launched in 2025, the Power Partners Program is available to homeowners and renters in qualified neighborhoods. The company offers free energy efficiency assessments to look for ways a home’s power usage could be reduced. The company may then pay for the cost of some home improvements, such as LED lighting, weather stripping and pipe wrapping and insulation.
Santee Cooper will publish more information on the program expansion at a later date.
Meanwhile, residential bills already climbed about 13% last year. Residential customers who used 1,000 kilowatt-hours a month — considered the industry standard — were asked to pay about $16 more per month after the utility came out of a court-mandated rate freeze.
Power customers had sued the Moncks Corner-based utility after cost overruns and mismanagement led to the 2017 abandonment of the V.C. Summer nuclear expansion project. That lawsuit led to the five-year rate freeze that began in 2020.
Since then, Santee Cooper has added 4,270 new customers between January 2025 and April 2026.

“Heating oil prices in Maine are now breaking records week after week, putting growing pressure on Maine [...]
text:
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. (Photo by gmnicholas/ Getty Images)The average price for heating oil reached a new high this week at $6.05 a gallon, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources. 
“Heating oil prices in Maine are now breaking records week after week, putting growing pressure on Maine families as temperatures continue to drop,” Celina Cunningham, acting commissioner of the department, said in a statement. 
The latest peak puts the average cost of heating oil up 82% from this time last year, the department reported. That means it will cost roughly $750 more to fill a standard 275-gallon oil tank. 
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. That number is down from 70% of households in 2010, according to the energy department.
The current peak is up one cent from the previous high of $6.04 set last week — that price surpassed the earlier record set Sept. 21 of $6.02. And prior to that, the record was $5.92 per gallon in 2022, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. 
Energy costs have soared this fall as the war in Iran restricts the flow of diesel and crude oil onto global markets and Russia has implemented an export ban on diesel after Ukrainian attacks on refineries. 
The latest price increases come after the U.S. Department of Energy last week announced it will release 315,000 barrels of heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, roughly a third of its supply, to help reduce the price of heating oil.

text:
Voter turnout was heavy on Election Day, Nov. 5, 2024, at Northview Church in south Fargo. The U.S. Department of Justice is sending a handful of election monitors to Cass County on Election Day this year, part of a nationwide effort. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)Department of Justice election monitors will observe polling locations in Cass County on Election Day as part of a nationwide effort.
The federal observers will be part of more than 1,000 election monitors being sent to polling locations across all 50 states on Election Day, an expansion of the department’s monitoring compared to 2022. In the 2022 midterms, observers were sent to 64 jurisdictions across 24 states.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The info you need to cast your ballot.]
Sarah Heinle, head election official for Cass County, North Dakota’s most populous county, said she spoke with Department of Justice officials Friday morning and learned the department will send a handful of election monitors on Tuesday.
The DOJ monitors will visit up to seven polling locations in Cass County and will observe for about an hour at each site to ensure compliance with federal election law, she said. Cass County, home to Fargo and West Fargo, accounted for about 22% of North Dakota voters in the 2022 midterms.
“They will be following standard election observer laws and rules for North Dakota just like anybody else going there,” Heinle said. 
She said the federal monitors want to ensure express voting options are available and observe whether polling locations allow assistance to be provided for people who request it.
“It’ll be just like when the ACLU or the League of Women voters, or anybody else, who monitors our polls goes out there,” Heinle said. 
North Dakota Secretary of State Michael Howe said he also participated on the call with Department of Justice officials Friday. 
Trump’s DOJ sends 1,000 election monitors to 50 states; locations not yet disclosed

“We had a lot of questions as to what are they going to be doing, and I feel comfortable with what they are trying to achieve,” Howe said. “They made it very clear that they will not be interrupting.”
Howe said DOJ officials were informed they cannot interact with voters within 100 feet of a polling location. Howe said he asked why monitors would need to interact with voters, and the DOJ officials indicated the department wants to know about the “voter experience,” especially if someone is turned away from the polls.
“They will be wearing the same election observer sticker that the ACLU will wear and the League of Women Voters will wear, and any other person that wants to be an election observer,” Howe said. He added Department of Justice officials said they wanted to be “as unobtrusive as possible.”
A spokesperson for the League of Women Voters of North Dakota said the group will also have election observers at polling locations in North Dakota on Election Day.
The Native American Rights Fund, a nonprofit headquartered in Colorado, will send about 300 poll watchers to nine states, including North Dakota, said Jacqueline De León, senior staff attorney for the organization.
Eighteen observers will be dispatched to nine locations in North Dakota, she said
“We are focused on areas that have significant Native American populations throughout the state,” De León said.
The poll watchers will be watching for a “smooth administration” of the elections, she said. The group’s election monitors also want to document if Native American voters needed to travel long distances to vote and are able to use their tribal IDs at polling locations, De León said.
The group encourages Native American voters who encounter difficulties casting ballots during the election to contact the nonprofit at 866-OUR-VOTE, or by email at vote@narf.org.
The American Civil Liberties Union of North Dakota will not have its own observers at election sites, but works collaboratively with the League of Women Voters to respond to election complaints or concerns, said Cody Schuler, advocacy manager for the ACLU of North Dakota.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

text:
A projection screen shows live footage of ballot drop box locations throughout Adams County at the Adams County Government Center in Brighton on Nov. 7, 2023. (Photo by Kevin Mohatt/Colorado Newsline)There could be up to 12 federal election monitors in Adams County on Election Day next week, though they will not be allowed to go inside polling locations.
U.S. Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels wrote in an email Friday that the department expects to deploy between four and 12 monitors to Adams. Justice originally intended to send four before it rejected terms from the secretary of state’s office that the monitors be accompanied by state representatives if the monitors enter voting centers.
Department lawyer Jake Bachand emailed Colorado election officials Thursday with the names of six additional monitors: DeAndre Adamich, Sarvenaz Danesh, Benjamin Essex, Michael Harris, Jorge Ortiz and Richard Roden. They will work in teams of two.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The federal monitors will be restricted to at least 100 feet away from buildings where election activity occurs, according to Colorado law.
​Federal officials reject ​Colorado’s conditions for election monitors in Adams County

They will “mostly be asking voters if they would voluntarily like to discuss their access to the polling location,” Pels said.
Justice planned to send monitors to Adams County to check compliance with federal voting rights laws, including accessibility for people with disabilities and Spanish-language availability. The county is a Democratic-leaning area of Colorado’s toss-up 8th Congressional District, where Republican Rep. Gabe Evans is facing a challenge from Democrat Manny Rutinel.
The federal government sent monitors to 64 counties in 24 states in 2022. The monitors are typically civil staff members, but some of the monitors this year are criminal prosecutors. The head of Justice’s Civil Rights Division said it plans to deploy around 1,000 monitors around the country Tuesday.
Various experts and officials worry that the large-scale operation could be a strategy to intimidate voters in a battleground race, amid other escalating actions by the Trump administration to control elections and cast doubt on results.
Election Day is Nov. 3. More information about how to register to vote and cast a ballot can be found at GoVoteColorado.gov.

A judge has ordered the owner of Jackson’s troubled Grand Chateau apartments be extradited and jailed after failing to comply with previous rulings to demolish the blighted property.
In an order released Thursday, Jackson Environmental Court Judge Jeffery Reynolds issued a “nonappealable judgment of conviction” against Ramesh Ramchandran, which requires the property owner to serve nearly two years in the Hinds County detention center in Raymond. 
The order comes after Ramchandran failed to comply with a previous order issued last month that required him to begin demolition or restoration of the property after incurring several building code violations. 
The previous order granted Ramchandran a 30-day suspension on the sentence contingent on progress made towards demolition or restoration. 
In his order, the judge called the property “a dangerous menace to the residents of the City of
Jackson,” adding that Ramchandran showed “criminal neglect.”
Ramchandran did not respond to numerous requests for comment.
The Grand Chateau is one of several complexes in legal limbo as the city pushes more aggressive efforts to fight against blighted properties plaguing the city. 
While the order sentenced Ramchandran to 630 days in jail, it remains to be seen how much time he will actually serve. As part of his ruling, Reynolds said early release would require his written authorization.
Ramchandran lives in Georgia, and is believed to have returned to his Alpharetta home after his initial sentencing in September. Due to this, a warrant for Ramchandran’s arrest would be required ifor Jackson Capitol Police officers to collect Ramchandran from his residence. 
Reynolds requested that Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp issue a warrant for Ramchandran’s arrest. The Fulton County Sheriff’s Department told Mississippi Today it cannot provide information regarding warrants. 
Ramchandran has owned the West Capitol Street property since 2021. It’s most notably known for recent controversy, in which Entergy cut power to the complex in July over alleged signs of meter tampering. 
The complex was supposed to be abandoned at the time of the power shutoff. However, over a dozen squatters were found still living on the premises.

text:
The Florida Capitol building on March 11, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)The artificial intelligence company targeted by a Attorney General James Uthmeier legal complaint says it is working with law enforcement, contrary to the A.G.’s claim.
A2E, an AI software that generates images, was subject of Uthmeier’s claim that its generating sexually explicit pictures of kids, a violation of state law.
Uthmeier: AI company allows people to generate sexually explicit pictures of kids

“We have learned about this news and we are consulting with the legal team,” A2E told the Phoenix in an email. “We have always been treating CSAM [child sexual abuse material] very seriously since the very beginning. We have been cooperating with law enforcement to detect and prevent all kinds of CSAM.”
Filed in state Circuit Court in Sarasota County, Uthmeier’s suit alleges A2E committed “unconscionable,” “deceptive,” and “unfair” practices under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.
The defendant is Rengstorff Consulting, a Nevada firm that owns A2E. The first allegation in the 26-page suit is that Rengstorff’s product lets “predators” “nudify non-consenting Floridians,” including children, and allows users to alter images of adults to feature child-like appearances.
“Just because you create the vehicle, it doesn’t give you exemption from liability. So while users might be providing images, at the end of the day, this AI software, this is the manufacturing hub that is actually churning out the child porn content. So we want to make them pay. We want to shut them down,” Uthmeier said during a news conference earlier this week announcing the suit in Orlando.
In 2025, Florida lawmakers approved a measure that requires social media companies to delete deepfakes, or AI-generated sexual depictions of people created without their consent.
The suit brings a few specific examples, including a Tampa man arrested earlier this year who Uthmeier alleges created more than “100 sexually explicit images of his 6-year-old stepdaughter and 10-year stepson, some with images of the two children performing oral and other sexual acts with him.”
“That predator was arrested thanks to the efforts of law enforcement – Defendant never reported the abusive and criminal images,” Uthmeier’s suit claims.

name: Missouri Independent
title: First MOScholars performance report exposes gaps in state oversight
description: State Treasurer Vivek Malek, pictured speaking in the Missouri State Capitol rotunda in 2025, shared the first annual performance report for the MOScholars voucher program Wednesday (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri’s first report on the academic performance of students in its MOScholars voucher program found encouraging test scores but also e[...]
text:
State Treasurer Vivek Malek, pictured speaking in the Missouri State Capitol rotunda in 2025, shared the first annual performance report for the MOScholars voucher program Wednesday (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).Missouri’s first report on the academic performance of students in its MOScholars voucher program found encouraging test scores but also exposed gaps in how the state collected the data, including information required by law that remains unavailable.
The report, released Wednesday by the Missouri Treasurer’s Office, found that students scored near the national average in reading and math during the program’s first three years. But researchers could validate test results for only 77% of students in testing grades, and the report lacked information about family income that state law requires.
The findings offer a baseline for measuring student performance but do not establish whether the program has improved academic outcomes or whether its students outperform those in public schools.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Researchers contracted to compile the report say they have an encouraging baseline to build on in future years. But the findings fall short of what some lawmakers expected from a program that has been operating for four years.
The law passed in 2021 that created the MOScholars program requires the state treasurer to “provide the test results and associated learning gains to the public via a state website after the third year of test and test-related data collection.”
Many expected this report last summer, immediately after the program’s third school year. When The Independent asked about the timing in April, the treasurer’s former chief of staff, Jackson Bailey, said the 2025-26 school year was “the fourth year of the MOScholars program, but is the third year of test and test-related data collection.” He said data for each school year is not collected until the following year.
But this was not always the office’s message.
When lawmakers were considering the expansion of the program in 2024, Senate Minority Leader Doug Beck asked State Treasurer Vivek Malek about the performance report during a Senate committee hearing.
“When I think of education, I think of accountability, and that is what I am curious about here,” Beck, a Democrat from Affton, said. “Do we know any of the educational outcomes of these students?”
Malek said his office “will have to produce a report after the third academic year, which will be ending in the academic year of 2024-25.”
“We are still getting all those scores and will be hiring a person who will be assessing all these scores and then analyzing and putting them together in report form,” he said.
Malek said this process would begin in the fall of 2024. The office, which has experienced considerable turnover since MOScholars’ creation, ultimately outsourced the report to the Saint Louis University PRiME Center, which conducts education policy research.
The PRiME Center was not hired until June 2025, according to the contract on the Missouri Office of Administration’s website.
 Missing and inconsistent test results

When the treasurer’s office sought a contractor in April 2025 to compile the report, it indicated that the existing data was disjointed and incomplete.
The request for proposals states there was “no standard format” for the test results.
“The current state of the data is that there are nine different tests being taken by thousands of different students… Right now, in its current state it is useless to measure anything,” it says.
By the time PRiME completed its report, researchers had identified 27 different test types students submitted — eight of which were not nationally norm-referenced assessments. By state law, MOScholars students in grades 3-10 should take “nationally norm-referenced tests that measure learning gains in math and English language arts” or the Missouri Assessment Program, commonly known as the MAP test.
Some students did not submit a score at all.
The statute puts the responsibility on the educational assistance organizations, which serve as intermediaries between voucher recipients and the treasurer’s office, to ensure students take a valid test. The organizations varied in compliance over the first three years of the program, although the share of students with valid results improved over time, the report notes.
On average, 77% of students required to take an assessment submitted valid results.
The Today and Tomorrow Educational Foundation, which is connected to the Archdiocese of St. Louis, had the worst response rate. In the 2024-25 school year, 14% of its students’ declined to submit scores, and 13% of scores were unable to be validated.
The PRiME Center expects better data collection going forward now that it has systems in place to guide the organizations and make the process easier.
“We have been able to construct a longitudinal data system that will serve the program forever,” PRiME Executive Director Collin Hitt told The Independent. “Now any student that is in the program we can track for as long as they are in the program and compare and look at their results over time.”
“Building these things takes time, but they are built now,” he said.
The office has also switched the software provider it uses to collect student data and help administer the program.
“The process in which these scores are collected and aggregated is complex,” MOScholars program specialist Meghan Rackers said in an emailed statement. “The program now has the proper policies, procedures and partners in place to work with educational assistance organizations to collect the assessment scores in a timely and accurate manner.”
 Income data remains unavailable

One piece of information required by state law is notably missing — family income level — and the office does not have a plan to address it.
State law requires that MOScholars reports aggregate data by “​​students’ grade level, gender, family income level, number of years of participation in the scholarship program and race.”
The PRiME Center report notes that “insufficient data were collected to accurately report this information.”
There are two ways families become eligible for MOScholars: either their income is below 300% of the federal poverty line or they have a child with an individualized education plan, which provides accommodations for students with disabilities. Those who qualify through having an IEP do not have to provide income information.
For those who meet income requirements, the data collection changed over time.
“This resulted in incomplete and inconsistent data that was therefore unable to be analyzed,” PRiME’s researchers wrote.
When asked whether this issue would be addressed, the treasurer’s office said “doing so would violate the common standard of only collecting information required to qualify for the program.”
“A common standard for privacy protections is that programs collect the least amount of information required to determine eligibility,” Rackers wrote.
Sen. Doug Beck questions State Treasurer Vivek Malek during a Senate Education and Workforce Development Committee hearing January 10, 2024. (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent)
The privacy of MOScholars students was called into question earlier this year when The Independent reported that students’ names and email addresses were inadvertently posted in a spreadsheet on the treasurer’s website.
The issue is one of several concerns state lawmakers have raised as they assess the administration of the program. Late in the legislative session, the Senate voted to move the program out of the treasurer’s office and into the hands of education officials. The proposal did not come up for a final vote, however, after pressure from a St. Louis archbishop to keep the program as-is.
Beck, who has been a vocal critic of the voucher program and  its administration by the treasurer’s office, said the performance report only amplified his disappointment with MOScholars.
“This report is incomplete, admits the Treasurer isn’t following the law, was outsourced to a third party and doesn’t answer key questions,” he told The Independent in a statement. “We are used to the Treasurer being incompetent, but this is starting to feel like a coverup. Something is going on with these vouchers and the public deserves to know the truth.”
 Encouraging results, but a limited picture

The report does not cover the 2025-26 school year, in which the program more than doubled in size. With more students in the program and more reaching the grades that require testing, there will be more data to work with.
“This testing sample is going to massively grow. So make it at what you will, but this is the baseline that we will see the future of the program being judged against,” Hitt said.
This initial report is “encouraging,” he said, adding that he is eager to get enough data to track student growth down the line.
The PRiME Center’s researchers translated scores into their national percentile rank. In English language arts, the average student score was in the 46th to 51st percentile. In math, they performed in the 47th to 49th percentile.
Missouri students in 4th and 8th grades take the National Assessment of Educational Progress, another nationally normed test. In 2024, Missouri students scored in the 45th to 47th percentile, according to PRiME’s analysis.
“As a scholar… if you told me that I was going to be looking at a program where 40% of the students had an IEP and the rest were from relatively low-income households, I would not have guessed that we would have seen test scores this high.”
Malek said in a news release that he is proud of the results.
“Behind these numbers are families who have been given the opportunity to find the right educational fit for their children, including students with special needs who deserve every opportunity to succeed,” he said. “These results reinforce why expanding educational opportunities and empowering parents to make the best decisions for their children is so important.”
The office also published a report detailing parent responses to a survey about the program, showing high parent satisfaction.
In total, 99% of those surveyed were satisfied with MOScholars. Some had complaints about a lack of communication and confusion about certain requirements but were overwhelmingly content.
“While participants may have provided areas for program improvement,” the report says. “Many of those same participants also voiced satisfaction with the program as a whole.”

text:
In the span of three weeks, 27 dairy farms in the state of Washington have tested positive for bird flu. (Photo by Kirsten Strough/USDA)Bird flu is hitting Washington dairy farms, and it’s spreading fast.
The Washington State Department of Agriculture confirmed the first detections in two Yakima County dairy herds in early October. On Oct. 26, the agency reported the highly pathogenic avian influenza in Benton County.
In the span of three weeks, 27 dairy farms tested positive for bird flu.
“The virus is moving fast … despite all the efforts that we’ve done within containment,” said Amber Itle, state veterinarian. “Right now, the risk for humans is very low.”
Milk from an infected dairy cow does not pose a risk for human consumption, Itle said. However, the department recommends drinking pasteurized milk because the virus will be killed during processing. The virus has not been found in meat, Itle said.
Containing the spread will be challenging because researchers don’t fully understand how highly pathogenic avian influenza transmission occurs, Itle said. Transferring sick dairy cows and contaminated equipment from one farm to another are known causes, but there’s likely many more.
“There’s been some studies that even suggest that flies can move this virus, the wind can move this virus, and possibly even … birds that maybe move from one farm to another,” Itle said.
Washington is the 20th state in the country to detect avian influenza in dairy cattle.
In the last two years, the Washington Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory conducted more than 7,000 bird flu tests on individual farms. Until three weeks ago, all tests came back negative, Itle said.
In response, “every farm in the targeted milkshed where we’re seeing spread is being tested on a weekly basis,” Itle added.
Symptoms of the disease include decreased milk production, changes in milk appearance, loss of appetite, fever, respiratory issues and changes in manure. When properly treated, most infected cattle recover within six weeks, according to the agency.
The Washington State Department of Agriculture recommends isolating animals suspected of carrying the disease and reporting the symptoms to the state by emailing ahealth@agr.wa.gov or by calling 360-902-1878.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Amendment 8 would keep ‘foreign adversaries’ from seizing Louisiana property
description: Railroad companies have expropriation authority in Louisiana, the state lawmaker who authored proposed Amendment 8 on the Nov. 3 ballot says it will prevent any foreign adversary that acquires a rail line from taking over  private property in the state. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/ New Jersey Monitor)Louisiana would join a trend among states that have banned ce[...]
text:
Railroad companies have expropriation authority in Louisiana, the state lawmaker who authored proposed Amendment 8 on the Nov. 3 ballot says it will prevent any foreign adversary that acquires a rail line from taking over  private property in the state. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/ New Jersey Monitor)Louisiana would join a trend among states that have banned certain foreign nations from gaining control of private property if its voters approve a change to the state constitution on Tuesday’s ballot. 
Amendment 8 specifically prohibits a “foreign adversary” or their representative from expropriating property. The list of countries considered adversarial is based on the U.S. Treasury’s official designation, which currently includes China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia and the regime of Venezuela’s former leader Nicolás Maduro. 
Expropriation is typically a power local or state governments wield when they want to justify the forced acquisition of private property for a greater common benefit, such as building out roads, drainage, water lines and other public infrastructure. The private owner has to receive fair compensation for the property being taken to comply with eminent domain laws that give governments expropriation power. 
“This is simply a wall of separation to make sure that they never get into the expropriation business, either them directly or indirectly through an intermediary or an agent,” said state Rep. Chuck Owen, R-Rosepine, who authored the amendment. “This is simply a wall of protection for the citizens of Louisiana.”
When he brought his bill before lawmakers this spring, Owen laid out a hypothetical example in which a foreign adversary buys a controlling stake in a Canadian railroad. Two such rail lines exist in Louisiana, and the state gives railroads expropriation power. The proposed amendment would provide “guardrails” to protect private property in such a situation, Owen said.  
Existing state law already prohibits foreign adversaries from expropriating property within 50 miles of a military base and from acquiring or leasing all immovable property in Louisiana. Owen’s proposal would bake this ban into the state constitution, making it harder for the legislature to change it moving forward. If Amendment 8 is approved, it would take another statewide vote to alter the constitutional provision.  
Since 2023, there has been a push among state legislatures to prohibit foreign adversaries from securing U.S. property for national security and economic reasons. There is no federal law banning such acquisitions, though the Agricultural Foreign Investment Disclosure Act of 1978 requires the deals to be reported to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Several government agencies track other types of commercial real estate transactions involving foreign buyers, but federal law protects the confidentiality of that data. The Bureau of Economic Analysis conducts foreign investment surveys every five years, but its publicly available summaries offer very limited insight into ownership.
Laws similar to the proposal Louisiana voters will consider Tuesday are already in place or proposed in at least 35 states, with some differences among them regarding the type of property to which the prohibition applies. 
For example, it’s illegal in North Dakota for China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea and Russia to acquire farmland. Indiana prohibits adversaries from buying property or leasing it for non-residential uses.
The bans also have compelled foreign-owned businesses to sell some of their U.S. holdings. 
After Arkansas put its law in place in 2023, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders ordered Sygenta, a Chinese-owned company, to sell 160 acres it owned there, and it was fined for failing to report to the state when it originally bought the land under a separate Arkansas law.  
Sygenta still owns property in five other states, though Chinese ownership of U.S. farmland totals less than 1%, according to the USDA. China’s biggest holdings are through pork and beef producer Smithfield Foods, which Shuanghui Group (now WH Group) acquired in 2013. Smithfield currently owns roughly 85,000 acres (0.004%) of U.S. land.
Foreign interests are not taking these laws sitting down. A group of Chinese citizens and a real estate business have sued in federal court to block Florida’s ban. Their case is currently before an appellate court. A similar lawsuit in Texas involving plaintiffs from China, North Korea and Russia landed before the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals, which ruled this month to uphold the state law.
USDA figures show international buyers — whether from a friend or foe nation — make up about 3.5% of U.S. agricultural landowners. Canadian interests hold the biggest share at 2.3%, and close to 100 other countries account for the remainder.
The National Agricultural Law Center, a nonpartisan research center, tracks state laws that deal with foreign ownership. Its director, attorney Harrison Pittman, said a potential pitfall in such measures is that they leave discretion over what countries are considered adversaries up to the president. 
“What if you have a state that has a lot of Saudi Arabian investment … like in the equine industry, and a future president labels Saudi Arabia as a foreign adversary? What does that do, like after the fact? That’s not what necessarily people had on their mind” when they approved the law, Pittman said.
There have also been questions about whether Amendment 8 is actually needed. 
In its analysis of the proposal, the progressive policy think tank Invest in Louisiana notes there is no evidence any foreign adversary has ever tried to seize property from anyone in the state. The group does not take a position on any of the amendments. 
Another progressive group, the Power Coalition for Equity and Justice, opposes the measure. 
“We don’t need to change the constitution for something that can be handled through regular state law,” the group wrote for its review of the amendment.
The Louisiana Association of Business and Industry, the state’s largest business lobby group, has not taken a position on the amendment.
Owen’s bill was approved without opposition or debate when it advanced through the legislature. Organizations whose representatives voiced support for it in committee included the Louisiana Citizens Advocacy Group, Louisiana Family Forum and the Louisiana Landowners Association. Those opposed were from the oil, gas and chemical industries as well as the regional economic development group Greater New Orleans Inc.
